Title: Ordinary General Meeting
text: Ordinary General Meeting of 29 March 2005 Introductory statement by Guy Quaden, Governor Ladies and Gentlemen, On my own behalf and on behalf of my colleagues on the Management Committee, I welcome you all to the Ordinary General Meeting of Shareholders of the National Bank of Belgium. Before giving the floor to Vice-Governor Luc Coene, who will present and comment on the results of the 2004 financial year, I will review with you the most significant aspects of the Bank's development over the past year. The year 2004 was mainly marked for our Institution by the strategic reflection it carried out on the future of its activities. This reflection has extended the strategic exercise already carried out in 2000, at the time of the creation of the euro and the 150th anniversary of our Institution. This first strategic exercise has generated many positive results, particularly in terms of human resources management, the Bank's image and the redeployment of some of its activities. Nevertheless, the speed with which its environment is changing has led our Institution to renew this exercise for the period 2005d02010. The reflection focused on all the tasks of the Bank, those related to the basic tasks of a central bank, namely essentially the preparation and execution of monetary policy decisions and the issue of banknotes, but also other missions of general interest, such as the processing of banknotes, numerous statistical and research activities, as well as services rendered to the State, businesses and individuals. The future of these tasks has been reassessed in the context of the Eurosystem, mainly with a view to improving the efficiency of the services offered. Particular attention has been paid to the organization of support activities, which are essential for carrying out the various missions, in order to optimize decision-making and the distribution of resources. The control of cos is indeed a fundamental concern of the Bank. In this connection, it should be noted that the restructuring of certain activities and productivity gains have made it possible to reduce the Bank's workforce from 2,533 full-time equivalents at the beginning of 1999 to 2,174 at the end of 2004. The target set in 2001 in the strategic plan was 2,200 full-time equivalents at the end of 2005. This objective is therefore already exceeded. The decisions taken in the strategic exercise are translated into quantifiable objectives and action plans to ensure the implementation of the new strategy. A number of adaptations have already been made to the organizational chart, in particular the redesign of three departments. Thanks to these decisions, the Bank can continue to adapt to its environment and guarantee the sustainability of its activities and the legitimacy of its action. Within the framework of the Act of 2 August 2002 on the supervision of the financial sector and financial services, the Bank has strengthened its links with the Banking, Finance and Insurance Commission. However, each of the two institutions retains its own responsibilities. The Financial Stability Committee, which brings together the management committees of the two institutions, is the cornerstone of the new architecture introduced in 2003. Its legal mission is to examine all matters of common interest to the Bank and the Banking, Finance and Insurance Commission. During the last financial year, he focused on crisis management, in particular by identifying the actors and functions critical to the proper functioning of the Belgian financial sector. Recommendations have been published on business continuity planning and a permanent structure for monitoring these recommendations has been set up. The Financial Stability Committee also coordinated the exercise of an International Monetary Fund team to assess the stability of the Belgian financial system, the results of which will be published in 2006. The Supervisory Board of the Financial Services Authority, which brings together the members of the Supervisory Board of the CBFA and the Regents of the Bank, was officially installed in early 2004. The Ministers of Finance, Economy and Consumer Protection have instructed me, in my capacity as President of this body, to set up a Steering Committee to reflect on the future of means of payment in our country. This round table, which brings together all the parties concerned, aims to make payments more efficient and accessible. Several topics have already been discussed, in particular the usefulness of 1 and 2 euro cent coins, the use of large denominations in trade and the launch of a comparative study on the cos and advantages of different means of payment. The merger between the CBFA and the Bank resulted not only in the establishment of this double dome, but also in the organization and management of certain synergies. For example, a "Prudential Policy" department now includes employees of both institutions and, in the course of 2004, the CBFA's IT infrastructure was transferred to the Bank's it centre. In the future, the pursuit of these synergies will make it possible to achieve optimally the two main objectives of the Law of 2 August 2002, namely the development of exchanges of information and expertise between the CBFA and the Bank to best guarantee the stability of the Belgian financial sector, and the multiplication of economies of scale between support services to contain the costs of increasingly demanding supervision. *** Although the Bank is constituted in the form of a public limited company, for it as for any central bank, the pursuit of profit is, from the outset, subject to the performance of tasks of general interest, whether these are related to monetary policy, the stability of the financial system or other tasks of general interest. Among the Bank's income, the most important are those derived from seigniorage, i.e. from the issuance of notes, from profitable assets held in return for them. But the performance and management of these assets are largely conditioned by the objectives and constraints of monetary and exchange rate policy, including for official reserves of gold and foreign currencies. In exchange for the concession it has made to it of the privilege of issuance, the State is entitled to the bulk of the financial proceeds of the Bank's profitable assets, beyond the share (the first 3%) that is left to the Bank to cover its operating costs, ensure its financial stability and remunerate its shareholders. The State is also entitled to a priority share in the profits. It is clear from the year under review that it is also the State that essentially bears the volatility of the Bank's results. In 2004, the Bank's performance was affected by the low level of interest rates on net assets in dollars and euros and by the depreciation of the dollar exchange rate. In accordance with the ESCB's accounting rules, potential foreign exchange losses must be recorded in profit or loss as at 31 December, while foreign exchange gains are only recorded once they are realised. These negative developments for the result were only partially offset by the additional monetary income resulting from the increase in the issuance of banknotes in the Eurosystem and thus from the Bank's share in this issue. The same reasons explain why the ECB is closing its 2004 financial year at a loss. In accordance with Eurosystem rules, this loss is borne by the national central banks, which has accentuated the unfavourable evolution of their results. Indeed, the ECB has not only retained its share of seigniorage income, which it normally distributes to the national central banks, but has also called on them. Once again this year, the Bank's prudent policy, particularly in terms of risk management and provisioning, allows it to redistribute a dividend to its own shareholders. The Bank thus remains one of the very few listed Belgian companies to have never stopped paying a dividend to its shareholders since 1948. This dividend, as usual, increases at the rate of inflation. *** The end of 2004 was also marked, for listed companies, by the publication of the Belgian Code of Corporate Governance, known as the "Lippens Code". The main objective of the non-binding Code is to enable companies to rely on a framework that stimulates efficiency and competitiveness while encouraging sound and transparent governance practices. The Lippens Commission has chosen a flexible approach that allows rules to be adapted to the size, activities and culture of each company, and based on the "comply or explain" system. The Bank has always been committed to respecting the fundamental ethical principles and values that underpin the development of corporate governance. In the coming year, as recommended by the authors of the Code, it will carry out a detailed analysis of the principles and recommendations of the Code, how they are already encountered within the Code and how to optimize its application while taking into account its specificities. It will draft and publish a corporate governance charter in due course. However, it already appears that certain principles and recommendations of the Belgian Corporate Governance Code cannot and cannot be applied to the letter to the Bank, as they are unsuited to the specific legal framework that governs it and to its particular position as the country's central bank. The main objective of the latter is not maximum profit but monetary and financial stability, and the legislature has entrusted it with other tasks of general interest. First of all, and this is fundamental, the Bank is not governed by the same legal texts as other public limited companies. As a member of the ESCB, it is governed firstly by the Treaty establishing the European Community and by the Protocol on the Statute of the ESCB and of the ECB annexed thereto, then by the Law of 22 February 1998 laying down its organic statute, and finally by its own statute. The provisions of the Companies Code and the other provisions on public limited companies apply to it only on a supplementary basis. The Corporate Governance Code is complementary to Belgian legislation. It is explicitly provided that none of its provisions may be interpreted as contrary to Belgian law. As far as the Bank is concerned, it is therefore even more than the Companies Code, of suppletive application. Secondly, and this is just as fundamental, the Bank does not have the same bodies as other public limited companies. Its organs are defined and organized by the Organic Law of 22 February 1998, which establishes their competences. While the organs of public limited companies under ordinary law are the Board of Directors, the General Assembly and, where appropriate, the Management Committee or the Managing Director, the Bank's organs are the Governor, the Management Committee, the Regency Council and the College of Censors. The Management Committee and the Regency Council of the Bank are specific bodies, organized by the Organic Law of the Bank, and which cannot be compared to the Management Committee and the Board of Directors of conventional public limited companies. Finally, the Bank's participation in the ESCB and the specific tasks of general interest entrusted to it, both at Belgian and European level, mean that it cannot be subject to the same operating rules and does not have the same objectives as other companies. The Bank has its own legal status, organs, operating rules, objectives and obligations which, although it has the legal form, the distinguish public limited companies under ordinary law. As a member of the ESCB, it is subject to specific rules and obligations which of course do not apply to public limited companies under ordinary law. This does not mean, on the contrary, that the fundamental ethical principles and rules of good corporate governance are absent from the Bank. The Bank has a clear structure, organized by a special law, the Organic Law. The resources of the various bodies are clearly defined, as are the procedures for appointing their members. It is directed and administered by a Collegial Management Committee which assumes most of the tasks of the Board of Directors and the management bodies of public limited companies under ordinary law. This committee meets once a week. Most of the counter-missions that the Corporate Governance Code recommends entrusting to independent directors are carried out by the Regency Council to the Bank. This very specific body carries out various tasks against which it is assigned by the organic law. In addition to the members of the Management Committee, it is composed of ten regents who are personalities external to the Bank, from Belgian socio-economic circles, and independent. The Regency Council meets at least twice a month. In addition to certain functions generally performed by the board of directors of conventional companies, the Regency Council is in charge of the missions traditionally reserved for the general meeting. Thus, it is he who is responsible for discussing and approving the annual report of the administration and the annual accounts, giving discharge to the management, deciding on the distribution of profits and the amount of the dividend, making proposals concerning the appointment of directors, fixing the remuneration of the members of the organs, and amending the statutes when it comes to bringing them into line with the organic law and international obligations. binding Belgium. The creation of the Regency Council and the procedures for appointing its members are the result of a choice by the legislator who wanted to entrust tasks under the Bank's counterpart to an independent body representing the interests of Belgian society as a whole. The explanatory memorandum to the 1948 law which amended the Bank's Organic Law states in this regard: "The proposed modalities, while allowing a wide choice of personalities, ensure the perfect independence of the Bank with regard to special interests ...". Other counter-effects are entrusted to the College of Censors, which supervises the preparation and implementation of the budget. Censors are chosen because of their counter skills. The general assembly, on the other hand, has limited powers. Its functions are to elect the regents from a double list, to elect the censors, to appoint the auditors of companies on presentation by the works council, to hear the report of the administration, and to amend the statutes in cases if the Regency Council is not competent to do so. In addition to the counters already mentioned, there are those exercised by company auditors. Like those of the other national central banks which are part of the ESCB, the Bank's accounts are, pursuant to Article 27.1 of the Protocol on the Statute of the ESCB and of the ECB, checked by external auditors. They have the right to examine the books and accounts of the Bank and to obtain any information on its operations. In addition to their tasks vis-88-vis the ESCB, they report to the Regency Council. In accordance with Belgian law, statutory auditors also carry out a specific task of counter-terrorism and information vis-88-vis the works council. Other cons are quite specific to the Bank. Thus, in particular, with the exception of those under the ESCB, the Bank's operations are supervised by the Government Commissioner on behalf of the Minister of Finance. A counter is also exercised by Parliament, whose competent committees may request to hear the Governor. All this shows that if they are organized in a different way from that of other public limited companies, cons of all kinds are present at the Bank! The Lippens Code recommends the creation of committees within the Board of Directors specialising in audit, appointment and remuneration. In the area of remuneration, a special committee already exists at the Bank. This is the Committee on budget and management remuneration, which gives an opinion to the Regency Council on these matters. It is composed of a member of the Management Committee, two regents, two censors and the Government Commissioner. In the field of audit, a series of internal counters are ensured and coordinated by the Internal Audit Service. Finally, as regards the appointment of the members of the bodies, the competence does not lie with the Management Committee. It is organized in a very specific way by the organic law. The creation of an internal committee would therefore have no reason to exist in that regard. With regard to its shareholders, the Bank is committed to disseminating relevant and quality information, while respecting the confidentiality of certain information, which is required by its status as a central bank. Its website contains extensive information for the public and shareholders. In addition, more specific information is made available to all in the annual report that the Governor submits in particular to Parliament. Finally, there are other areas in which the Bank is subject to stricter rules than other listed companies. Thus, it is the only listed company whose directors will have filed this year with the Court of Auditors declarations of mandates and assets. *** For several years now, the Bank has been working within a new framework, the Eurosystem, composed of the thirteen central banks that together conduct the new European monetary policy. Institutions set up to carry out tasks of general interest, they now pursue common objectives defined by the Treaty establishing the European Community. These objectives are specified in a very explicit Mission statement. I thank you for your attention to this presentation, which may be a little didactic but probably useful since the specificities of the Bank, although they always end up being recognised by court decisions, are sometimes misunderstood when we consider our institution too partially.

En ce qui concerne la Banque, il est donc, davantage encore que le Code des soci<8e>t<8e>s, d'application suppl<8e>tive. Ensuite, et c'est tout aussi fondamental, la Banque n'a pas les m<90>mes organes que les autres soci<8e>t<8e>s anonymes. Ses organes sont d<8e>finis et organis<8e>s par la loi organique du 22 f<8e>vrier 1998, qui fixe leurs comp<8e>tences. Alors que les soci<8e>t<8e>s anonymes de droit commun ont pour organes le conseil d'administration, l'assembl<8e>e g<8e>n<8e>rale et, le cas <8e>ch<8e>ant, le comit<8e> de direction ou l'administrateur d<8e>l<8e>gu<8e>, la Banque a pour organes le Gouverneur, le Comit<8e> de direction, le Conseil de r<8e>gence et le Coll<8f>ge des censeurs. Le Comit<8e> de direction et le conseil de r<8e>gence de la Banque sont des organes sp<8e>cifiques, organis<8e>s par la loi organique de la Banque, et qui ne peuvent pas <90>tre compar<8e>s au comit<8e> de direction et au conseil d'administration des soci<8e>t<8e>s anonymes classiques. Enfin, la participation de la Banque au SEBC et les missions sp<8e>cifiques d'int<8e>r<90>t g<8e>n<8e>ral dont elle est investie, tant au niveau belge qu'au niveau europ<8e>en, font qu'elle ne peut <90>tre soumise aux m<90>mes r<8f>gles de fonctionnement et qu'elle n'a pas les m<90>mes objectifs que les autres soci<8e>t<8e>s. La Banque a un statut juridique, des organes, des r<8f>gles de fonctionnement, des objectifs et des obligations propres qui, bien qu'elle en ait la forme juridique, la distinguent des soci<8e>t<8e>s anonymes de droit commun. En tant que membre du SEBC, elle est soumise <88> des r<8f>gles et <88> des obligations sp<8e>cifiques qui ne s'appliquent bien entendu pas aux soci<8e>t<8e>s anonymes de droit commun. Cela ne signifie pas pour autant, au contraire, que les principes <8e>thiques fondamentaux et les r<8f>gles d'une bonne gouvernance d'entreprise soient absents de la Banque. La Banque est dot<8e>e d'une structure claire, organis<8e>e par une loi sp<8e>ciale, la loi organique. Les res des diff<8e>rents organes sont clairement d<8e>finis, de m<90>me que les modalit<8e>s de d<8e>signation de leurs membres. Elle est dirig<8e>e et administr<8e>e par un Comit<8e> de direction coll<8e>gial qui assume la plupart des missions du conseil d'administration et des organes de gestion des soci<8e>t<8e>s anonymes de droit commun. Ce comit<8e> se r<8e>unit une fois par semaine. La plupart des missions de contre que le Code de corporate governance recommande de confier aux administrateurs ind<8e>pendants sont <88> la Banque assum<8e>es par le Conseil de r<8e>gence. Cet organe tout <88> fait sp<8e>cifique exerce en effet diff<8e>rentes missions de contre qui lui sont assign<8e>es par la loi organique. Outre les membres du Comit<8e> de direction, il est compos<8e> de dix r<8e>gents qui sont des personnalit<8e>s externes <88> la Banque, issues des milieux socio-<8e>conomiques belges, et ind<8e>pendantes. Le Conseil de r<8e>gence se r<8e>unit au moins deux fois par mois. Outre certaines fonctions g<8e>n<8e>ralement assum<8e>es par le conseil d'administration des soci<8e>t<8e>s classiques, le Conseil de r<8e>gence a en charge des missions traditionnellement r<8e>serv<8e>es <88> l'assembl<8e>e g<8e>n<8e>rale. Ainsi, c'est lui qui est charg<8e> de discuter et d'approuver le rapport annuel de l'administration et les comptes annuels, de donner d<8e>charge <88> la direction, de d<8e>cider de la r<8e>partition des b<8e>n<8e>fices et de la hauteur du dividende, de faire des propositions concernant la nomination des directeurs, de fixer la r<8e>mun<8e>ration des membres des organes, et de modifier les statuts lorsqu'il s'agit de les mettre en conformit<8e> avec la loi organique et les obligations internationales liant la Belgique. La cr<8e>ation du Conseil de r<8e>gence et les modalit<8e>s de d<8e>signation de ses membres r<8e>sultent d'un choix du l<8e>gislateur qui a voulu confier des missions relevant du contre de la Banque <88> un organe ind<8e>pendant repr<8e>sentatif des int<8e>r<90>ts de l'ensemble de la soci<8e>t<8e> belge. L'expos<8e> des motifs de la loi de 1948 qui a modifi<8e> la loi organique de la Banque pr<8e>cise <88> ce sujet : "Les modalit<8e>s propos<8e>es, tout en permettant un large choix de personnalit<8e>s, assurent la parfaite ind<8e>pendance de la Banque <88> l'<8e>gard des int<8e>r<90>ts particuliers ...". D'autres missions de contre sont confi<8e>es au Coll<8f>ge des censeurs qui surveille la pr<8e>paration et l'ex<8e>cution du budget. Les censeurs sont choisis en raison de leurs comp<8e>tences en mati<8f>re de contre. L'assembl<8e>e g<8e>n<8e>rale, quant <88> elle, a des comp<8e>tences limit<8e>es. Elle a pour fonctions d'<8e>lire les r<8e>gents sur une liste double, d'<8e>lire les censeurs, de nommer les r<8e>viseurs d'entreprises sur pr<8e>sentation du conseil d'entreprise, d'entendre le rapport de l'administration, et de modifier les statuts dans les cas ole Conseil de r<8e>gence n'est pas comp<8e>tent pour le faire. Outre les contres d<8e>j<88> cit<8e>s, il y a ceux exerc<8e>s par les r<8e>viseurs d'entreprises. Comme ceux des autres banques centrales nationales qui font partie du SEBC, les comptes de la Banque sont, en vertu de l'article 27.1 du protocole sur le statut du SEBC et de la BCE, contr<8e>s par des auditeurs externes. Ceux-ci ont le droit d'examiner les livres et les comptes de la Banque et d'obtenir toutes informations sur ses op<8e>rations. Outre leur mission vis-<88>-vis du SEBC, ils rendent compte au Conseil de r<8e>gence. Les r<8e>viseurs d'entreprises exercent <8e>galement, conform<8e>ment <88> la loi belge, une mission sp<8e>cifique de contre et d'information vis-<88>-vis du conseil d'entreprise. D'autres contres sont tout <88> fait sp<8e>cifiques <88> la Banque. Ainsi notamment, <88> l'exception de celles qui rel<8f>vent du SEBC, les op<8e>rations de la Banque sont surveill<8e>es par le Commissaire du Gouvernement pour le compte du Ministre des finances. Un contre est en outre exerc<8e> par le Parlement, dont les commissions comp<8e>tentes peuvent demander <88> entendre le Gouverneur. Tout ceci d<8e>montre que s'ils sont organis<8e>s de fa<8d>on diff<8e>rente de celui des autres soci<8e>t<8e>s anonymes, les contres de toute nature sont bien pr<8e>sents <88> la Banque ! Le Code Lippens recommande la cr<8e>ation au sein du conseil d'administration de comit<8e>s sp<8e>cialis<8e>s en mati<8f>re d'audit, de nomination et de r<8e>mun<8e>ration. En mati<8f>re de r<8e>mun<8e>ration, un comit<8e> sp<8e>cial existe d<8e>j<88> <88> la Banque. Il s'agit de la commission du budget et des r<8e>mun<8e>rations de la direction, qui donne un avis au Conseil de r<8e>gence en ces mati<8f>res. Elle est compos<8e>e d'un membre du Comit<8e> de direction, de deux r<8e>gents, de deux censeurs et du Commissaire du Gouvernement. En mati<8f>re d'audit, une s<8e>rie de contres internes sont assur<8e>s et coordonn<8e>s par le Service Audit interne. Enfin, en ce qui concerne la nomination des membres des organes, la comp<8e>tence n'en revient pas au Comit<8e> de direction. Elle est organis<8e>e de mani<8f>re tout <88> fait sp<8e>cifique par la loi organique. La cr<8e>ation d'un comit<8e> interne n'aurait d<8f>s lors <88> cet <8e>gard aucune raison d'<90>tre. A l'<8e>gard de ses actionnaires, la Banque a <88> c<cf>ur de diffuser des informations pertinentes et de qualit<8e>, tout en respectant la confidentialit<8e> de certaines informations, ce que lui impose son statut de banque centrale. Son site internet contient une large information destin<8e>e au public et aux actionnaires. Par ailleurs, une information plus sp<8e>cifique est mise <88> la disposition de tous dans le rapport annuel que le Gouverneur pr<8e>sente en particulier au Parlement. Enfin, il y a d'autres domaines dans lesquels la Banque est soumise <88> des r<8f>gles plus strictes que les autres soci<8e>t<8e>s cot<8e>es. Ainsi, elle est la seule soci<8e>t<8e> cot<8e>e dont les dirigeants auront d<8e>pos<8e> d<8f>s cette ann<8e>e <88> la Cour des Comptes des d<8e>clarations de mandats et de patrimoine. *** Depuis d<8e>j<88> plusieurs ann<8e>es, la Banque travaille dans un nouveau cadre, l'Eurosyst<8f>me, compos<8e> des treize banques centrales qui conduisent ensemble la nouvelle politique mon<8e>taire europ<8e>enne. Institutions cr<8e><8e>es pour accomplir des t<89>ches d'int<8e>r<90>t g<8e>n<8e>ral, elles poursuivent d<8e>sormais des objectifs communs d<8e>finis par le trait<8e> instituant la Communaut<8e> europ<8e>enne. Ces objectifs sont pr<8e>cis<8e>s dans une Mission statement tr<8f>s explicite. Je vous remercie de votre attention pour cet expos<8e> peut-<90>tre un peu didactique mais probablement utile d<8f>s lors que les sp<8e>cificit<8e>s de la Banque, si elle finissent toujours par <90>tre reconnues par les d<8e>cisions de justice, sont parfois mal comprises lorsqu'on envisage notre institution de mani<8f>re trop partielle.

Title: SEPA Financial Forum Symposium
text: 2006-05-30 FINANCIAL FORUM SYMPOSIUM ON SEPA Key-note speech by Guy QUADEN, Governor of the National Bank of Belgium Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a pleasure for me to open this colloquium on SEPA or Single Euro Payments Area. Recently, SEPA (Single Euro Payments Area) has rightly become one of the main priorities of commercial banks and central banks in the euro area. In addition, SEPA is increasingly being made aware of itself as a project with a societal dimension, in which actors who do not come from the banking world are called upon to participate closely. This symposium is therefore timely to allow all these actors to express themselves and address different aspects of SEPA. Thanks to SEPA, it will be possible to make payments throughout the euro area by bank transfer, direct debit or payment card as easily as it is today within the borders of the same country. There can be no doubt about the macroeconomic benefits of a single payments area in Europe, in which the same technical standards are used and the same regulatory framework applied. More effective competition in the payment services sector must ultimately lead to greater efficiency, better service and, finally, savings for the end user. The European authorities therefore rightly see SEPA as an important objective within the framework of the so-called "Lisbon Agenda", the aim of which, let us remember, is to increase the competitive capacity of the European economy. The National Bank of Belgium fully supports the objectives of SEPA, not only as a member of the Eurosystem, but also as a continuation of the policy it has always pursued at national level. Belgium now has one of the best payment systems in terms of efficiency, ease of use and co. Well-informed and critical observers such as the European Commission have repeatedly confirmed this. It is undeniable that this success is largely due to interbank cooperation. Indeed, almost all the innovations have been achieved through interbank agreements, in other words through self-regulation, so that the Belgian banking sector is a pioneer in terms of banking standards and payment automation. Although the banknote is its main product, and even as it continues to be appreciated and demanded by the public, the National Bank, an institution of general interest, whose modernization, efficiency and security of payment systems is a major concern, has largely contributed to the development of electronic payments in our country. We take a similar approach to SEPA and are happy to make ourselves available to the banking sector to support it in this regard. The transition to SEPA is complex and requires vigorous and coordinated action by many stakeholders. It is essential that the proper functioning of payment systems remains ensured throughout the transition process. Only in this way will all parties have the guarantee that SEPA will deploy its European dimension, with everyone bringing their enthusiastic cooperation to it. The banking sector and all the other actors involved in the SEPA project are therefore facing great challenges. Let me briefly touch on the main ones. Communication boulevard de Berlaimont 14 tel. 32 2 221 46 28 VAT BE 0203.201.340 Banque Nationale de Belgique s.a. BE-1000 BRUXELLES RPM Brussels To begin with, SEPA is a crucial challenge in terms of banking and interbank infrastructure. The adaptation of technical standards for non-cash payments has an impact on a large number of banking applications. The management of current accounts and the related payments system are now at the very heart of banking activities and represent a substantial part of the banks' cos structure. The list of adaptations made necessary by SEPA is long: the replacement of the national account number by an international account number, the adaptation of the formats of transfers and direct debits, the necessary technical adjustments in order to be able to use all cards on all payment terminals, the modification of customer interfaces for electronic banking operations, the adaptation of contracts with customers, etc. Interbank clearing houses and card schemes will need to convert their infrastructure. All of this involves considerable short-term investments for the banking sector and other payment service providers, who will only see the results in the longer term. The introductory text to this colloquium indicates that the investments that are needed in SEPA will be greater than those required by the introduction of the euro. To tell the truth, I do not yet have precise information that would allow me to confirm or qualify this statement. But, in any event, it is indisputable that SEPA is a project that is both vast and complex, which needs to be carried out with a firm hand. This brings me to the second challenge: managing SEPA governance. Several parties play a role in this respect: the banking sector, under the leadership of the European Payments Council (EPC), the national banking communities, the European Commission, the European Parliament, the ECB and the Central Banks of the Eurosystem. Since 2002, the European banking sector has made it clear that SEPA has become one of its objectives, which it aims to achieve by 2010. This objective would be achieved essentially through self-regulation, i.e. through interbank arrangements at European level. The sector therefore created the European Payments Council or CEP, which has since made considerable progress under the SEPA project. Cep has successfully designed a set of SEPA standards for credit transfers and direct debits and has created a framework for payment cards. This is a major achievement in the European banking landscape, which still has significant national differences. Even within the banking sector, some are wondering whether this capacity for self-regulation of banks will be sufficient to carry out the SEPA project. The problems to be solved are, in fact, multiple and the resistance to change is often quite great. But if I refer to the Belgian experience, I am convinced that this European interbank collaboration will be the key to SEPA's success. The European Commission and the Eurosystem have repeatedly stressed that it is the banks that are leading the SEPA project; the fact remains that each of these authorities has a role to play. The European Commission is responsible for defining the legal framework and removing obstacles to open competition. The Eurosystem supports the implementation of SEPA through a forum for consultation between the different parties and, if necessary, by helping to find common solutions. Mr Godeffroy will certainly come back to this Eurosystem issue shortly. The national central banks are also crucial in drawing up and implementing national SEPA transition plans. The colloquium will discuss in more detail how the SNB is carrying out this task in practice, both with regard to the banking sector and with regard to actors outside the sector. The CEP, the national banking communities, the national central banks and the European authorities each have their responsibility in the SEPA project. It is also essential that all these parties work together towards the same objectives. Too little self-regulation of the European banking sector or insufficient collaboration between the bodies listed above could lead to the failure of SEPA or heterogeneous implementation in different countries. Such phase shifts in the introduction of the system would create a delicate situation for some countries to take the necessary steps to achieve SEPA in a timely manner, while others would do so incompletely or too late. This would have the effect of punishing the "best students", who would have made the necessary investments for SEPA without being able to reap the benefits, because of the delay of others. This is a major concern of the Belgian banking sector, which at European level is one of the most active. In this context, it is therefore essential to use the same definition of SEPA everywhere and to always go through its stages simultaneously. Communication boulevard de Berlaimont 14 tel. 32 2 221 46 28 VAT BE 0203.201.340 Banque Nationale de Belgique s.a. BE-1000 BRUXELLES RPM Brussels The third challenge concerns the impact of SEPA on services and prices for the end user. As I said at the beginning of my presentation, more open competition and an extension of scale at European level must ultimately lead to a better quality/price ratio for the end user. However, it is currently difficult to predict what the concrete impact will be on the different types of end-users in each European country. In my opinion, however, there can be no doubt about the final objective: SEPA must take the best current systems as a reference and cannot be satisfied with a kind of European average. In addition, sufficient space for innovation within SEPA should be left to meet the new needs of end-users. Close involvement of their representatives (companies and consumers) throughout the process offers the best guarantee in order to achieve this objective. This brings me to the fourth challenge: SEPA as a project with a social dimension. SEPA is not just about the banking world, because ultimately all users will have to deal with the new instruments. All actors will be forced to adapt and some of them, such as companies and public authorities, will have to invest in it. The success of SEPA depends on the willingness of all actors to make the necessary adjustments in time within the framework of national transition plans. These plans must be drawn up in consultation with all parties and then involve their coordinated action. Two weeks ago, the SNB brought together all stakeholders for the first time to draw up the Belgian transition plan. The public authorities play an important role in this context. First of all, it is essential that a process of social transformation of this magnitude receive the explicit support of the highest political authorities. In addition, public authorities, as an important end-user of payment services, can set an example for all other parties. If public policy operations are rapidly converted to European formats, this will go a long way towards reaching the critical mass that will make the switch to SEPA irreversible. Finally, I would like to briefly highlight the strategic aspects of SEPA. SEPA is much more than a technical conversion for the use of new payment instruments. It is much more than an additional cost. It offers new opportunities to those who wish to seize them and are willing to adapt. Banks will have to answer strategic questions such as these: as a bank, do we want to be active in the European market for payment services? What are our strengths, what are our handicaps? What steps need to be taken to reach new customers and retain existing ones? What investments should be made to make the project a success? What (European) infrastructure will we need to connect to? How to reduce our overall cos?, etc. Bank customers will now be able to search for the best payment service providers in an open competitive space. It is above all companies with an international vocation that will be able to greatly simplify their internal administration thanks to the adoption of European standards and the free choice of their banker. In this more competitive market, Belgian banks undoubtedly have the necessary assets in hand, thanks to the efficiency of their current payment systems. SEPA is therefore a challenge on several levels. Let us not be impressed by the difficulties of the transition process, but let us look together for the opportunities that may arise. This colloquium will undoubtedly give us the necessary inspiration to work towards the realization of SEPA, with all the necessary enthusiasm. Comment r<8e>duire nos cos globaux?, etc. Les clients des banques pourront d<8e>sormais rechercher les meilleurs prestataires de services de paiement au sein d<d5>un espace concurrentiel ouvert. Ce sont surtout les entreprises <88> vocation internationale qui pourront simplifier fortement leur administration interne gr<89>ce <88> l<d5>adoption des normes europ<8e>ennes et au libre choix de leur banquier. Le SEPA constitue donc bien un d<8e>fi <88> plusieurs niveaux. Title: What an economic and monetary europe
text: 2006-05-31 WHAT ECONOMIC AND MONETARY EUROPE? Speech by Guy Quaden, Governor of the National Bank of Belgium Monetary union is more than seven years old now. The euro has become the single currency of more than 300 million Europeans and one of the world's two major currencies. The creation of the euro owes nothing to chance but everything to will. In these times of European gloom, it is good to remember this. Europe demonstrated on this occasion that, when it wanted to, when a number of European countries wanted to, they could carry out a major project. In the last ten years of the previous century, it took the governments of the time in twelve countries - and there were all political colours of them - unwavering ambition and obstinacy to make the Treaty signed at Maastricht a reality, and in particular to fulfil the famous criteria. And the introduction of the euro - in two phases, as we know: early 1999 in financial life, early 2002 in everyday life - was also a huge technical challenge. Not only for central banks, but for all banks, all economic and financial actors and, ultimately, the entire population. A challenge successfully met. Was it worth the effort? What has the euro brought us? First of all, the euro brought monetary peace to Europe. More generally, this is also the first contribution of European integration: it has brought us peace. Our children, my children, find it difficult to imagine that, for many centuries, France, Germany and the other great European powers could have waged war against each other, often on Belgian territory today, especially here in Waterloo... This seems unthinkable, absurd to the younger generations of Europeans. Born in August 1945, I did not know the two intra-European wars that my father had known. But, during the first part of my career as an economist, I experienced the conflicts, let us say rather the monetary turbulence that disrupted economic relations between our countries: the succession of devaluations and revaluations, in particular the great and last crisis within the European Monetary System in 1992-1993. Today, complete monetary peace prevails between twelve countries whose national currencies have disappeared since 2002 and have merged into the euro. It was too quickly forgotten but, for our companies, which trade mainly within the European area, it is the most painful source of monetary instability that has disappeared. The second contribution of the euro is price stability. This is the objective assigned by the Maastricht Treaty - the European Monetary Constitution - to the European Central Bank and the national central banks, which together constitute the Eurosystem in charge of the single monetary policy. In the interests of transparency, the European Central Bank has defined price stability very precisely as inflation below 2% in the medium term but close to this amount (because the Eurosystem fights against both deflation and inflation). Since its creation, the Eurosystem can be considered to have generally fulfilled its mandate. Admittedly, a central banker can never be fully satisfied, especially since the target has been slightly exceeded in recent years (with average inflation in the euro area of 2.1% in 2004 and 2.2% in 2005). But these results were achieved in a context marked by a sharp rise in the prices of oil and many other commodities over which monetary policy has no control. Recent inflation rates, however, have been out of step with those observed during previous oil shocks. Let me begin by saying that we are simply carrying out the mandate that has been given to us. European central bankers are said to be independent because, once appointed by the political power, they make their decisions independently, in their soul and conscience, without asking for or receiving instructions. A bit like judges. But, like judges, central bankers do not make laws, they apply them: it is the parliaments and the peoples who make the laws and, in particular, the Maastricht Treaty, which entrusted us with the primary responsibility for price stability. Moreover, Treaty or not Treaty, it seems to me that, in all countries, the population tends to consider that the first duty of a central bank is to preserve the stability of the purchasing power of the currency it issues. That said, would too much attention to moderation in inflation be detrimental to economic growth? Without being a sufficient condition for growth, price stability is a necessary condition. Moderate inflation is desirable to maintain consumer confidence. However, in our countries, household consumption expenditure is still the main item of national or domestic product. When inflation rises, the consumer loses confidence. Moreover, we could observe a phenomenon of this kind just after the introduction of the euro at a time when not the overall and actual inflation, but the inflation felt by many consumers, who focused on a few prices that indeed increased at the time, increased significantly. On the other hand, the control of inflation allows all economic agents, companies, households and public authorities to benefit from relatively low interest rates, a factor that is certainly favourable to growth. Central banks set short-term interest rates, those relating to the loans they grant to other financial institutions. But medium- and long-term interest rates are set by the markets, based on different factors, the most important of which is operators' inflation expectations. The more the saver anticipates a significant deterioration in the purchasing power of his capital at a certain maturity, the higher he will require a high interest rate to lend it. Thus one lends at lower rates to a country where inflation is traditionally low. That is why, and not out of Germanophilia, Belgium had linked the fate of its franc to that of the 1990 German mark. And this is the third contribution of the euro and the monetary policy that has accompanied it since its creation: historically very low interest rates, favourable to demand and employment, whether short rates or long rates. This low interest rate is due, at least in large part, to the confidence of economic operators in the European Central Bank's ability to control inflation in line with its medium-term objective. It is therefore important to carefully preserve this credibility. For many months, the European Central Bank has maintained its main interest rate at 2%, a level that is actually below the rate of inflation. The so-called real interest rate was therefore negative. Such a situation can only be exceptional. Adjustment was needed as inflationary risks intensified and economic activity strengthened. The adjustment process began last December without a pre-established timetable for subsequent increases. The Governing Council takes its decisions at its own pace, without haste but also without procrastination. Each month, the Council assesses the latest data and new prospects for inflation and growth in the euro area. It is not excluded that a new increase will be decided at its next meeting in early June. But even in such a case, the Interest Rate of the European Central Bank would continue to compare favourably with those in force in our countries before the transition to monetary union and could not be regarded as a handicap for economic growth. *** Although monetary union has proved to be positive for our countries, and if they are currently enjoying a cyclical recovery, we must not hide the fact that Europe has a structural problem of insufficient growth in the medium and long term. In most of our countries - because there are exceptions, I will come back to this - we are able, for a certain period of time, to record an economic growth rate of 2%, the so-called potential growth, but we only very exceptionally rise to higher levels and too often we fall back to lower levels. Let us not compare, of course, european or Belgian growth rates with Chinese or Hindu rates. These are countries that are emerging as they say. But, in the last fifteen years, Europe, the eurozone in particular, has experienced growth - overall and per capita - significantly lower than that of the United States. However, this country was, at the beginning, already richer and the gap has therefore widened even more. We work less in Europe than in most other parts of the world, the United States in particular. In most European countries, participation rates, i.e. the proportion of people of working age who are actually in the labour market, are lower. And people who work work fewer hours a week, fewer days a year, and fewer years in their lives. This situation, which is not new but has not improved, has long been offset by higher labour productivity in European countries, particularly in Belgium. We work less, but we worked better. There are two problems though. One: this high level of productivity, which also compensates for heavier wage costs, was achieved by the elimination of the least productive jobs and therefore at the cost of a large amount of employment. Two: in the last ten years, productivity gains have been greater in the United States thanks to the faster and more massive introduction of new information and communication technologies in American companies, which have thus closed part of the gap in this area. Another characteristic of Europe is the cumbersome nature of the regulations. In this connection, reference is generally made to the labour market, where rigidities are more pronounced in Europe than in most other regions of the world. But the lack of flexibility is not limited to this aspect of things alone. Consider, for example, the rules that limit the establishment of new retail spaces or restrict the opening hours of stores. European countries generally have a lower propensity to work and a higher propensity to regulate than most other regions of the world. It would be a perfectly respectable societal choice, I would like to say, if we accepted all the consequences. Because, according to the saying goes, one cannot have both the butter, the money of the butter and, moreover, the smile of the creamer, one cannot, under such conditions, aspire to a rate of growth of the product or income that is equal to those of the regions ola propensity to work is stronger and the propensity for regulation is lower. And, more seriously, in a demographic context the relationship between the active and the inactive is set to deteriorate, it will become increasingly difficult, without a change in behaviour, to preserve social protection systems that are more generous than in the rest of the world, another characteristic of Europe of which it can legitimately be proud. However, as the work of Professor Sapir, whom I think you invited earlier to your rostrum, has clearly shown, the notion of the 'European social model' can be misleading. Europe is in fact home to different social models that are distinct in characteristics and performance, in terms of efficiency and equity. Within the euro area itself, two countries have consistently posted above-average economic growth: Ireland and Finland. To attract investment and jobs, Ireland has played mainly on a low tax burden and therefore also on reduced public spending. On the other hand, Finland, like the other Nordic countries, continues to offer an advantageous but dynamic social protection system and, although public expenditure is not lower than in continental Europe, it is of better quality, more oriented towards training and innovation. The diagnosis of the weak economic dynamism in Europe was made some time ago in Lisbon. An agenda has been drawn up, recently revised. The problem is the implementation of reforms. Progress has been made, but progress has been uneven across countries, and overall too slow. The example mentioned of the best European countries from which others should draw inspiration, however, indicates that it is possible to combine efficiency and equity. And, going back to my starting point, the euro, I would say that it is difficult to imagine, let alone admit, that, ten years after having been able to carry out this ambitious project, our countries have become incapable of undertaking other important reforms that should enable them to reap all the potential benefits of the single market and monetary union and also to face the great challenges of external competition and internal ageing. Title: Monetary policy and the role of central banks over the next ten years
text: 24/10/2006 DEPARTMENT OF STUDIES Cl.: I.A.4.e. INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION AND FINANCIAL STABILITY DEPARTMENT MONETARY POLICY AND THE ROLE OF CENTRAL BANKS OVER THE NEXT TEN YEARS Speech by Mr Guy Quaden, Governor of the National Bank of Belgium, on the occasion of the 70th anniversary of the "Banking and Financial Review" and "Banking and Financial Law", Belgian Financial Forum, 26 October 2006 Ladies and gentlemen I am pleased to share with you some thoughts on monetary policy. -especially that of the Eurosystem - and the role of the central banks. The organizers of this celebration of the 70th anniversary of the "Banking and Financial Review" and "Banking and Financial Law" wanted to turn our eyes to the future. The idea is excellent but the exercise is perilous: according to the famous joke, forecasting is difficult, especially when it concerns the future. Thus, ten years ago, many still thought that European monetary policy would not see the light of day. I was not, which, of course, does not protect me from the surprises that history can have in store for us. Yet the saying goes with good reason that to govern is to foresee. I also believe that it means taking into account the uncertainty that surrounds any forecast and acting accordingly. In particular, it is up to central banks to make every effort to properly assess risks, in the exercise of their two main tasks, which I shall address in turn: ensuring monetary stability and financial stability. * * * The main objective of the Eurosystem's monetary policy is to maintain price stability in the euro area. I do not think it will be called into question because that would require amending the European Treaty. Above all, I do not want to believe that the lessons learned from the bitter experience of deflation and inflation of the past century, nor those given by many economists, including Phelps (recent Nobel laureate), on the importance of the expectations of economic agents and the inefficiency, even the nuisance of policies tried to overexploit the short-term trade-off between inflation and chage will be forgotten. Is it necessary to recall that controlling inflation and supporting activity are not contradictory but, on the contrary, price stability is the necessary - although obviously not sufficient - condition for sustainable growth? It benefits economic activity in the medium and long term, by supporting consumer confidence, and therefore their demand, and by reducing, to the benefit of investment, the risk premiums incorporated in long-term interest rates. So far, the institutional provisions of the Treaty, such as the independence granted to the Eurosystem, and the monetary policy strategy adopted by the Governing Council of the ECB, in particular the definition of price stability, have served remarkably as an anchor for inflationary expectations, thus providing significant flexibility in the conduct of this policy, despite slight but repeated exceedances of the 2 p.c. threshold by current inflation, in a context marked by the sharp increase in oil prices. Will it be the same in the future? Does the apparent success of this policy not contain certain dangers? To what extent will the conduct of European monetary policy be affected by the ongoing structural changes? I will briefly discuss the possible impact of some of these changes: globalisation, changes in productivity and demography and the growing growth of financial markets. The emergence of large countries such as China and India on the world economic stage has caused radical changes in relative prices. On the one hand, contributing to a strong growth of the world economy, it has led to a rise in the price of raw materials, including oil, even if geopolitical tensions and speculation have also played a role. On the other hand, it has exerted downward pressure on the prices of labour-intensive manufactured goods and even certain services. Beyond the direct effects of import prices, globalization has increased aggregate supply and competitive pressures. Along with the credibility of monetary policy, it may have helped to muzzle the second-round effects of the oil shock and mitigate the impact of domestic capacity utilization d1capital and labord1 on inflation, what economists call a flattening of the Phillips curve. It is not true that this adjuvant to maintaining price stability will remain in the coming decade, especially if protectionist resistance were to prevail. In any case, accurately assessing the changes in economic relations brought about by globalisation will be a major challenge for the Eurosystem. Globalization is also financial and implies the possibility of better risk sharing, more efficient allocation of resources and easier financing of current account balances. The current pattern of external imbalances is paradoxical, however, since, in the words of Kenneth Rogoff, the United States benefits from the largest foreign aid program in world history. Indeed, Asian countries have so far shown a preference for export-led growth and the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves, and oil-producing countries are also building up growing external debts, while to the weakness of private savings in the United States, linked in particular to the wealth effects of rising house prices, In addition, there was a considerable public deficit. Financing of net U.S. imports has so far been smooth and at remarkably low interest rates, thanks to the excess of savings over investment outside the U.S., but the U.S. economy cannot accumulate external debt indefinitely. Over the past two years, a first easing of exchange rate policy and the declared desire to promote the development of rural areas in China, a recovery in domestic demand in Japan and the euro area, the return of monetary policy to neutrality and the cooling of the real estate market in the United States have all been encouraging signs on the way to a reduction of imbalances. However, more needs to be done to avert the risk of a sharp correction, through excessive movements in exchange rates and a rebound in long-term interest rates. Europe must take part in the concerted effort, promoting investment and growth through structural reforms. Within the euro area, the synchronization of business cycles appears to have increased, but persistent growth gaps remain. On the one hand, this is a normal phenomenon, even desirable in case of "catching up". For the rest, it is up to the national authorities and social partners to address the structural problems of their economies. The Eurogroup should strengthen itself, not to interfere in monetary policy, which is in any case excluded by the Treaty, but for a critical examination and better coordination of other policies. The political leaders of European nations are indeed faced with the challenges of preparing public finances for the effects of an ageing population and of implementing the Lisbon Agenda. Because Europe should be able, without giving up good social protection, to increase its productivity, in particular by taking full advantage of the new information and communication technologies, like the American economy. A more flexible and dynamic economy should allow for higher growth and lower inflationary pressures, which monetary policy will take into account where appropriate. As for demographic change, which is relatively slow, its implications for the conduct of monetary policy are in principle quite limited. Central banks will, however, be alert to the possibility of more abrupt changes in the demographic transition phase. Today, the high level of savings in some countries, which also contributes to low interest rates, could be linked to the propensity to save of the still-working baby boom generation and uncertainties about the evolution of public pension systems. How the authorities ensure the future of these systems will be decisive. On the other hand, population ageing is likely to alter the transmission mechanism of monetary policy, reducing the importance of the credit channel and increasing the importance of wealth effects. This brings us to the latest structural change I wanted to mention, the growing growth of the financial markets. This has many implications for monetary policy. I will mention only two: taking account of asset price developments and the importance of communication. While price stability, by ruling out disruptions due to unanticipated fluctuations in inflation, contributes to the stability of financial markets, it is not a guarantee of this. The anchoring of inflationary expectations, under the combined effect of the increased credibility of monetary policies and globalization, is sometimes even suspected of constituting fertile ground for risk undervaluation and financial exuberance. According to some, central banks, reassured by the short-term inflation outlook, would allow debt to grow and financial bubbles to erupt. These developments could lead to financial crises or even subsequent deflation. Central banks would also tend to react asymmetrically, offsetting above all the effects of a fall in asset prices and giving rise, by the assurance they seem to give in this way (we have spoken of a "Greenspan put"), a problem of moral hazard. There is no doubt that the debate on how to take asset price developments into account in the conduct of monetary policy will continue in the coming years, as the difficulties of preventive action are not negligible, both in terms of diagnosing possible overvaluations and the prognosis and dosage of appropriate monetary policy tightening. In any event, beyond assessing the short- and medium-term risks to price stability resulting from supply and demand shocks affecting the economy, the Governing Council of the ECB is also attentive to the more distant risks arising from a possible accumulation of imbalances, while recognising the difficulty of determining equilibrium values. Monetary analysis can play a role in this respect. Admittedly, the link between the evolution of M3 and that of prices in the medium term seems to have become distended, precisely because of the increasing impact of portfolio considerations on the demand for money, or even a break due to the change in the monetary regime. On the other hand, the study of credit and liquidity data, together with that of indicators relating to the assessment of asset prices and the macroeconomic environment, can shed light on the possible accumulation of financial imbalances: a field of research is opening up on this subject. Finally, while the analysis is necessarily complex, it must also be clearly communicated. The independence of the Eurosystem requires it to be accountable to the public for the results achieved. The importance of the financial markets in the transmission of its policy - after all, it only narrowly counteracts the very short-term interest rates of the money market - also requires a high degree of transparency as to the reasons for monetary policy decisions. The press conference immediately following the meetings of the Governing Council of the ECB on monetary policy is exemplary in this respect. The Council took a further step this year by providing guidance on the future direction of interest rates, subject to the achievement of a baseline macroeconomic scenario. This conditional character must be strongly emphasized. The predictability of monetary policy decisions actually comes first and foremost from the clarity of strategy. * * * Monetary policy alone cannot ensure monetary stability and financial stability. As long as financial markets did not experience major shocks, and this was the case in the first decades of the post-war period, the theme of financial stability was able to take a back seat. However, since the end of the 70s, deregulation, the internationalization of activities and markets and, above all, the increasing sophistication of financial techniques and products have completely changed the situation. While business cycles have tended to lose momentum, shocks to financial markets have multiplied: banking crises in Japan and the Scandinavian countries in the early 90s; secondly, the Asian crisis, the default on russian and Argentine debts and the bankruptcy of LTCM; more recently, the stock market crisis, the attacks of September 11, accounting scandals in the United States. This more turbulent environment has attracted the attention of central banks, which have been led to rethink their contribution to financial stability. The reflections were essentially based on two main axes. Based on the premise that prevention is better than cure, central banks have developed macro-prudential supervisory structures to detect warning signs of vulnerability in the financial system. As these structures will never make it possible to protect oneself, in all circumstances, against possible accidents, it is also necessary to put in place crisis management procedures and mechanisms. I would like to briefly outline these two main modalities of action. Some central banks, especially in the euro area, have already been in charge of the so-called micro-prudential counter-supervision of financial institutions for a long time. The few examples I have just given are sufficient proof of the need to complement this surveillance of individual bankruptcy risks with monitoring of the macroeconomic implications that may result from turbulence or accidents affecting the entire financial system. This macro-prudential approach has become one of the main tasks of central banks, whether or not they are charged with the counter-against individual institutions. The specificity of macro-prudential analysis is not just a question of scale. It is also a question of perspective. For a supervisor, the macroeconomic environment and financial markets are considered exogenous variables that can affect the situation of individual banks. In a macro-prudential approach, these variables are made endogenous in order to take into account the impact that the overall behaviour of financial intermediaries may have on financial markets and the economy in general. Market operators today react much more quickly than in the past to common sources of information. This increases the risk of widespread behaviours which, even if justified at an individual level, could generate systemic problems if adopted simultaneously by a large number of institutions. A good understanding of the dynamics of market behaviour is not easy to develop. Much progress remains to be made. At the international level, the International Monetary Fund's Financial Sector Assessment Programme (FSAP) provides a stimulus for this type of analysis and allows the authorities both to benefit from an outside perspective and to compare the domestic financial system with others. Belgium has recently submitted to this programme profitably and successfully. At the same time, many central banks, including the National Bank of Belgium, make sure to communicate their own analysis and assessment of the national financial system through specific publications, the "Financial Stability Review" or "Report". In these publications, they focus on the links and interdependencies between institutions, the channels and processes of contagion or the cases of exposure to common risks. Preventive analyses and countermeasures cannot exempt the authorities from preparing to carry out, if necessary, a more curative remedy. Here we join the second axis of central banks' action in the field of financial stability, namely crisis management and resolution, in particular through the function of lender of last resort. Central banks are rightly very cautious and want at all costs to avoid maintaining the anticipation by market participants of rapid or even automatic intervention by the authorities to solve a problem as soon as it grows. They also want to take as much as possible solutions put in place by the markets which, in many cases, themselves have the resources and skills to react and adapt to shocks. However, the need for public intervention cannot be ruled out. This possibility must go hand in hand with a very clear principle. It is the problem institutions, their managers, their shareholders and, where appropriate, their creditors who will have to bear, to the maximum degree, the financial consequences of resolving a crisis. The classic constructive ambiguity often put forward by central banks must be coupled with this harsh certainty. At the international level, preparations for crisis management have progressed greatly through the organization of simulation exercises. Such exercises have recently been carried out by the Eurosystem, for the euro area, and between central banks, supervisors and treasuries, for the European Union as a whole. They highlighted the need for good coordination, the interactions between prudential authorities and market participants, but also the inevitable conflicts of interest that will arise in the event of a crisis. It therefore seems crucial to build mutual trust through regular contacts. This applies, of course, and even above all, at national level. It is also important for the National Bank of Belgium to maintain high-level contacts with the country's main banks, those with the greatest systemic weight. The information that is exchanged during these contacts, the concerns that are expressed on these occasions are essential elements for the proper exercise of our mission of financial stability. Des relations fortes doivent aussi exister entre la banque centrale et les autorit8es de supervision. Je ne r8esiste pas ici 88 l'envie de citer un de nos illustres compatriotes et coll8fgues, Alexandre Lamfalussy: "To take the right decision in a situation where central banks would be called upon to pump liquidity or, in extreme case, to provide emergency liquidity, central banks need a "real time" insight into the working of the financial system as a whole, and of banks in particular. The organisation of the channels through which such insight is obtained is an extremely difficult task. My concern is that those central banks which do not have an operational involvement in bank supervision would find it hard to gather the appropriate information". "Operational involvement" is not synonymous with taking charge of the function, but must go much further than simple contacts and exchanges of information. This is the main objective of the reform of the institutional supervisory landscape in Belgium implemented by the 2002 law and the raison d'90tre of strengthening the links and synergies between the National Bank of Belgium and the Banking, Finance and Insurance Commission. The achievement of a good balance and the conduct of this extremely difficult task will, in my view, make it necessary to carry out, in the near future, an evaluation of the application of the 2002 law and the architecture it has defined. Nor will Economic and Monetary Union be able to avoid a similar examination. To quote another quote from Alexandre Lamfalussy, "To act swiftly and efficiently in a potential crisis situation, you need few interlocutors and simple communication lines. With those objectives in mind, we should have a hard look at our current institutional arrangements in the field of crisis prevention and management. These arrangements seem to me, to put it mildly, sub-optimal". * * * At the end of this overview of some of the major trends at work in the economy and finance, I will not pretend to have defined precisely what European monetary policy and the re of central banks will be in ten years' time. But if there is an easy prediction, it is that we will continue to live in an uncertain world. It is therefore important that central banks remain providers of stability, basing their risk assessment on the most thorough analyses. Rest assured that the National Bank of Belgium and the Eurosystem will be actively engaged in this.

L'Union <8e>conomique et mon<8e>taire ne pourra d'ailleurs pas non plus faire l'<8e>conomie d'un examen similaire. Pour reprendre une autre citation d'Alexandre Lamfalussy, "To act swiftly and efficiently in a potential crisis situation, you need few interlocutors and simple communication lines. With those objectives in mind, we should have a hard look at our current institutional arrangements in the field of crisis prevention and management. These arrangements seem to me, to put it mildly, sub-optimal". * * * Au terme de ce survol de quelques grandes tendances <88> l'<cf>uvre dans l'<8e>conomie et la finance, je n'aurai pas la pr<8e>tention d'avoir d<8e>fini pr<8e>cis<8e>ment ce que seront la politique mon<8e>taire europ<8e>enne et le re des banques centrales dans dix ans. Mais s'il est une pr<8e>vision facile, c'est que nous continuerons <88> vivre dans un monde incertain. Il importe d<8f>s lors que les banques centrales restent des pourvoyeuses de stabilit<8e>, en appuyant leur <8e>valuation des risques sur les analyses les plus fouill<8e>es. Soyez assur<8e>s que la Banque nationale de Belgique et l'Eurosyst<8f>me s'y emploieront activement.

Title: General Assembly 2007
text: 2007-03-26 GENERAL MEETINGS 2007 Introductory statement by Governor Guy Quaden Ladies and Gentlemen, I welcome you, on my own behalf and on behalf of my colleagues on the Management Committee, to this ordinary general meeting of shareholders of the National Bank of Belgium. As is tradition, I would like to briefly retrace for you the most significant events of the year under review, before giving the floor to the Deputy Governor who will present and comment on the annual accounts for the financial year 2006. We will then answer your questions in a climate that we hope will be serene. Earlier this year, we celebrated the fifth anniversary of the introduction of euro notes and coins. Thirteen countries now share the same currency and their central banks are participating, together with the ECB, in the development and implementation of a common monetary policy. Thanks to the active collaboration of the central banks concerned, the Eurosystem is successfully carrying out the tasks entrusted to it by the Maastricht Treaty: to define and implement the monetary policy of the euro area, to conduct foreign exchange operations, to hold and manage the official foreign exchange reserves of the Member States and to promote the proper functioning of payment systems. The Eurosystem is working well. However, it is evolving. In its dimension first. It welcomed a new member in January 2007, Slovenia, and is likely to join others as early as next year. He also evolves in his organization. One of the basic principles of the functioning of the Eurosystem is the strong decentralisation of tasks, in particular in contacts with financial institutions and national economic agents. This principle of decentralization, however, has evolved towards more specialization and new forms of collaboration between central banks. In this context, the SNB has increased its specialization in certain activities of the system, in particular the processing of banknotes, the management of guarantees related to monetary policy and the collection of statistical data. In the area of banknotes, the Bank has developed a computer tool that manages the flow of banknotes and coins both within the Bank and between the Bank and financial institutions and cash carriers. This application, called "cash", has provided significant productivity gains as well as increased transaction security. The Bank offers other central banks the possibility to use this application. A partnership was concluded in 2006 with the Nederlandsche Bank and the Banque centrale du Luxembourg, which the Bank of Finland has just joined. The management of the sretes is more directly concerned with the execution of monetary policy. The loans granted to financial institutions must be guaranteed by appropriate safeguards. The Bank has developed a new IT application to ensure effective management of these guarantees. This platform, called the "Euro Collateral management system", allows an almost fully automated management of these sets and an improvement of the services provided to financial institutions. The advantages offered by this platform have aroused the interest of other central banks and, here too, a partnership has been concluded with the Nederlandsche Bank. Finally, a third application for which the Bank has know-how that may be of interest to other partners concerns the collection of statistical information. This is the computer application called "Central server for statistical reporting", which facilitates the transmission and reception of data Communication boulevard de Berlaimont 14 tel. 32 2 221 46 28 VAT BE 0203.201.340 Banque Nationale de Belgique s.a. BE-1000 BRUXELLES RPM Brussels statistics via the internet. This tool is already in use at the Bank in most statistical areas that require the collection of data from both financial and non-financial enterprises. These examples demonstrate the Bank's concern to further improve the quality of its services to the country and the Eurosystem through increased specialisation through the use of new technologies and the dynamic management of its human resources. The evolution of the various activities in 2006 is presented in the annual report that was sent to you before the meeting or given at the entrance, and which is also available on our website. * * * An event of which I must inform the Assembly occurred after the publication of this report. This is the judgment delivered on 9 March 2007 by the Commercial Court of Brussels in the case between a small group of shareholders and the Bank and the State, concerning three laws that occurred between 1996 and 2002 and which transferred to the Treasury capital gains realized by the Bank on gold sales. This judgment is the fifth court decision in disputes between the Bank and some of its shareholders. It is also a fifth confirmation of the merits of the arguments that the Bank has always defended. The Court of First Instance dismissed the plaintiffs' application that the capital gains realized on the disposals of gold must be shared among the shareholders. He agreed with the Bank and the State and confirmed that the shareholders have no right to the capital gains that the Bank realizes on its gold sales. You will find in the report that has been given to you the details of the evolution of the judicial cases. I will not call them back. The various judgments, however, confirm three things: 1. whereas the Bank is a special institution and a specific company with its own laws and statutes; 2. whereas foreign exchange reserves constitute an asset allocated to the missions of general interest entrusted to the Bank; 3. that the Bank did not commit any fault, since, in accordance with its duty, it applied the laws. Finally, I must inform the Assembly of a very recent judicial event, since it concerns an interim order issued on 23 March by the President of the Commercial Court of Brussels. On 21 March, 22 shareholders had submitted several requests to it, based on the judgment of 9 March 2007, including that of suspending and postponing the holding of this ordinary general meeting. The Chairperson rejected this request. The other requests submitted to the President by these few shareholders are still pending and will be the subject of a future order. I will therefore not speak about it, but the Bank is confident that its position will once again be confirmed judicially. * * * I shall now give the floor to the Deputy Governor for a detailed presentation of the annual accounts for the financial year 2006. In his presentation, he will already answer a large number of questions received from shareholders prior to the meeting. Your other questions may be addressed as part of the question and answer session. I thank the shareholders who sent us their questions in advance and in writing, which facilitates the preparation and smooth running of this meeting. Thank you for your attention.
