Title: Gouverneur Pierre Wunsch van de Nationale Bank wikt de stand van het land - 'Er is iets in de mensen geslopen dat wij niet goed begrijpen'
text: Interview with Governor Wunsch - De Morgen - 23.12.2023 Bart EECKHOUT and Lotte BECKERS Pierre Wunsch, Governor of the National Bank, assesses the state of the country - 'Something has crept into people that we don't really understand' Budget deficits are rising, the climate is changing and wars are raging at Europe's borders. However, Pierre Wunsch, Governor of the National Bank, is most concerned about something else. "A lot of people even refuse to accept facts." There are few places in Belgium that are as reminiscent of a palace in a former Soviet republic as the main building of the National Bank. A messenger in a grey suit guides us through a labyrinth of long corridors. Along the way, an employee shows up, with a stack of paper under his arm, on his way to another employee with a stack of paper. In that beige-coloured decor, Pierre Wunsch is a fresh appearance. The 56-year-old governor of the National Bank of Belgium has a good, bilingual chat - too good, according to some politicians. His political background is French-speaking liberal, but he combines it with a certain obsession with climate politics. One of his concerns is that future governments will have to set aside extra money for the green transition. Money that is not there, while the country's economy is doing quite well. So the first question is obvious: is Belgium in good shape or not? "If you only look at the short term, you have to say that the Belgian economy is holding up well," Wunsch begins. "We are doing better than many other European countries. This is partly due to automatic wage indexation, which protects people's purchasing power and thus stimulates private consumption. But business investment has also risen by more than 10 percent this year and last year combined. That's an exceptional amount. Research also shows that over the last few years, the wages of the less skilled workers have risen faster than average." Why? "Workers have gained more power in the labor market due to the scarcity. We are coming out of a period in which inequality increased as a result of globalization, with higher growth but also with access to cheap Chinese products and cheaper labor from other countries. So now it seems to be going in the other direction, partly due to the combination of higher minimum wages and lower unemployment." You are basically saying: the labour market shortage is good for people at the bottom of the labour market. But not for growth. "At the end of the day, economics is about the people, not about itself. I would rather have an economy with a tight labour market where companies have to invest in digitalisation and a reduction in inequality than an economy that increases inequality. It's a challenge for companies, but it's good news for the people who work in those companies." So Belgium is doing quite well. How is that possible? "When the European economy is not doing so well, Belgium always does a little better than many other countries. And now noticeably better. Because the people are well protected. There is wage indexation, social spending is quite high and there were the extra measures to cushion the energy shock." Institutions such as the IMF have always been critical of these so-called automatic stabilizers. Now they appear to be keeping the economy afloat. "Well, yes, in the short term. (smiles) Jusqu'ici tout va bien. This protection costs the government a lot of money. I'm not going to announce a crash here. Belgium is not going to be bankrupt in two years' time. But there is a wall, and if we don't change course, we are guaranteed to run into it. "Just stabilizing the budget deficit at the current, far too high level will cost the next government 10 billion in five years. Because the ageing population is going to cost more money anyway and because we have to pay interest on our debt. I do not want to dramatize the situation, but I also do not want to give the impression that everything is fine. The Netherlands and Germany do have the budget and national debt under control, and these are not social deserts. Bon, this is Belgium. The political solution will always be a little... be anything. The employment rate is also a challenge. We are moving in the right direction, but slower than we should be. The regional differences are huge." Why can't we get that resolved? "One of the problems is the lack of incentives to go to work. I have experienced this myself with three Ukrainian refugees that we have taken care of at home for a while. They could not believe that they would receive money from the OCMW. 800 euros, that's a full wage in Ukraine, isn't it? But two years later, they still weren't working. They were not stimulated, they did not learn enough French and Dutch. In the Netherlands, almost 70 percent of Ukrainian refugees were working at the beginning of this year, here in the Netherlands it would fluctuate around a quarter at the time." Should we be afraid of a long government formation? "Yes and no. Yes, because current affairs by definition means that policy remains unchanged and that the budget deficit will therefore continue to rise. But no, because there is no reason to panic. I think that the rating agencies have already included these complex government formations in their calculations for Belgium." You said this week: wage indexation is here to stay. That's a different language than last year. "We shouldn't be silly about the fact that automatic indexation costs us competitiveness. But I immediately said at the start of the energy crisis that companies' profit margins are historically high and that there was therefore capacity to absorb the shock. At a certain point, there was a sharp acceleration in inflation. If energy prices had pushed inflation up for another six months, we would have had a real problem. At that time, I did indeed suggest that the modalities of indexation should be adjusted. Subsequently, gas prices plummeted, (dry) My timing was not right. "I'm not going to repeat that the wage index has to be adjusted. Due to the indexation, there is little room to do anything else in wage policy. That makes the labor market rigid. But at the same time, the macroeconomic problem is quite limited. Exports are suffering, but domestic consumption remains strong, and in the long run the differences with the other countries will level out again." You mean: if there are no additional wage increases, above the index. "It's not up to me to give advice on that, but indeed: according to our calculations, the margin would be at least to zero. Otherwise, the gap with neighbouring countries will remain too wide." Would you rather be governor of the National Bank of the Netherlands? "I couldn't do that accent (laughs). I don't envy my Dutch colleague. After the elections, it will not be so easy to implement policy there either. "I'm 'just' governor. I don't have to make decisions with seven parties around the government table. If everything is going well and there is no inflation, my job is not that difficult. The crises and structural challenges make it difficult, but also interesting. Certainly the climate challenge is a bit of an obsession for me. I'm pretty optimistic about the technology. I don't know if we'll be able to keep warming to 2 degrees, but don't forget that we're coming from estimates, twenty years ago, of 5 degrees. What makes me less happy is the political side of the story." "If overfishing is the problem, subsidizing chicken doesn't help," you said of climate politics. What do you mean by that? "The expression comes from a Swedish colleague. What I mean by that is that it is not useful to just give a lot of subsidies for green investments, without at the same time increasing the cost of fossil fuels. That's what President Biden is doing in the U.S. right now. At some point, people will have to go to an increase in the price of oil and gas in order to literally price fossil fuels out of the market." These American subsidies are a problem for our industry. "We will lose part of the value chain. The question now is whether that affects the entire industry. Are companies bringing hydrogen to Europe or is industry moving to places where there is hydrogen? Business leaders in the port of Antwerp are relatively optimistic. Europe will lose market share in energy-intensive industry, but it is possible that the port areas will gain. Because large investments will be made first where there is already a lot of industrial activity. Antwerp then has an advantage." The energy crisis has shaken many people's belief in the green transition. "That crisis was a supply shock. Our society was not yet ready to let go of fossil fuels. On the contrary, this crisis has reminded us that the transition is far too slow. When I look at the political trends in Europe, I get gloomy. The green parties are struggling, the populist ones are winning. That is why it is important that the European 'fit for 55' legislation is anchored (a package of green measures that aims to reduce emissions by 55 percent by 2030, BE/LB). That's all there is to it for the time being. In addition, you must have the flexibility to replace a contested measure. People revolt when the transition starts to cost them too much. Then you risk having a backlash, which takes you even further from home." Belgium is lagging behind in home insulation, but investment in renovation is still declining. "The degree of insulation is far too low. At the same time, we are making our standards stricter than necessary. Is that smart? People have to make heavy investments and are not even sure that they will get that A-label. I've experienced it myself with a property in France. Two bathrooms insulated, had to spend a lot of money, but the result is insufficient. "At some point, we will have to make diagnoses almost house by house: insulate here, better a heat pump there, and wait and dismantle there for twenty years." What lingers anyway is the geopolitical uncertainty. "I'm more concerned about the polarization. This links Trump's comeback to Wilders in the Netherlands, but also to the public debate here. It is very difficult to come up with a balanced story in the media. I read titles over pieces that don't make sense and that lead to clicks and then everyone starts tweeting angrily about the titles. "There's nothing wrong with a robust debate, but in the past, discussions started on the basis of facts. Now many refuse to accept the facts themselves. Everywhere I go, I hear the same concern. Not about the facts, but about how people experience them. Something has crept into people that we don't really understand. "We shouldn't be afraid of the future. Our economy is resilient. The situation on the job market is completely different now than it was when I was young. Now that was a crisis. If you wanted a job - at the postal service, at the Planning Bureau - you had to take an exam in Heysel by the thousands." One moment when you clashed with the media was when you allegedly said that the government bond could not be repeated. What about now? "I said that it was not worth repeating in the sense of: no three times 20 billion from the banks. But I wasn't against that government bond, and I understand why so many people signed up for it. My message has long been that the banks have room to do more. I was one of the first to say that publicly in Belgium, long before it became a political issue. The government bond has sent a clear signal to the banks. And it has arrived." Is that so? The interest rate on savings deposits is still meagre. "The banks can't do much more, because they have taken out a large volume of fixed-rate mortgage loans. If the banks go to 4 percent interest, they are bankrupt. If the Belgian wants to buy a house, he will go to two or three banks to get a good loan. The competition is very strong there. But it does mean that banks have less margin to give a lot of interest on savings deposits, because those deposits finance the loans in the longer term. You could say that's a social choice." According to economist Paul De Grauwe, you protect the banks more than the citizens. "Paul is abusing his academic title for fairly cheap attacks. The beginning of his story is always correct, but then he exaggerates. To say that we are giving billions as a gift to the banks is simply nonsense. Subtract the gifts that the national banks in Europe are supposedly giving to the banks from the profits of those banks and we are in a banking crisis. Paul knows that too." Your mandate will expire in 2024. Are you going for an extension? "That's up to the government to decide" But if they ask you, you say yes. "Yes, I think this is a very exciting job. There is the international dimension, the task of leading a company of almost two thousand people and the role I play in the public debate on macroeconomics. I'm happy to do that." Too much, says PS chairman Paul Magnette. "Oh well, I understood him. If I had really said what I had said according to a certain press release, then he had every reason to be angry. Only I hadn't said that. "Actually, I said exactly the same thing then as I do now. The situation is stable, but public finances are not sustainable in the long term. And so, sooner or later, we will have to take a radically different approach to our budget. In the French-language Belga report, the headline suddenly became 'Wunsch attacks Vivaldi: need for radically different politics'. I hadn't said a word about Vivaldi!" Is fuss the most annoying part of your job? "I like to communicate, but it gets tricky when you lose control of the content of what you've said. Especially now, in a society that is becoming increasingly polarised, institutions such as the National Bank should play their part in interpreting what is happening. With all the nuances. But I'm not complaining. Politicians are in the middle of it every day. I don't envy them."
text_original: Interview Gouverneur Wunsch - De Morgen - 23.12.2023 Bart EECKHOUT en Lotte BECKERS Gouverneur Pierre Wunsch van de Nationale Bank wikt de stand van het land - 'Er is iets in de mensen geslopen dat wij niet goed begrijpen' De begrotingstekorten lopen op, het klimaat verandert en er woeden oorlogen aan de Europese grenzen. Toch maakt gouverneur Pierre Wunsch van de Nationale Bank zich het meeste zorgen over iets anders. 'Veel mensen weigeren zelfs feiten te aanvaarden.' Er zijn weinig plekken in Belgi die zozeer doen denken aan een paleis in een voormalige Sovjet- republiek als het hoofdgebouw van de Nationale Bank. Een bode in grijs pak gidst ons door een labyrint van lange gangen. Onderweg duikt een medewerker op, met een stapel papier onder de arm, op weg naar een andere medewerker met een stapel papier. In dat beigekleurig decor is Pierre Wunsch een frisse verschijning. De 56-jarige gouverneur van de Nationale Bank van Belgi heeft een goede, tweetalige babbel - te goed, volgens sommige politici. Zijn politieke achtergrond is Franstalig liberaal, maar die combineert hij met een zekere obsessie voor klimaatpolitiek. Dat volgende regeringen extra geld opzij zullen moeten zetten voor die groene transitie is een van zijn bezorgdheden. Geld dat er niet is, terwijl 's lands economie best wel draait. Dus ligt de eerste vraag voor de hand: staat Belgi er nu goed voor of niet? "Kijkje enkel naar de korte termijn, dan moetje zeggen dat de Belgische economie goed standhoudt", begint Wunsch. "Wij doen het beter dan vele andere Europese landen. Dat heeft deels te maken met de automatische loonindexering, die de koopkracht van de mensen beschermt en zo de privconsumptie stimuleert. Maar ook bedrijfsinvesteringen zijn dit en vorig jaar samen met meer dan 10 procent gestegen. Dat is uitzonderlijk veel. Onderzoek toont ook dat over de laatste jaren bij ons de lonen van de korter geschoolde arbeiders sneller zijn gestegen dan gemiddeld." Hoezo? "Werknemers hebben door de schaarste meer macht gekregen op de arbeidsmarkt. We komen uit een periode waarin de ongelijkheid toenam als gevolg van de globalisering, met een hogere groei maar ook met toegang tot goedkope Chinese producten en goedkopere arbeidskrachten uit andere landen. Nu lijkt het dus de andere richting uit te gaan, mede door de combinatie van hogere minimumlonen en lagere werkloosheid." U zegt eigenlijk: de arbeidsmarktkrapte is goed voor mensen aan de onderkant van de arbeidsmarkt. Maar niet voor de groei. "Uiteindelijk draait economie om de mensen, niet om zichzelf. Ik heb liever een economie met arbeidsmarktkrapte waar ondernemingen moeten investeren in digitalisering en een vermindering van de ongelijkheid dan een economie die de ongelijkheid vergroot. Voor bedrijven is het een uitdaging, maar voor de mensen die in die bedrijven werken, is het goed nieuws." Belgi doet het dus vrij goed. Hoe kan dat? "Als het minder goed gaat met de Europese economie doet Belgi het altijd een beetje beter dan vele andere landen. En nu merkelijk beter. Omdat de mensen goed beschermd zijn. Er is de Page 1 of 5 loonindexering, de sociale uitgaven liggen vrij hoog en er waren de extra maatregelen om de energieschok te dempen." Instellingen zoals het IMF zijn altijd kritisch geweest voor die zogenaamde automatische stabilisatoren. Nu blijken ze de economie overeind te houden. "Welja, op korte termijn dus. (glimlacht) Jusqu'ici tout va bien. Die bescherming kost de overheid veel geld. Ik ga hier geen crash aankondigen. Belgi gaat niet bankroet zijn over twee jaar. Maar er staat wel een muur, en als we de koers niet bijsturen, lopen we er gegarandeerd tegen. "Alleen al het begrotingstekort stabiliseren op het huidige, veel te hoge niveau zal de volgende regering in vijfjaar tijd 10 miljard kosten. Omdat de vergrijzing sowieso meer geld gaat kosten en omdat we rente moeten betalen op onze schuld. Ik wil de situatie niet dramatiseren, maar ik wil ook niet de indruk wekken dat alles in orde is. Nederland en Duitsland hebben de begroting en staatsschuld wel onder controle en dat zijn toch geen sociale woestijnen. Bon, dit is Belgi. De politieke oplossing zal altijd een beetje... van alles zijn. De tewerkstellingsgraad is ook een uitdaging. We gaan in de goede richting, maar trager dan zou moeten. De regionale verschillen zijn groot." Waarom krijgen we dat niet opgelost? "Een van de problemen is het gebrek aan prikkels om te gaan werken. Ik heb dat zelf meegemaakt met drie Oekraense vluchtelingen die wij thuis een tijdje hebben opgevangen. Zij konden niet geloven dat ze geld zouden krijgen van het OCMW. 800 euro, dat is een volwaardig loon in Oekrane, h. Maar twee jaar later werkten ze nog altijd niet. Ze werden niet aangespoord, ze leerden onvoldoende Frans en Nederlands. In Nederland was begin dit jaar bijna 70 procent van de Oekraense vluchtelingen aan het werk, hier bij ons zou dat toen rond een kwart schommelen." Moeten we bang zijn voor een lange regeringsvorming? "Ja en neen. Ja, omdat lopende zaken per definitie betekent dat het beleid ongewijzigd blijft en dat het begrotingstekort dus zal blijven oplopen. Maar ook neen, omdat er geen reden tot paniek is. Ik denk dat de ratingbureaus die complexe regeringsvormingen al in hun berekeningen voor Belgi hebben opgenomen." U zei deze week: de loonindexering is here to stay. Dat is andere taal dan vorig jaar. "Dat de automatische indexering ons concurrentiekracht kost, daar moeten we niet flauw over doen. Maar ik heb bij het begin van de energiecrisis meteen gezegd dat de winstmarge van ondernemingen historisch hoog ligt en dat er dus capaciteit was om de schok op te vangen. Op een bepaald moment zat er wel een forse versnelling in de inflatie. Als de energieprijzen nog zes maanden langer de inflatie omhoog geduwd hadden, hadden we echt een probleem gehad. Toen heb ik inderdaad gesuggereerd om de modaliteiten van de indexering aan te passen. Vervolgens zijn de gasprijzen gekelderd, (droog) Mijn timing was niet goed. "Dat de loonindex moet worden aangepast, ga ik niet meer herhalen. Door de indexering is er wel weinig marge om nog iets anders te doen in de loonpolitiek. Dat maakt de arbeidsmarkt rigide. Maar tegelijk is het macro-economische probleem vrij beperkt. De uitvoer lijdt eronder, maar de binnenlandse consumptie blijft sterk, en op termijn raken de verschillen met de andere landen weer uitgevlakt." Page 2 of 5 U bedoelt: als er geen extra loonsverhogingen komen, boven de index. "Het is niet aan mij om daarover advies te geven, maar inderdaad: volgens onze berekeningen zou de marge minimaal tot nul zijn. Anders blijft de kloof met de buurlanden te breed." Zou u liever gouverneur van de Nationale Bank van Nederland zijn? "Dat accent, dat zou ik niet kunnen (lacht). Ik benijd mijn Nederlandse collega niet. Na de verkiezingen wordt het daar ook niet zo gemakkelijk om beleid te voeren. "Ik ben 'maar' gouverneur. Ik moet geen beslissingen nemen met zeven partijen rond de regeringstafel. Als alles goed gaat en er geen inflatie is, is mijn job niet zo moeilijk. De crises en structurele uitdagingen maken het lastig, maar ook interessant. Zeker de klimaatuitdaging is een beetje een obsessie voor mij. Ik ben vrij optimistisch over de technologie. Ik weet niet of we de opwarming op 2 graden zullen kunnen houden, maar vergeet niet dat we komen van schattingen, twintig jaar geleden, van 5 graden. Wat me minder vrolijk stemt, is de politieke kant van het verhaal." 'Als overbevissing het probleem is, helpt het niet om kip te subsidiren', zei u over de klimaatpolitiek. Wat bedoelt u daarmee? "De uitdrukking komt van een Zweedse collega. Ik bedoel ermee dat het niet nuttig is om enkel veel subsidies te geven voor groene investeringen, zonder tegelijk de kostprijs van fossiele brandstoffen te verhogen. Dat is wat president Biden in de VS nu doet. Ooit zal men naar een verhoging van de olie- en gasprijs moeten gaan om fossiel letterlijk uit de markt te prijzen." Die Amerikaanse subsidies zijn een probleem voor onze industrie. "Wij zullen een deel van de waardeketting verliezen. De vraag is nu of dat de hele industrie aantast. Laten bedrijven waterstof naar Europa komen of verhuist de industrie naar plaatsen waar waterstof is? De bedrijfsleiders in de Antwerpse haven zijn relatief optimistisch. Europa zal in de energie-intensieve industrie marktaandeel verliezen, maar het is wel mogelijk dat de havengebieden erbij winnen. Omdat men grote investeringen eerst zal doen waar er al veel industrile activiteit is. Antwerpen heeft dan een voordeel." De energiecrisis heeft bij velen het geloof in de groene transitie geschokt. "Die crisis was een aanbodschok. Onze samenleving was nog niet klaar om fossiel los te laten. Die crisis heeft ons er juist aan herinnerd dat de transitie veel te traag gaat. Als ik dan kijk naar de politieke trends in Europa, dan word ik somber. De groene partijen hebben het moeilijk, de populistische winnen. Daarom is het belangrijk dat de Europese 'fit for 55'- wetgeving verankerd is (een pakket groene maatregelen dat de uitstoot met 55 procent moet verminderen tegen 2030, BE/LB). Meer zit er voorlopig niet in. Bovendien moetje de flexibiliteit hebben om een gecontesteerde maatregel te vervangen. Mensen komen in opstand als de transitie hen te veel gaat kosten. Dan riskeer je een terugslag te krijgen, waardoor je nog verder van huis bent." Belgi loopt achter met woningisolatie, maar de investeringen in renovatie lopen nog terug. "De isolatiegraad ligt veel te laag. Tegelijk maken we onze normen strenger dan nodig is. Is dat wel slim? Mensen moeten zware investeringen doen en zijn niet eens zeker dat ze dat A-label gaan halen. Ik heb het zelf meegemaakt met een eigendom in Frankrijk. Twee badkamers gesoleerd, veel geld moeten uitgeven, maar het resultaat is onvoldoende. Page 3 of 5 "Op een bepaald moment zullen we bijna huis per huis diagnoses moeten maken: hier isoleren, daar beter een warmtepomp, en ginds twintig jaar wachten en afbreken." Wat sowieso blijft hangen, is de geopolitieke onzekerheid. "Ik maak me meer zorgen over de polarisering. Dat verbindt de comeback van Trump met Wilders in Nederland, maar ook met het publieke debat hier. Het is heel moeilijk om nog met een evenwichtig verhaal te komen in de media. Ik lees titels boven stukken die nergens op slaan en die leiden naar clicks en dan begint iedereen boos te tweeten over de titels. "Er is niets mis met een stevig debat, maar vroeger begonnen discussies op basis van feiten. Nu weigeren velen de feiten zelf te aanvaarden. Overal waar ik kom, hoor ik diezelfde bezorgdheid. Niet over de feiten, maar over hoe mensen die ervaren. Er is iets in de mensen geslopen dat wij niet goed begrijpen. "We moeten niet bang zijn voor de toekomst. Onze economie is veerkrachtig. De situatie op de arbeidsmarkt is nu totaal anders dan toen ik jong was. Dat was pas een crisis. Als je een job wou - bij de post, bij het Planbureau - moest je met duizenden tegelijk een examen afleggen in de Heizel." Een moment waarop u in de clinch lag met de media was toen u gezegd zou hebben dat de staatsbon niet voor herhaling vatbaar was. Hoe zit het nu? "Ik heb gezegd dat het niet voor herhaling vatbaar was in de zin van: geen drie keer 20 miljard weghalen bij de banken. Maar ik was niet tegen die staatsbon, en ik begrijp waarom zoveel mensen erop ingetekend hebben. Mijn boodschap was al langer dat de banken ruimte hebben om meer te doen. Ik ben een van de eersten die dat in Belgi publiekelijk gezegd heeft, lang voor het een politiek thema werd. De staatsbon heeft een duidelijk signaal aan de banken gegeven. En het is aangekomen." Is dat zo? De rente op spaardeposito's is nog altijd magertjes. "Veel meer kunnen de banken niet doen, omdat ze een groot volume hypotheekleningen aangegaan zijn met vaste rente. Als de banken naar 4 procent rente gaan, zijn ze failliet. Als de Belg een huis wil kopen, zal hij naar twee, drie banken gaan om een goede lening te krijgen. Daar speelt de concurrentie heel sterk. Maar het betekent wel dat banken minder marge hebben om op spaardeposito's veel rente te geven, want die deposito's financieren de leningen op langere termijn. Je zou kunnen zeggen dat dat een maatschappelijke keuze is." Volgens econoom Paul De Grauwe beschermt u de banken meer dan de burgers. "Paul misbruikt zijn academische titel voor vrij goedkope aanvallen. Het begin van zijn verhaal is altijd correct, maar dan overdrijft hij. Zeggen dat wij miljarden cadeau geven aan de banken is gewoon onzin. Trek de cadeaus die de nationale banken in Europa zogezegd aan de banken zouden geven af van de winsten van die banken en we zitten in een bankcrisis. Paul weet dat ook." In 2024 loopt uw mandaat af. U gaat voor een verlenging? "Dat is aan de regering om te beslissen" Page 4 of 5 Maar als ze het u vragen, dan zegt u ja. "Ja, ik vind dit een enorm boeiende job. Er is de internationale dimensie, de opdracht om een onderneming van bijna tweeduizend mensen te leiden en de rol die ik speel in het publieke debat over de macro-economie. Ik doe dat graag." Te graag, vindt PS-voorzitter Paul Magnette. "Ach, ik begreep hem wel. Als ik echt had gezegd wat ik volgens een bepaald persbericht had gezegd, dan had hij alle reden om boos te zijn. Alleen had ik dat dus niet gezegd. "Eigenlijk zei ik toen exact hetzelfde als nu. De situatie is stabiel, maar op termijn zijn de overheidsfinancin niet houdbaar. En dus zullen we vroeg of laat op een radicaal andere manier onze begroting moeten aanpakken. In het Franstalige Belga-bericht werd de kop plots 'Wunsch valt Vivaldi aan: nood aan radicaal andere politiek'. Ik had geen woord over Vivaldi gezegd!" Is ophef de vervelendste kant van uw job? "Ik communiceer graag, maar het wordt lastig als je de controle verliest over de inhoud van wat je hebt gezegd. Juist nu, in een maatschappij die steeds meer polariseert, zouden instellingen zoals de Nationale Bank hun rol moeten spelen om te duiden wat er gebeurt. Met alle nuances. Maar ik klaag niet. Politici staan er elke dag middenin. Hen benijd ik niet." Page 5 of 5

Title: Pierre Wunsch, gouverneur de la Banque nationale, sur les taux, lconomie, la polarisation de la socit  - Elon Musk naurait pas pu faire Tesla  partir de lEurope
text: Interview with Governor Wunsch - Trends Tendances - 28.12.2023 Daan KILLEMAES & Pierre-Henri THOMAS Pierre Wunsch, governor of the National Bank, on interest rates, the economy, the polarisation of society... - "Elon Musk could not have made Tesla from Europe" Seeking a second term at the NBB, Governor Pierre Wunsch does not want to endorse markets that expect a rate cut in March. And he questions this European culture that often prefers stability and consensus to disruption. We met with the Governor of the National Bank of Belgium (NBB), Pierre Wunsch, at a time when the government had not yet formally taken the decision to renew his mandate. The meeting was an opportunity to discuss topics that go far beyond the framework of strict monetary policy and to talk in particular about how he approaches his role as governor. "With my background, a doctorate in economics, eight years' experience in various ministerial cabinets, experience in the private sector (at Tractebel, editor's note), my job as governor allows me to make the most of these ultimately very diverse experiences," he says, adding: "Many economists have a clear idea of what needs to be done. But with these years in cabinets, I sometimes have a better sense of what is politically feasible." TRENDS-TENDANCES. You are considered more of a hawk on the Governing Council of the European Central Bank. That's right? PIERRE WUNSCH. I am indeed classified as such. I was more of a "dove" at first, but the facts change and you change your mind. This reputation is somewhat linked to the fact that I disagreed with the decisions of the Board of Governors twice in 2021. I don't regret it. There is a consensus today that the forward guidance at the time was a little too aggressive, which is part of the reason why we reacted too slowly. And the last round of quantitative easing decided in December 2021, when inflation was already at 5%, was really not justified. And today, the situation is reversed. The markets are even pricing in a first rate cut in March. If inflation comes down, we will move in that direction at some point. But after four years of inflation above 2% (in 2021, 2022, 2023 and again in 2024, when the European Central Bank forecasts inflation of 2.7% for the euro area, editor's note), we must not declare victory too soon. Markets tend to overreact a little bit. Even if we think that this is going in the right direction, we should not say it too loudly. Our attention is focused on the evolution of wages. Negotiations are continuing today with a target of wage growth in the euro area of around 4.5 to 5%. This is not consistent with our 2% target. Some of my colleagues say that there is a huge risk that we will do far too much. I do not think so. We have a forecast of up to 2% inflation in 2025. It depends on moderating wage growth and reducing companies' profit margins (so that companies absorb part of the wage increase rather than raising their prices, editor's note). This is a reasonable baseline scenario. And in this scenario, we should not raise interest rates again, unless there is a shock. But to deduce from this that we will start cutting rates in March... When you look at the Belgian economy, you see a strange landscape: household confidence indices are up, but business confidence is not good. Still, business investment has increased by 8.6% this year and is expected to grow by another 4.7% next year. Indeed, there is a larger-than-usual gap between confidence indicators and growth. If we look at the figures of corporate purchasing managers, we should have been in recession for a year. But defining what is happening at the investment level is not easy. And frankly, we don't have a good explanation. In part, there is the fact that companies had very good profitability (it has since declined), and had accumulated a lot of liquidity. They may have borrowed a little too much because it was cheap. They therefore had a lot of internal resources to invest. The other part of the story could be that when you can't find workers, when energy is more expensive, when you anticipate the fact that the state will have to improve its finances and will have to go and get money from you at some point, you think about increasing your productivity and therefore investing. As for the difference in confidence between households and businesses, I explain it by the geopolitical uncertainty that affects businesses more. They are facing multiple risks: climate, energy crisis, geopolitical crisis, etc. And if you look at the media and the press, everything is bleak. Is there a responsibility of the media? What I have noticed, and this is personal, is that you have less and less control over your message. Sometimes I reread an article, I'm satisfied. Then a title, which sometimes has almost nothing to do with the article, appears for people to click through. And if politicians start tweeting about the subject without having read the article, the message is lost. Are you adapting your communication strategy to this new reality? It's difficult. We are really trying to find a balanced language. And it is also the role of an institution like the National Bank to explain that the world is complex. However, if you always have to get to the heart of the main things about tweets and headlines, it's no longer possible, especially in a society that is becoming more and more polarized. I will take the example of the climate. We decided that the ECB would be much more ambitious on climate than other central banks. But what we do is ultimately limited, almost symbolic. We have greened our securities purchases a little, for 2% of our collateral. I wasn't very convinced by the idea that central banks play a role in allocative efficiency, but we made the decision and we're doing it. However, NGOs in Belgium are actively campaigning against my second term. However, I have spent the last two or three years reading a lot about the climate. I think we need to do things in this area, I work a lot on the subject. I pleaded for a carbon tax, I pleaded for a carbon price, I wrote a thesis on the economics of the environment 30 years ago. I have a certain international recognition: the Peterson Institute invited me to Washington in June for the opening speech of a climate conference, followed by an interview with the economist Jean Pisani-Ferry, who is rather center-left. But if you don't agree 100% with some activists, you're on the wrong side. Because from now on, to have an impact in the media, you have to attack the person, you have to designate an enemy. This is the way our society works and it is a bit worrying. It is generally observed that in times of crisis, and this was again the case this time, Belgium resists better than its neighbours thanks to its automatic stabilisers, the automatic indexation of wages and the budgetary support of the public authorities. But we also observe that when the crisis is over, there are no measures in the opposite direction. Is this sustainable in the long term? It must indeed be symmetrical. If we want to do more in times of crisis, we need to replenish our reserves. In fact, we have done so in the past. Previous governments have taken measures to rectify the situation and restore corporate profitability. This made it possible to absorb a significant automatic indexing without too many problems. As far as public finances are concerned, Belgium has for years been one of the few countries to have achieved a primary surplus of more than 5% of its GDP. Public finance specialists know this, even at the global level! Before the covid crisis, our deficit was close to zero. This trajectory must be resumed, but it seems increasingly difficult due to the fragmentation of the political landscape. During the next legislature, you will therefore have to continue to warn every year against the slippage of public finances? I am not only a governor, I also chair the High Council of Finance. So that's my role, which I try to play in a calm and balanced way. I repeat every time that we are not going to be bankrupt in two years, but that is no excuse for doing nothing. Because at the end of the day, if we do nothing, we will hit a wall and the cost of sanitation, of rehabilitation, will weigh much more heavily on people, especially the most vulnerable. The sooner the better. We will be able to spread the effort over time, with less negative impact on people. Europe's recommendations on our budget could require the next legislature to make an effort of 25 billion? It depends on the ambition we want to have, but indeed, with no change in policy, the deficit increases from year to year by about 0.4%, so by 2 billion per year. So, over a legislature, we already need 10 billion just to stabilize the deficit. So I am asked if we have the means to make this effort. I can't say what should be done. But I can say that we have had a problem in recent years, which is that public spending systematically increases faster than growth. And this leads mathematically to a dead end. Germany, where there are also high regional inequalities, and the Netherlands have deficits clearly below 3%. Their savings are rotating. These are not social deserts. If it's feasible in their country, it must be feasible in our country. Leaving problems fallow is not unique to Belgium. ECB President Christine Lagarde, at the end of the last Governing Council meeting of the year, criticised "a certain level of procrastination" on the part of Europe on certain issues "that have been pending for far too long and are essential to support the competitiveness of the euro zone. Whether it's the Capital Markets Union, the Banking Union or the whole Market Union and the free movement of goods and services, there is still a lot of progress to be made," she says. Are you worried about that too? This speech was intentional. We discussed this in the Board of Governors. We realise, certainly in Belgium, that we are going to come up against demographic constraints more and more. We have the climate issue. We decided to be ambitious. But this will weigh on our growth potential, because it is a negative productivity shock. In Europe, we like to play the security and stability card. I believe that we are not good at disruptive industries because we don't like disruption. However, technical progress - artificial intelligence, GAFA, etc. - is increasingly disruptive. But Europe is struggling in this direction because it likes things that are predictable, under control, consensual. We can respect it. But can we at the same time want to be the most innovative region in the world? I think we will have to ask ourselves the question for a moment: are we not putting too many brakes on the dynamism of companies? Maybe the answer is no, and too bad if we are not the first on the ball. But I have the impression that sometimes we want everything and its opposite. I remember an article in the Harvard Business Review that asked this question: the fashion is for consensual management, the "manager coach", but when you look at the most successful companies, their management style is exactly the opposite. Why is that? Take Elon Musk. He did his business in the United States and then came to Europe where he is now in confrontation with the Swedish and German unions. Elon Musk would have created his business from Europe, he would not have made Tesla, or at least not in his own way. Is there a debate about the deposit facility and the remuneration, currently at 4%, of banks' excess liquidity? Some see this as a gift to banks and would like to raise the ratio of non-interest-bearing reserve requirements that banks must deposit with the Eurosystem. Which camp are you on? I think we need to sequence the debates. If we need to reduce excess liquidity, the first thing to do is to look at the PEPP (the "pandemic emergency purchase programme" launched in March 2020, editor's note) and to look at the pace at which liquidity needs to be reduced. But if we increase the reserve requirement ratio, it is a form of tax on banks: they received 4%; they will receive zero. The ECB can tax the banks, but I believe that this is more a matter for elected governments. I spent time explaining that the National Bank was making losses because our objective was to achieve 2% inflation without taking into account the impact of our instruments on our results. Now, I should explain that we can't make too many losses? The next time we do quantitative easing, the banks will say to themselves: central banks take a big position in interest rate risk, but if it goes badly, they will tax us. So we have to be very careful. I therefore think that the rules of engagement must be defined, and that taxing banks, just like taxing CO2 for that matter, is a political matter.
