Title: Where does the Belgian economy stand?
text: Speech by Jan Smets, Governor of the National Bank of Belgium, on the occasion of the Start Event 2018-2019 of the Union of Self-Employed Entrepreneurs (Unizo) Brussels, 13 September 2018 Ladies and gentlemen, I would like to thank UNIZO for inviting you to address you today on this run-off after the summer recess. Where does the Belgian economy stand? Where is she going? But also, what is needed to steer her further in the right direction? Those are the questions I want to raise today. I firmly believe that you have the same questions. I will not come up with a ready-made answer for everything. Many challenges are situated in policy areas that are not those of a central banker. But I would like to point out a few lines of action. I begin my story in the euro area because the fate of the Belgian economy is closely linked to that of the currency union to which it belongs. As you may know, this morning in the Governing Council of the ECB we decided to reduce net asset purchases to 15 billion per month from October and if everything goes as expected, we will no longer buy additional assets next year. We took that decision on the basis of the strength of the recovery in the euro area. From this, we draw confidence that inflation will converge sustainably towards our objective. The fact that the economic engine has started to run at somewhat lower speeds this year has of course not escaped our notice. Growth during the first two quarters of 2018 and the latest business cycle indicators point in this direction. Nevertheless, we think that this is mainly a normalization, after the very high growth rates at the end of 2017. For the euro area, we now expect growth to slow slightly from 2% this year to 1.7% in 2020. That is still higher than the long-term potential. Incidentally, these growth forecasts were only revised downwards to a limited extent between June and September. Also for Belgium d0 for which I do not currently have recent estimates d0 the National Bank's spring forecasts, with a growth of around 1.5%, are still fairly accurate. Moreover, partly as a result of the recovery in competitiveness, the tax shift and the activation policy, this growth is particularly labour-intensive. The normalisation of monetary policy may have begun, but, as we have explained in detail, it will be very gradual. The crisis - tomorrow it will be exactly ten years ago that Let us not forget that this crisis was primarily a financial crisis which, as you know, also hit the Belgian banking sector hard. Today, however, the excessive leverage in bank balance sheets has been reduced, solvency and liquidity have been restored and the profitability of Belgian banks is among the better in the euro area. This could be achieved without reducing the supply of credit for Belgian companies, which is one of the factors why Belgium has weathered the crisis relatively well. In addition, stricter standards for financial institutions have been developed on an international scale. In addition, banking supervision in the euro area was transferred to the Single Supervisory Mechanism and a Single Resolution Mechanism and Resolution Fund were set up. For both, the National Bank is the Belgian partner. This is an important step towards a banking union tailored to the monetary union, although this process still needs to be deepened. After all, the banking union is not yet complete today, and that is a handicap when we have to tackle the next crisis. Furthermore, as one of the important lessons we have learned from the crisis, macroprudential policy was developed to mitigate systemic risks. It is in this context that the National Bank has asked Belgian banks to create an additional buffer for their portfolio of loans for residential real estate. I am convinced that all these reforms will enable the financial system to continue to play its role as a financier of the economy. Is there no dirt in the air at all? Nothing could be further from the truth. If domestic growth dynamics remain robust in the euro area and also in our country, clouds have also appeared on the international stage. Some of them are in Europe. I am thinking of the turmoil in the financial markets over Italian fiscal policy, where the government has fortunately confirmed its commitment to debt reduction plans. And of course also to the fear of a 'no deal' Brexit. With its high degree of openness -the United Kingdom is also our fourth largest market - Belgium is vulnerable to such shocks. Many Belgian companies export - either themselves or indirectly because they are a link in the Belgian part of a wider international value chain. But there is more going on in the global economy. Protectionism is emerging for the first time in a long time, and that is a pity because it ultimately leads to loss for everyone. Higher trade tariffs will also increase prices at a time when pro-cyclical expansionary fiscal policies in the United States could already fuel inflation. This can lead to greater imbalances - in countries, but also between countries. We are already noticing that the synchronous world growth of 2017 is not being extended and that a number of emerging economies are continuing. Of course, protectionist tendencies are preferably reversed on the international stage. But at the same time, these uncertain times also indicate how important it is that we fully work on our adaptability and increase the strength of our own economy. That is a lever that we have fully in our own hands. It is the key that allows us to both deal appropriately with economic hardship and to take full advantage of the positive impulses that we also see. Digitalisation, for example, is essentially a boon for a society that has to look for productivity gains due to the ageing of its population. But it can also become a problem if the economy fails to integrate it smoothly, due to a lack of the right structures, due to inertia or because not everyone is up to date with the latest developments. For me, that is where the biggest challenge for the Belgian economy lies: making mutations run smoothly and, yes, even playing change as an asset. This requires a smooth dissemination of novelties in the economy. Initiative must be easy to develop, but equally it must be possible to deal smoothly with activities without a future. If capital and labour remain trapped there for too long, this not only has an immediate impact on productivity developments. For the long term, there is also the risk of losing touch with more promising activities. Economic growth, the employability of employees and, in combination, their remuneration therefore benefit from smooth transitions. However, I note that both the start-up rate and the cessation rate of companies in Belgium are relatively low. This may indicate that the process, which austrian economist Schumpeter called creative destruction, is insufficiently developed. Nevertheless, it is encouraging that the start-up rate of companies has recently increased and that self-employment is on the rise. In order for such transitions to run smoothly, a well-functioning labour market is crucial. I have already pointed out that in recent years there has been a strong focus on job creation. By the end of this year, there will be more than 200,000 more jobs than four years earlier and job creation will continue in the coming years, albeit at a slower pace. The unemployment rate has now fallen to 6.2% in the first quarter, compared to 8.6% in 2015. Nevertheless, some groups show a particularly low employment rate, while companies are finding it increasingly difficult to fill their vacancies. The coordination between supply and demand on the labour market is difficult and this needs to be improved. This is a story that starts with the training of young people in education d0 where early drop-out must decrease d0 then involves the stepping stone to work - for example through forms of alternating learning - and must result in lifelong learning. In this way, employees will be able to successfully work for a whole career even now that the policy is aimed at career extension. This extension is necessary in order to curb the reduction in the labour supply associated with the ageing of the population. Already today we see that, as a result of the policy pursued, the participation rate of the older age groups is rising. So a lot has already happened and a new job deal is in the pipeline. However, no effort is too much to ensure that the hitherto untapped labour potential can actually be used. This will also benefit social inclusion. After all, ensuring that everyone's talent can and remains employable in an economy that is constantly changing is the means par excellence to let everyone reap the benefits of economic and technological progress. I see other important bottlenecks where a forward-looking strategy is required. Traffic congestion is an example of this. It is a cost to companies, a burden to employees and is increasingly becoming a factor that makes investment unattractive. Energy supply is another domain with very high needs. And in both cases, economic efficiency and environmental sustainability must be reconciled. This is not an easy task, but requires creative solutions. An efficient infrastructure d0 also in domains other than the one I have mentioned d0 acts as a catalyst for economic growth and productivity. With wage moderation and tax cuts on labour, great efforts have been made in recent years to restore competitiveness in terms of wage costs. It is not just a matter of consolidating that progress now within the improved framework of the Competitiveness Act. Its effectiveness must be further strengthened by also taking due account of all other, sometimes less tangible, aspects of competitiveness, and in particular the dissemination of innovation and, of course, entrepreneurship. The investment pact presented earlier this week seems to me to be very opportune in this respect. Let me also take a moment to reflect on public finances and the role that the government has to play in supporting growth potential. By controlling government spending and reducing interest charges, the budget deficit was reduced to 1% of GDP and the dynamics of public debt were reversed, although the latter is still above 100% of GDP. At the same time, the tax shift and the corporate tax reform provided important impulses to make public spending more growth and employment-friendly. These plans cover several years and must therefore continue to be implemented, albeit in circumstances that do not jeopardise the achievement of a structural budget balance. In my opinion, there is also room on the expenditure side for growth-friendly shifts, in particular towards more public investment and - I have already mentioned this - to support labour supply. In addition, work must be done to ensure that government action is more efficient and high-quality. This not only creates budgetary margins, but will also lead to a I conclude. Ten years after the start of the crisis, the Belgian economy is doing quite well. The financial system has been restructured and prudential policy has been significantly strengthened. There has been a resumption of decent growth rates and employment is increasing sharply, partly as a result of the policy pursued. Furthermore, the budget deficit has decreased and pension reforms have significantly reduced the budgetary cost of an ageing population. However, the work is far from finished. Adjusting the biotope in which companies and employees operate in such a way that mutations run more smoothly can both increase productivity and mobilize the still untapped labour potential. The labour market deserves special attention. Removing bottlenecks in the outdated infrastructure, increasing the efficiency of government action and managing the transition to an economy that emits fewer greenhouse gases are other important challenges. This must not jeopardise the further consolidation of public finances. After all, it is time for fiscal policy to create buffers for the future. All in all, Belgium has weathered the crisis well. Let us use the better times to further strengthen ourselves structurally, and to seek maximum complementarity between the various actions d0 to increase the resilience of our economy and social inclusion.
text_original: Toespraak door Jan Smets, Gouverneur van de Nationale Bank van Belgi<91>, naar aanleiding van het Startevent 2018-2019 van de Unie van Zelfstandige Ondernemers (Unizo) Brussel, 13 september 2018 Dames en heren, Ik stel er prijs op UNIZO te danken voor de uitnodiging om vandaag het woord tot u te richten op deze rentr<8e>e na het zomerreces. Waar staat de Belgische economie? Waar gaat ze naartoe? Maar ook, wat is nodig om haar verder in de goede richting te sturen? Dat zijn de vragen die ik vandaag wil aankaarten. Ik ben er rotsvast van overtuigd dat u met dezelfde vragen zit. Ik zal niet voor alles met een pasklaar antwoord komen. Tal van uitdagingen situeren zich overigens in beleidsdomeinen die niet die van een centrale bankier zijn. Maar ik wil wel enkele krachtlijnen aangeven. Ik begin mijn verhaal in het eurogebied omdat het lot van de Belgische economie nauw verbonden is met dat van de muntunie waartoe ze behoort. Zoals u mogelijk weet, hebben we vanochtend in de Raad van Bestuur van de ECB besloten de netto-aankopen van activa vanaf oktober terug te schroeven tot 15 miljard per maand en indien alles naar verwachting verloopt, zullen we volgend jaar niet langer activa bijkopen. We hebben die beslissing genomen op grond van de kracht van het herstel in het eurogebied. Daaruit putten we het vertrouwen dat de inflatie op duurzame wijze zal convergeren naar onze doelstelling. Dat de economische motor dit jaar op wat lagere toeren is gaan draaien, is ons uiteraard niet ontgaan. De groei tijdens de eerste twee kwartalen van 2018 en de recentste conjunctuurindicatoren wijzen in die richting. Niettemin denken we dat dit vooral een normalisering is, na de wel z<8e><8e>r hoge groeicijfers aan het eind van 2017. Voor het eurogebied gaan we er nu van uit dat de groei licht vertraagt van 2 % dit jaar tot 1,7% in 2020. Dat is nog altijd hoger dan het lange termijnpotentieel. Overigens werden die groeiprognoses tussen juni en september slechts in beperkte mate neerwaarts herzien. Ook voor Belgi<91> <d0> waarvoor ik momenteel niet over recente ramingen beschik <d0> zijn de voorjaarsprognoses van de Nationale Bank, met een groei van om en bij de 1,5%, nog steeds vrij accuraat. Bovendien is die groei, mede als gevolg van het herstel van het concurrentievermogen, de taxshift en het activeringsbeleid, bijzonder arbeidsintensief. De normalisering van het monetair beleid mag dan wel begonnen zijn, toch zal ze, zoals we uitvoerig hebben toegelicht, zeer geleidelijk verlopen. De crisis - morgen is het precies tien jaar geleden dat Laten we niet vergeten dat die crisis in eerste instantie een financi<91>le crisis was die, zoals u weet, ook de Belgische banksector zwaar heeft getroffen. Vandaag is de excessieve schuldhefboom in de bankbalansen evenwel teruggeschroefd, zijn de solvabiliteit en de liquiditeit hersteld en behoort de rentabiliteit van de Belgische banken bij de betere in het eurogebied. Een en ander kon worden bewerkstelligd zonder het kredietaanbod voor Belgische bedrijven in te krimpen en dat is een van de factoren waarom Belgi<91> de crisis relatief goed heeft doorstaan. Bovendien werden op internationale schaal strengere standaarden voor de financi<91>le instellingen uitgewerkt. Daarnaast werd het bankentoezicht in het eurogebied overgeheveld naar het Gemeenschappelijk toezichtmechanisme en werden een Gemeenschappelijk resolutiemechanisme en resolutiefonds op poten gezet. Voor beide is de Nationale Bank de Belgische partner. Daarmee zijn belangrijke stappen gezet in de richting van een bankenunie op maat van de monetaire unie, al moet dat proces nog verder worden uitgediept. Vandaag is de bankenunie immers nog niet volledig, en dat is een handicap wanneer we een volgende crisis moeten aanpakken. Verder werd, als <8e><8e>n van de belangrijke lessen die we uit de crisis hebben getrokken, het macroprudentieel beleid uitgewerkt om systemische risico<d5>s in te dijken. Het is in die context dat de Nationale Bank de Belgische banken heeft gevraagd een extra buffer aan te leggen voor hun portefeuille leningen voor residentieel vastgoed. Ik ben ervan overtuigd dat al deze hervormingen het financieel stelsel in staat zullen stellen zijn rol van financier van de economie te blijven spelen. Is er dan helemaal geen vuiltje aan de lucht? Niets is minder waar. Blijft de binnenlandse groeidynamiek in het eurogebied en ook in ons land robuust, dan zijn er ook wolken verschenen op het internationale toneel. Voor een deel zitten die in Europa. Ik denk aan de onrust op de financi<91>le markten over het Italiaanse begrotingsbeleid, waar de regering gelukkig haar gehechtheid aan de plannen tot schuldvermindering heeft bevestigd. En natuurlijk ook aan de vrees voor een 'no deal' Brexit. Met zijn hoge openheidsgraad -het Verenigd Koninkrijk is bovendien onze vierde afzetmarkt - is Belgi<91> kwetsbaar voor dergelijke schokken. Vele Belgische bedrijven exporteren - ofwel zelf, ofwel indirect omdat ze een schakel zijn in het Belgische deel van een ruimere internationale waardeketen. Maar er is meer aan de hand in de wereldeconomie. Protectionisme steekt voor het eerst sinds lang de kop op, en dat is jammer want het leidt uiteindelijk tot verlies voor iedereen. Hogere handelstarieven zullen bovendien prijsverhogend werken, op een moment dat een procyclisch expansief begrotingsbeleid in de Verenigde Staten de inflatie al zou kunnen aanwakkeren. Een en ander kan uitmonden in grotere onevenwichten -in landen, maar ook tussen landen. Nu al merken we dat de synchrone wereldgroei van 2017 niet wordt doorgetrokken en dat een aantal opkomende economie<91>n door Uiteraard worden de protectionistische tendensen bij voorkeur gekeerd op het internationale toneel. Maar tegelijkertijd geven deze onzekere tijden ook aan hoe belangrijk het is dat we voluit werk maken van ons aanpassingsvermogen en de kracht van de eigen economie vergroten. Dat is een hefboom die we zelf volledig in handen hebben. Het is de sleutel die toelaat zowel gepast om te gaan met economische tegenspoed, als voluit profijt te halen uit de positieve impulsen die we eveneens zien. Digitalisering bijvoorbeeld is in wezen een zegen voor een samenleving die door de vergrijzing van haar bevolking op zoek moet gaan naar productiviteitswinst. Maar ze kan evengoed een probleem worden indien de economie er niet in slaagt ze vlot te integreren, bij gebrek aan de juiste structuren, als gevolg van inertie of omdat niet iedereen mee is met de nieuwste ontwikkelingen. Daar ligt voor mij de grootste uitdaging voor de Belgische economie: mutaties vlot laten verlopen en, ja, verandering zelfs uitspelen als troef. Daartoe is een vlotte verspreiding van nieuwigheden in de economie nodig. Initiatief moet makkelijk ontplooid kunnen worden, maar evenzeer moeten activiteiten zonder toekomst vlot kunnen worden afgewikkeld. Indien kapitaal en arbeidskrachten er te lang blijven vastzitten, heeft dat niet alleen een onmiddellijke weerslag op het productiviteitsverloop. Voor de lange termijn ontstaat ook het risico voeling te verliezen met meer belovende activiteiten. De economische groei, de inzetbaarheid van werknemers en, daarmee gepaard gaand, hun verloning zijn dan ook gebaat bij vlotte transities. Ik stel evenwel vast dat zowel de oprichtingsgraad als de stopzettingsgraad van ondernemingen in Belgi<91> relatief laag is. Dat kan erop wijzen dat het proces, dat door de Oostenrijkse econoom Schumpeter creatieve destructie werd genoemd, onvoldoende ontwikkeld is. Toch is het bemoedigend dat de oprichtingsgraad van ondernemingen recent is toegenomen en dat zelfstandige arbeid in de lift zit. Om dergelijke transities vlot te laten verlopen is een goed werkende arbeidsmarkt cruciaal. Ik heb er al op gewezen dat er de jongste jaren met succes sterk is ingezet op het scheppen van werkgelegenheid. Aan het eind van dit jaar zullen er ruim 200.000 banen meer zijn dan vier jaar eerder en de werkgelegenheidscreatie zal ook de komende jaren doorgaan, zij het in een lager tempo. De werkloosheidsgraad is inmiddels teruggevallen tot 6,2% tijdens het eerste kwartaal, terwijl die in 2015 nog 8,6% beliep. Toch vertonen sommige groepen een bijzonder lage werkzaamheidsgraad, terwijl ondernemingen het steeds moeilijker krijgen om hun vacatures op te vullen. De afstemming tussen vraag en aanbod op de arbeidsmarkt verloopt moeilijk en daar moet beterschap in komen. Dat is een verhaal dat begint bij de opleiding van jongeren in het onderwijs <d0> waar het vroegtijdig afhaken moet dalen -, vervolgens de opstap naar werk behelst - bijvoorbeeld via vormen van alternerend leren - en moet uitmonden in levenslang leren. Aldus zullen werknemers met succes een hele loopbaan lang aan de slag kunnen blijven, ook nu het beleid gericht is op loopbaanverlenging. Die verlenging is nodig om de verschraling van het arbeidsaanbod die met de vergrijzing van de bevolking gepaard gaat, in te dijken. Vandaag al zien we dat, ingevolge het gevoerde beleid, de participatiegraad van de oudere leeftijdsgroepen de hoogte in gaat. Er is dus al heel wat gebeurd en een nieuwe jobdeal staat in de steigers. Geen inspanning is echter te veel om ervoor te zorgen dat het tot op vandaag onaangesproken arbeidspotentieel daadwerkelijk kan worden benut. Dat zal ook de maatschappelijke inclusie ten goede komen. Ervoor zorgen dat eenieders talent inzetbaar is <8e>n blijft in een economie die voortdurend verandert, is immers het middel bij uitstek om iedereen mee de vruchten van de economische en technologische vooruitgang te laten plukken. Ik zie nog andere belangrijke knelpunten waar een toekomstgerichte strategie zich opdringt. De verkeerscongestie is daar een voorbeeld van. Ze is een kost voor de ondernemingen, een last voor de werknemers en wordt steeds meer een factor die investeren onaantrekkelijk maakt. Energiebevoorrading is een ander domein met zeer grote noden. En in beide gevallen moeten economische effici<91>ntie en ecologische duurzaamheid met elkaar in overeenstemming worden gebracht. Dat is geen eenvoudige opdracht, maar vereist creatieve oplossingen. Een effici<91>nte infrastructuur <d0> ook in andere domeinen dan die welke ik heb aangehaald <d0> werkt als een katalysator voor economische groei en productiviteit. Met de loonmatiging en de lastenverlagingen op arbeid zijn er de jongste jaren grote inspanningen geleverd om de concurrentiekracht inzake loonkosten opnieuw te herstellen. Het is niet alleen zaak die vooruitgang nu te consolideren binnen het verbeterde raamwerk van de wet op het concurrentievermogen. De slagkracht ervan moet verder versterkt worden door ook voldoende oog te hebben voor alle andere, soms minder tastbare, aspecten van de competitiviteit, en met name de verspreiding van innovatie en, natuurlijk, ondernemerschap. Het eerder deze week gepresenteerde investeringspact lijkt me in dat opzicht heel opportuun. Laat me ook even stilstaan bij de overheidsfinanci<91>n en de rol die voor de overheid is weggelegd in het ondersteunen van het groeipotentieel. Door een beheersing van de overheidsuitgaven en de daling van de rentelasten werd het begrotingstekort teruggebracht tot 1% bbp en werd de dynamiek van de overheidsschuld omgebogen, al bedraagt die laatste nog steeds meer dan 100% bbp. Tegelijk werden met de taxshift en de hervorming van de vennootschapsbelasting belangrijke impulsen gegeven om het overheidsbeslag groei- en werkgelegenheidsvriendelijker te maken. Die plannen beslaan meerdere jaren en moeten dus verder worden uitgevoerd, zij het in omstandigheden die de realisatie van een structureel begrotingsevenwicht niet in het gedrang brengen. Naar mijn oordeel is er ook aan de uitgavenzijde ruimte voor groeivriendelijke verschuivingen, meer bepaald in de richting van meer overheidsinvesteringen en - ik heb het daar al over gehad - ter ondersteuning van het arbeidsaanbod. Bovendien moet werk gemaakt worden van een effici<91>nter en kwaliteitsvoller overheidsoptreden. Zulks cre<91>ert niet alleen budgettaire marges, maar zal ook tot een Ik concludeer. Tien jaar na het begin van de crisis gaat het vrij goed met de Belgische economie. Het financieel systeem is geherstructureerd en het prudentieel beleid is aanzienlijk versterkt. Er is opnieuw aangeknoopt met behoorlijke groeicijfers en de werkgelegenheid neemt sterk toe, mede ingevolge het gevoerde beleid. Verder is het begrotingstekort teruggelopen en hebben de pensioenhervormingen de budgettaire kost van de vergrijzing aanzienlijk verlicht. Het werk is evenwel lang niet af. De biotoop waarin bedrijven en werknemers opereren z<97> bijsturen dat mutaties vlotter verlopen, kan zowel de productiviteit verhogen als het nog onaangesproken arbeidspotentieel mobiliseren. De arbeidsmarkt verdient daarbij bijzondere aandacht. Knelpunten in de verouderde infrastructuur verhelpen, de effici<91>ntie van het overheidsoptreden vergroten en de transitie naar een economie die minder broeikasgassen uitstoot in goede banen leiden, zijn andere belangrijke uitdagingen. Een en ander mag de verdere gezondmaking van de overheidsfinanci<91>n niet in het gedrang brengen. Voor het begrotingsbeleid is het immers tijd om buffers voor de toekomst aan te leggen. Belgi<91> heeft de crisis al bij al goed doorstaan. Laat ons de betere tijden aangrijpen om ons verder structureel te versterken, en maximaal complementariteit te zoeken tussen de verschillende acties <d0> om de veerkracht van onze economie <8e>n de maatschappelijke inclusie te vergroten.

Title: What are the challenges for economic policies, now and in the future?
text: 16/05/2019 What are the challenges for economic policy, today and tomorrow? Quels defis pour les politiques economiques, aujourd'hui et demain? Speech following the lunch conference of the Cercle de Lorraine, Brussels, 16 May 2019 Pierre Wunsch, Governor of the National Bank of Belgium Ladies and gentlemen, It is with pleasure that I address you. I would like to talk about the main challenges for economic policy, starting with those of a cyclical nature because they are the most urgent today. It is also on this cyclical dimension that the focus of monetary policy lies. Indeed, economic developments in the euro area and, linked to this, the convergence of inflation towards the objective of price stability determine the decisions of the Governing Council of the ECB. However, I would like to add at the outset that many policy challenges are structural in nature. I am thinking, for example, of the need to take further steps towards an inclusive labour market, of the impact of the digital revolution, of the ageing of the population, as well as of global warming. I will come back to that later. We are living  and I say this without any exaggeration  in a particularly uncertain time from an economic point of view. Protectionism is regaining new life, after a long period of economic advances and innovations fuelled by the success of free trade and globalisation. Not only is a trade war threatening to break out between the US and China, but trade with the EU is also in the crosshairs. China's economy is also facing significant challenges of a more domestic nature: the debt ratio of state-owned enterprises is rising rapidly and the country has embarked on a profound transition aimed at reducing dependence on exports and investment. All these factors have caused a considerable slowdown in growth. Other emerging economies, such as Argentina and Turkey, are also facing severe difficulties. Closer to home, uncertainty about Brexit remains high. Moreover, many national democracies - not just the British ones - are finding it increasingly difficult to pursue decisive policies. There is a feeling among the population that globalisation has been at the expense of reduced control, increased inequality and an inability to meet the demands for living standards. This affects trust and leads to immobilism. Investments suffer greatly from that kind of uncertainty. In this context, economic activity in the euro area surprised unfavourably from the second half of last year, whereas it had achieved particularly solid results before. This weakening was partly due to more specific factors in some countries or sectors. This is why it was initially assumed that the incidence would be short-lived. Gradually, however, the slowdown in growth proved to be more persistent. In particular, trade, and with it activity in manufacturing, declined sharply. Given its current account surplus, the euro area is particularly exposed. Germany in the first place, exports and manufacturing industry occupy a prominent place and exports also focus heavily on capital goods, cars and the Chinese market. The German engine of growth was therefore the first to stall, but with repercussions in other euro area countries. In fact, they are largely integrated into the value chains that feed the German manufacturing industry. As a result, trade flows within the euro area have also contracted significantly. Until the end of 2018, the Belgian economy slowed down more slowly, in particular because it had benefited less from the strong surge in exports in 2017. In the first quarter, however, growth returned to 0.2% on a quarterly basis. Nevertheless, it seems that the spring projections currently being prepared by the SNB's staff will only need to be revised down slightly from the previous growth estimate of 1.4% for 2019. Indeed, signs of resilience are also emerging. Activity indicators in the services sector are holding up much better, as is domestic demand, which is supported by rising wage increases and continued strong job creation. Despite the slowdown in growth, the unemployment rate in the euro area continued to contract, returning to 7.7% in March. In Belgium too, employment has continued to recover and the unemployment rate has since fallen to 5.7%. Half a century ago such a low rate was no longer observed in Belgium. The favorable financial conditions are another supporting factor. The Eurosystem's monetary policy in recent years has not only provided a strong stimulus, it has also been able to maintain that stimulus in the difficult circumstances of recent months. In response to the deteriorating cyclical environment, the Governing Council announced last March that policy rates will remain at their current levels at least until the end of 2019, and in any case for as long as necessary to ensure a sustained convergence of inflation to levels below, but close to, 2 % over the medium term. Previously, that was until the summer of 2019. A new series of tltros (targeted longer-term refinancing operations) was also announced. With both the growth and inflation projections set to decline further, the Governing Council stands ready to adjust all its instruments if necessary. This realization has led to a further fall in interest rates on the financial markets. Moreover, unlike at the end of last year, risk premiums have remained low. These developments provide a powerful counterbalance and help support growth and inflation. While smoothing the business cycle and seeking price stability are important goals, they are not enough to achieve a well-functioning and inclusive economy that also addresses the many long-term challenges. This requires the use of other economic policy levers, mainly at national level. It may seem contradictory to stress the importance of national economic policies in a globalized world, but this is not the case. The sometimes widespread idea that we have become victims of globalization, that it would leave us destitute to face the challenges of tomorrow, seems to me both false and dangerous. False because national policies always make a difference! One only has to look at the disparities within the European Union to be convinced of this. Also, whether we are talking about training, climate issues, the functioning of the labour market, social protection or innovation, it is almost always the same countries that are cited as examples: Denmark, Finland, Sweden. Or small economies open to the world... This is obviously no coincidence! A misconception, therefore, that would make us helpless victims... But also dangerous if it becomes an excuse to justify immobility or lack of choice. So, yes, Belgium can do more and better. And our starting point is also quite favorable: we enjoy a high level of productivity, a skilled workforce and, unlike in other countries, we have not seen a sharp rise in income inequality in recent decades. The reforms initiated since the crisis are also moving in the right direction. One area in which great strides have been made is the labour market. In the last four years, 220,000 jobs have been created in Belgium. The economic recovery that followed the crisis has contributed greatly to this, but economic growth is also much more job-intensive than before. This last point is undoubtedly due to the policy pursued to stimulate both the demand for and the supply of labour. The strengthening of competitiveness, the tax shift, the activation of managers and the lengthening of careers have all contributed to the exceptional growth in employment. Over time, these developments have also led to changes in our vision of the labour market. At the end of my studies, the idea was still widespread that the volume of work was determined and that unemployment could be combated by containing the supply of work (by means of early retirement or reduction of working hours). But the reality is quite different. It is now clear that a broadening of the labour supply may indeed be accompanied by a reduction in chage. This benefits not only the economy, but also social cohesion. Having a job increases social inclusion, reduces the risk of poverty and strengthens the basis for public administrations to finance their missions. Nevertheless, the underutilized labour potential in Belgium remains large, so that there is still room for improvement. All in all, only 70 % of the population aged between 20 and 64 is in work. In Brussels and Wallonia, the low employment rate is the result of both a low participation rate and a high unemployment rate. In Flanders, on the other hand, the unemployment rate is low, but the participation rate remains weak. The shortage on the labour market is the most pronounced. This increases the chance of an acceleration of wage increases. In the companies, sectors or regions that are growing strongly and are confronted with shortages, this is normal. Higher wages can help attract those sought, either from sectors or locations where unemployment is prevalent, or by encouraging more people to enter the labour market. However, these wage increases should not automatically be copied in places where the economy is not doing so well. That would only increase their own problems and weaken the incentives for more labour mobility. In a labour market that is tightening and at the same time showing large differences in both sectoral and geographical dimensions, this should be an important focus in order to be able to perpetuate job creation. Another point of attention is the impact of technological progress and digitalization on our economies. In recent months, we have all been able to read in the media the long list of jobs that would be will disappear in the coming years: accountants, documentalists, cashiers... most routine tasks would be threatened. This impression that technical progress has never been so rapid and threatening is a source of concern for many people. Paradoxically, however, we are currently seeing the opposite: in reality, job creation has rarely been so vigorous and productivity developments so weak. Thus, technical progress measured at the macroeconomic level is now close to zero! The challenge is therefore to find the path of faster productivity gains. Once the labour potential is fully mobilized, these gains are indeed the only sustainable source of economic growth and income generation. Put more clearly, without productivity gains, no long-term growth, no sustainable wage increases or increased purchasing power. With this in mind, the increasing digitalisation of our economy is an opportunity to be seized. It will naturally leave its mark on the labour market. Some jobs will indeed disappear, but others will develop in their place. The nature of employment is also likely to change, with the pressure of our predictable career model, largely based on seniority. The training challenge therefore goes beyond learning digital techniques as such  even if it remains important  and must be broadened in order to allow workers to remain open to change. This implies a less linear view of our professional life and the evolution towards continuous learning. Productivity gains also need to be made as the ageing of the population increasingly depresses labour supply. Moreover, there is no escaping a continuation of the policy of career extension. Here too, important steps have already been taken and we see the employment rate of the older age groups steadily increasing. This will increase once the pension reform reaches cruising speed. The benefits are twofold: with more people in work, the capacity to pay pensions increases, while at the same time keeping the number of pensioners in check. This is much more favourable for purchasing power than a scenario in which the pension reform would place the full weight on the amount of the benefit. And not reforming or scaling back reforms will inevitably compromise the sustainability of public finances or lead to other policy priorities, such as education, infrastructure or the energy transition, being pushed into the background. Let us not forget that budgetary expenditure related to ageing is already increasing by 0.2 percentage points of GDP per year. By 2040, they will be more than 3 percentage points higher than today. That is why it is so important that buffers for the future are created at budgetary level and that a credible path towards a structural budget balance is put in place as soon as possible. This would also provide more margin to absorb periods of cyclical downturn. To conclude, I would like to say a few words about the climate issue. I am afraid that this is hardly original. And it might give the impression that I'm succumbing to a fad. Nevertheless, I am convinced that the subject is important and confronts us with enormous challenges. As proof, the SNB will devote its next colloquium to this theme. What to tell you that has not already been said? I believe above all that this is a subject of extreme complexity that does not fit well with a reduction to a few slogans. How best to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, or at the lowest cost? It is a question that concerns many aspects of our economic life: our production methods, our energy mix, or the response to our mobility and housing needs... However, to date, the debate cannot, in my view, be sufficiently based on a clear analytical framework with a sufficiently broad consensus. Two quick examples in this area. First example: we have tried to explain, at the National Bank, the very sharp rise in real estate prices in Belgium in recent years. We came to the conclusion that 75% of this increase was explained by the increase in the price of building land. In other words, the desire to densify buildings for the purposes of mobility and environmental protection may lead to problems of access to housing if we are not careful. A comprehensive approach is therefore needed. Second example: the government recently asked us if we could simulate the proposals made under the climate pact. Our answer: unfortunately no. Our models are not granular enough to do this. For the time being, the empirical material available to support the debate is therefore not sufficient. In addition, the temporal dimension is essential. Once a certain threshold is reached, global warming risks turning into an irreversible process. Therefore, it is a priori important to obtain results relatively quickly. On the other hand, taking more time would allow more benefit from technological advances, which could facilitate the transition and make it less coeuse. Moreover, technological progress and its diffusion are not independent of the policy pursued and have everything to gain from a clear framework, setting guidelines for a long time. Beyond the political debate, a major analytical effort is therefore necessary, involving intense coordination at the Belgian level. To close the circle, I would like to return to monetary policy and address the question of whether it is necessary to print money for the climate. The idea looks attractive, partly because of its simplicity. In reality, however, it is not that simple. After all, let us not forget that monetary policy is already very accommodative today. To put it bluntly, a lot of money has already been created. Indeed, between March 2015 and December 2018, the Eurosystem purchased assets on a large scale in order to ensure further quantitative easing at a time when the policy rate was already negative. Even though net purchases have stopped, the program itself is far from over. After all, the portfolio of purchased assets will be kept fully up to date for some time to come. This perpetuates its downward impact on financing conditions, which is and remains an important component of our monetary policy calibration. The assets held by the Eurosystem are of secondary importance. Because central bank purchases give rise to a whole series of portfolio rearrangements, they basically affect the price of all assets and lead to a generalized easing of financing conditions. In other words, the central bank does not necessarily have to buy so-called climate-friendly assets so that they benefit from the easing and would provide an incentive for such investments. So there is already an incentive today. Let that be clear. What is missing, and this is exactly the point I have just made, is an integrated vision that gives investors clear direction so that this incentive actually results in investments. Achieving this is not the task of the central bank, but is intrinsically within the competence of the elected governments. Thank you for your attention.

Speech naar aanleiding van de lunchconferentie van de Club van Lotharingen/Le Cercle de Lorraine, Brussel, 16 mei 2019 Pierre Wunsch, gouverneur van de Nationale Bank van Belgi<91> Dames en heren, Het is met genoegen dat ik het woord tot u richt. Title: Current and emerging challenges for monetary policy
text: Ladies and gentlemen It is a pleasure for me to participate in this conference. I would like to thank the organisers for inviting me to share some considerations on the topic "Current and emerging challenges for monetary policy". In my presentation, I will not limit myself to the current issues  and there are many of them. I will also address some of the new challenges facing monetary policy in the near future where more reflection, research and debate is needed. PP 2 1. THE CURRENT MACROECONOMIC SITUATION, THE EUROSYSTEM'S PROJECTIONS AND THE RISK ASSESSMENT But first I would like to focus on the challenges that the current macroeconomic situation presents for monetary policy in the euro area. PP 3 As you know, the euro area has gone through two crises  the global financial crisis in 2008 and the sovereign debt crisis around 2012  but it has shown positive growth over the past six years. There is no doubt that the economy has benefited from a robust recovery, thanks in part to our supportive monetary policy measures. The growth rate for the first quarter of 2019 turned out to be higher than expected, and was supported by strong domestic demand, particularly consumption. The labour-intensive services sector, by far the largest sector in the euro area economy, also continues to grow. In a context of good performance in the domestic economy, the unemployment rate continues to decline: in April, it stood at 7.6%, its lowest level since August 2008, i.e. since the early stages of the crisis. In this tighter labour market, wages continue to rise. In terms of employment, we are now in a better position than we have ever been in the last ten years. Despite these positive developments, several reasons for concern remain. Economic growth has slowed since the end of 2017. While some slowdown could be expected after a fairly long period of expansion, economic indicators have sent worrying signals since 2018. This is also reflected in the Eurosystem's latest macroeconomic projections, which show a slowdown in the recovery for 2019 and beyond. In addition, these projections carry risks that could further weaken economic activity. We face significant uncertainties related to the continued threat of protectionism, as well as broader geopolitical uncertainties. Their persistence is already weighing on the euro area economy, and on the manufacturing sector in particular. This could lead to the paralysis of investment and the decline in world trade. For a central bank whose main objective is to ensure price stability, the behaviour of inflation is very important. And here too, there are reasons to worry. The risk of deflation disappeared after the 2015 launch of the asset purchase programme, but euro area inflation remains low despite the economic recovery: total inflation fell to 1.2% in May. This level is still too low compared to our definition of price stability  that is, below, but close to, 2% in the medium term. Excluding the more volatile components of the overall indicator (i.e. food and energy), inflation has hovered around 1 per cent for most of the past six years. These developments are somewhat difficult to interpret. As I mentioned, the deceleration in growth and the persistence of uncertainties may explain, to some extent, slightly lower inflation rates than expected. Nevertheless, recent economic weakness seems insufficient to justify the extent to which and the duration of inflation remains disconnected from our target, given the strong recovery and dynamic labour market that the euro area has enjoyed in recent years. When thinking about inflation, usually in the context of a Phillips curve, it is important not only to consider the cyclical state of the economy. The trend level of inflation  where it would be on the horizon when all shocks have dissipated  is also important. The absence of inflation despite a long recovery could mean that it has fallen. This could be explained by the fact that a very long period of low  too low  inflation may have contaminated the expectations of the general public in this regard: financial markets, but also companies and workers, who negotiate wages taking into account how they think inflation will evolve. A perceived decline in trend inflation would be of great concern to the ECB, as it would further complicate the achievement of the inflation target. PP 4 How concerned should we be? The analysis of the behaviour of inflation expectations, especially at more distant horizons, is an essential ingredient of such an assessment. Prices for long-term inflation protection in financial markets, such as inflation swap markets, which had recovered somewhat since the end of 2016, started to fall again at the end of last year. If we take them literally, their recent levels and developments are indeed a source of concern. However, surveyed inflation expectations have remained at levels closer to our definition of price stability. It is possible that the difference between the signals relating to market-based and survey-based inflation expectations is related to the presence of risk premia  in this case, negative inflation risk premia  that weigh on inflation swap prices. To some extent, this situation could be seen as encouraging: we can say that true inflation expectations are not too low and remain well anchored. However, the presence of such negative premiums could be a concern in itself: they may indicate that if lower-than-expected inflation rates were to emerge, this would happen in times of adverse economic conditions. 2. THE GOVERNING COUNCIL ADOPTED ADDITIONAL MEASURES Of course, the Governing Council of the ECB is concerned about these developments. That is why we have taken additional measures in recent months that will continue to support the euro area economy and create the necessary conditions for inflation to return to a level close to 2%. PP 5 First, we have decided to extend the period during which policy rates will remain at their current, historically low levels. In March, this period was extended until the end of 2019. In June, as it turned out that the uncertainties I mentioned were not a temporary phenomenon, we extended it until at least the first half of 2020; and, in any case, for as long as it is necessary to ensure that inflation continues to converge steadily towards our target. Extending this period will also extend the period during which we will reinvest in full the principal of the bonds acquired under the asset purchase program, when they mature. Indeed, full reinvestments will continue for an extended period beyond the date on which we begin to raise policy rates. This will ensure that financial conditions remain very favourable: maintaining this large stock of assets on the Eurosystem's balance sheet contributes to lower term premiums. This reduces the level of long-term rates, which are relevant to the investment and consumption decisions of households, corporations and governments. PP 6 Second, we have decided to propose a new round of targeted longer-term refinancing operations, or TLTROs, to be launched in September. These operations provide liquidity to euro area banks, in order to prevent them from suffering financing constraints that could lead them to limit their lending to households and businesses. The final details of these operations were decided a few weeks ago. The base borrowing rate is 10 basis points above the average MRO rate observed over the two-year term. Like their predecessors, TLTRO-III allows banks to benefit from a lower rate if their lending is sufficiently dynamic. This favorable rate can go down to 10 basis points above the (average) deposit facility rate. TLTRO-III will therefore be relatively generous compared to alternative sources of funding. In this way, they will support growth and inflation in the euro area by maintaining accommodative financing conditions for the private sector. In addition, the Governing Council is determined to act if adverse circumstances materialise. In such a case, we would be prepared to adjust all instruments in order to continue to support the economy and the convergence of inflation towards our target. If necessary, we could consider further extending the forward guidance, but also resuming net asset purchases or lowering rates again. At the same time, we must ensure that all of our policies remain effective and continue to support growth and inflation. This can be particularly relevant when it comes to negative rates: in some cases, they could threaten money transmission by banks or lead to financial instability. That is why we continue to monitor their impact. PP 7 Indeed, these negative nominal rates are peculiar, as many depositors and investors would prefer to hold cash rather than receive a negative return. At the same time, banks want to prevent their customers from withdrawing their money, to avoid facing insufficient or less stable funding. As a result, they have been reluctant to apply negative rates to certain categories of retail deposits. This implies that negative rates are not fully reflected in all bank funding costs. Banks with a higher percentage of personal deposits may be the most exposed to such an effect: the share of funding for which costs remain at or above zero is larger. In Belgium, regulated savings accounts, which account for a quarter of banks' funding, must  legally  offer a positive interest rate of at least 0.11%, 51 basis points higher than the current rate on the ECB's deposit facility. This limits the benefits that banks can derive from lower funding costs. Ultimately, the impact may extend beyond credit institutions to their customers. If banks lower their lending rates in line with policy rates and market rates, their interest margins could come under pressure. Ultimately, their profitability could suffer. In extreme scenarios, in order to avoid this negative impact on their profits, banks could decide to reduce (or even increase) their lending rates less. As a result, the cost of debt financing would rise for households and businesses, depriving them of the benefits of loosening monetary policy. The story does not end with this possible effect on the profits of banking institutions, nor does it necessarily materialize immediately after the introduction of negative rates. Negative interest rates affect banks' profitability through different channels, which have different dynamic profiles. As a rule, profits materialize in the first place, while losses extend over a longer period. For example, credit institutions finance themselves largely through short-term debt, the prices of which adjust immediately to a fall in interest rates. Their holdings are generally longer-term assets and, initially, interest margins widen. However, as assets are replaced by other assets with lower returns, margins tighten. Also, the lower the interest rates or the lower the interest rates, the greater the potential negative impact on the profits of institutions. That is why we believe it is important to closely monitor the profitability of banks in order to avoid a situation in which our measures could have a negative, rather than a positive, impact on the macroeconomy. So far, there is no evidence that negative interest rates impede the transmission of monetary policy in the euro area, either by restricting borrowing or driving up lending rates. Lending rates have fallen in the wake of the cuts in policy rates and remain at unprecedented low levels. Business credit has evolved in a manner consistent with the business cycle. In fact, in recent years, banks' profitability has benefited from renewed momentum in economic growth and loan demand, as well as a decrease in the risk of default among borrowers, and Belgium has been no exception. However, this situation could change, in particular if adverse events materialise and the Governing Council were consequently led to further lower policy rates or further extend the period of low interest rates. If we were to observe that negative interest rates could begin to hamper the transmission of monetary policy to the real economy, we could consider adopting compensatory measures to ensure that our policy rates do not become restrictive; in other words, to ensure that households and businesses continue to benefit from our measures. However, while the banking sector plays a fundamental role in the transmission of monetary policy in the euro area, it is not the only channel through which our measures have their impact. Negative interest rates also make market financing cheaper for the public sector (relieving fiscal policies) as well as for many private sector entities, especially companies. Even if downward pressure from negative interest rates on banks' profitability were to limit their transmission to borrowing  and this is only an assumption for the time being  negative policy rates would still have a largely positive impact on macroeconomics. In addition, negative interest rates are only one measure among all those we are putting in place at the moment. The securities acquired by the Eurosystem, our forward-looking guidance and the provision of financing to banks at negative rates are all contributing to supporting growth and inflation and to reducing banks' funding costs. Through these channels, these measures can contribute positively to banks' profitability, even in the event that banks no longer benefit from the policy of negative interest rates. As I indicated earlier, banks can respond to a likely squeeze on their profits by raising their lending rates. Another possibility is for banks to come to run greater risks, by extending their credit, so that they can compensate for the tightening of margins with larger volumes. From a monetary policy perspective, this can be a positive development: it can counteract too little risk-taking and facilitate access to credit for businesses and households. But this behavior has the disadvantage that banks may have to take "excessive" risks, which would increase financial instability. However, this scenario is not reserved for credit institutions or negative interest rates. Similar behaviour could also be observed in other financial markets when interest rates are very low, especially if they remain at this level over an extended period of time. In such cases, prudential (and I am focusing on macroprudential) and supervisory policies are the first line of defence: by targeting specific pockets of risk without having to tighten the stance of monetary policy, they avoid stifling the positive impact of low interest rates on the economy. Prudential policies can therefore provide additional scope for monetary policy to remain adequately accommodative. It is in this context that the National Bank of Belgium, like several of its counterparts, has adopted a series of macroprudential measures  the last of which was a year ago  to ensure that banks remain well protected, in particular against risks related to the residential real estate market. In addition, the NBB is ready to activate the countercyclical capital buffer in response to the acceleration of the credit cycle. Banks are required to build up additional capital buffers based on loans they grant to the Belgian non-financial private sector. Thus, they are better equipped to deal with adverse shocks and to absorb credit losses, which safeguards the provision of credit to the real economy throughout the cycle. PP 8 3. NEW CHALLENGES FOR MONETARY POLICY These are the most immediate challenges we face today. However, these are part of a context of other, more structural transformations that could strongly influence monetary policy in the coming decades. PP 9 The first of these "new" developments that I will mention is not, strictly speaking, entirely new since it has been observed throughout the last 30 years. This is the decline and the current very low level of natural or equilibrium real interest rates. There are many definitions of this abstract concept. In the current context, it can be seen as the interest rate that balances the supply of savings and the demand for investment in the economy. At this equilibrium point, the economy is growing at its potential pace and inflation is stable. In recent decades, the global supply of savings has increased, while the demand for investment has declined. Demographic changes, inequality, falling prices of capital goods and declining public investment, among other factors, may explain these trends. As a result, the natural interest rate has slowly moved downwards. When the crisis erupted, cyclical obstacles exacerbated this decline. The estimates shown on the graph  mostly made in the context of a European task force to which Bank experts have also contributed  reflect this development for the euro area over the past 20 years. Why is this situation problematic? To stimulate the economy in times of crisis, central banks lower real rates below the level of the natural rate. But policy rates cannot sink too far into negative territory. As we have seen before, a very negative rate, or even a slightly negative rate maintained for a very long time, could tighten rather than ease financial conditions. If inflation is also low, which is usually the case during crises, central banks may not have enough room for manoeuvre. Continued weakness in the natural rate could increasingly hamper monetary policy. To ensure an adequate stance, central banks may have no choice but to extend the period of low policy rates further or to resort to other means, such as asset purchases. These measures lower long-term rates rather than short-term rates. However, if they have been effective in recent years, they are not unlimited in all cases and, if they are implemented very often or over long periods of time, they can have undesirable side effects. As I have said before, prudential policies (and, in particular, macroprudential policies) could help limit these side effects, allowing monetary policy to remain accommodative for longer. But they could also prove useful in another, more preventive way: by increasing the resilience of the financial system, prudential policies could help avoid crises. In this way, monetary policy would have to be used less often and the effective lower bound of nominal interest rates would be reached less frequently. Other policy areas also have a key role to play. Structural measures, in particular, can help to increase potential output and thus raise the equilibrium rate, for example by promoting productivity and competition. Indeed, advanced economies, including Belgium, have seen a slowdown in employment growth and total factor productivity. Reversing this trend would not only be beneficial for prosperity as such, it could also have a positive impact on the conduct of monetary policy. Fiscal policies can play multiple roles. Ex ante, sound public finances help reduce the likelihood of crises, as the public sector is more resilient to shocks. Ex post, fiscal policies can play an important stabilizing role: and, the healthier the ex-ante fiscal situation, the more room there is to assume this role. In the current context, this means that countries with fiscal space can use it  and they should when growth is below potential  when needed to support monetary policy. Finally, monetary policy should also be open to adapting its strategy, if necessary, to the new conditions created by a permanent reduction in the natural rate. In this regard, I note with great interest the CURRENT review by the US Federal Reserve of its monetary policy strategy, including the impressive academic work done in this context. Further discussions will help us better understand the options available for monetary policy to remain effective in the context of the so-called "new normal." Under our current strategy, it is clear that pursuing our inflation target of close to 2% symmetrically is a prerequisite for safeguarding enough room for monetary policy. Further debate and analysis is also greatly needed for central banks to meet the next two challenges I would like to mention today. PP 10 The first concerns the diffusion of new technologies and the transition to the digital economy. Digitalisation could affect the conduct of monetary policy in the coming years, through its impact on potential output, the break-even rate and inflation dynamics. Its ultimate impact, however, is uncertain at this time. Several possibilities can materialize. For example, digitalization could increase productivity or increase competition, as consumers can now access and compare more online sellers. Both higher productivity and increased competition could translate into lower prices and higher output. Especially when total demand recovers at the same pace as supply, this is undoubtedly an encouraging development, which should lead to an increase in equilibrium interest rates. However, as I have already mentioned, productivity growth has weakened in most advanced economies, including Belgium. This raises a paradox: while workers fear that robots will take their jobs, job growth is surprisingly dynamic and it is the evolution of productivity that is disappointing. Further research, particularly in the area of productivity measurement in the digital age, is needed to understand how these phenomena will manifest themselves. In addition, while new technologies could intensify competition in some sectors (such as retail), they could have the opposite effect in others: for example, if technologies lead to higher fixed costs, this will promote economies of scale. This "superstar effect" could hamper competition and growth, while prices would rise, amounting to a negative supply shock. Of course, the impact may also depend, to a large extent, on how authorities respond to these new developments, for example by adapting competition or labour market regulations. In any case, a more in-depth analysis is still needed to understand all the implications that the current technological development process will have for the economy and for monetary policy. PP 11 Another challenge with equally uncertain consequences for monetary policy is climate change. Last year, when he was awarded the Alfred Nobel Prize in Economics, Professor Nordhaus called it "the ultimate challenge for the economy." I fully agree: its impact could be enormous, profound and long-lasting. I do not pretend to provide here a complete analysis of the consequences of climate change. In many ways, we are still studying what they would be. Instead, I will look at some of the main channels through which climate change and the policies adopted to combat it could affect the economy, and what this could mean for monetary policy. Climate change covers various phenomena related to global warming, such as sea level rise, more extreme weather events and related natural disasters; climate change in some regions could induce strong waves of migration and reduce agricultural production. All of this could translate into price increases, permanent economic losses, lower productivity and investment, and greater financial instability, all in a context of heightened uncertainty. In the euro area, the impact could be more negative for the countries of the South than for those of the North, which would exacerbate fragmentation. However, efforts to reduce fossil fuel consumption and avoid such disastrous outcomes can also have far-reaching economic repercussions. A transition to a greener economy will involve profound changes in current economic structures and relative prices. Some technologies may not be sufficiently advanced to ensure that greener energy will ensure a similar level of production. In this case, growth would decline in the short term, while prices would rise. The more sudden the transition, the higher the risks. At the same time, investment in new technologies could also be a source of economic prosperity to maintain sustainable living standards. Like digitalization, climate change raises fundamental questions about the measurement of macroeconomic aggregates, such as output and inflation. For example, we can think of how a (hypothetical) regulation that forces households to switch to more expensive electric cars would affect the consumer price index. Electric cars will replace gasoline-powered cars in the price index as if they were a different product: in this case, the price index will not jump. The negative effect on household purchasing power is therefore not visible in the consumer price index. This is of course not a new phenomenon, but it could happen more often as regulations force the abandonment of carbon-based technologies. These issues should be considered to ensure that our measures of inflation continue to reflect economic realities. While the ultimate impact of climate change and policies to mitigate it remains uncertain, it will be a key driver of economic (and social) change in the coming decades. Even if the transition to cleaner energy sources were perfect, it could have far-reaching consequences for economic policy. The authorities, including central banks, should not neglect this. But what can central banks do about it? Like other institutions, businesses and even households, central banks can adopt a more sustainable behavior on a daily basis. For many years, the National Bank of Belgium has been involved in initiatives to make it more environmentally friendly. It has obtained three stars in the "Ecodynamic Company" label of the Brussels Region and is a certified "CO2 neutral" company. Last year, the Bank integrated the use of environmental, social and governance criteria into the management of a non-monetary policy portion of its portfolio to help support the transition to a more sustainable financial model. Together with other central banks, the Bank participates in international groups to learn more about the risks and consequences of climate change and the transition to a greener economy. For example, we participate in the Network for Greening the Financial System, a network of 40 central banks and supervisors whose mission is to identify and promote best practices and conduct analytical work on the issue. The Bank will also dedicate its 2020 International Conference to the potential impact of climate change on macroeconomics and financial markets. In its role as supervisor and macroprudential authority, the Bank has taken action to identify, measure, manage and mitigate financial stability risks related to climate change. In addition to these initiatives, central banks were called upon to do more, including through the use of monetary policy instruments. As we shall see, a number of these proposals would pose significant problems for the conduct of monetary policy. I will go through some of them, ranging from the narrowest to the broadest actions. A first option is to adjust the valuation of assets used as collateral, taking into account the higher implicit risk that surrounds industries with higher carbon emissions. For example, assets related to "brown" activities would suffer a higher discount. As a result, banks that give them as collateral would receive less liquidity in exchange. This would better protect central banks against the risks of climate change. But it would also encourage banks to hold "green" bonds, making it cheaper to finance green sectors. However, there is, at this stage, no standard on how to properly define green and brown assets, and climate-related risks have not (yet) been incorporated into risk assessments. Central banks could either wait for credit rating agencies to incorporate these risks or take the initiative to assess them themselves. A bolder proposal suggests reorienting our monetary policy portfolios towards low-carbon assets. As I am sure you are aware, the Eurosystem holds a large stock of bonds as a result of purchases made to support the rise of inflation towards its target. The Eurosystem holds almost 20% of all eligible green bonds under the corporate sector purchase programme, amounting to around 2 billion. This amount shall be proportional to the share of green bonds in the bond market eligible under the corporate sector purchase programme, one of the principles of that programme being to be as market neutral as possible. Through our purchases, we have also helped to reduce the cost of financing green activities, and the increase in private sector issuance of green bonds will mean that the Eurosystem holds a greater amount of green bond. Yet, for some, we should go further and further rebalance our purchases in favor of green bonds. With regard to public sector initiatives, I would like to highlight the fact that our accommodative policies have created considerable additional financial room for manoeuvre that governments can use to finance green public investments. Some proposals, however, go even further and suggest that central banks directly finance such public sector initiatives, through a a new "green quantitative easing" or a "green monetary helicopter". Such initiatives are often part of the "Modern Monetary Theory". However, we must not lose sight of the fact that our main task is to maintain price stability and that all our initiatives must first and foremost respect it. On the other hand, the latter type of proposal could dangerously mix monetary policies and objectives with fiscal policies and objectives. Let us see, for example, what the proponents of modern monetary theory advocate. The essential point of this theory is that a sovereign who issues his own currency cannot fail. It can therefore increase its debt at will, since, if necessary, the central bank can print money to repay it. The government could thus take ambitious initiatives to promote the transition to a greener economy (or pursue other objectives) without worrying about the sustainability or otherwise of its debt. As attractive as it may seem, such a framework raises several problems. To begin with, the debt of the various countries of the euro area is not denominated in a national currency but in that of the monetary union, and the Member States cannot "print it at will". This is why the Stability and Growth Pact is crucial to ensure the sustainability of public finances. In addition, the Treaty prohibits monetary financing to preserve "monetary dominance". More generally, the economics envisaged in the context of modern monetary theory should be examined with caution. In fact, "printing money" means that the central bank's own funds are transformed into interest-bearing reserves held by the private sector. When interest rates rise from their current negative levels, it imposes a cost on the central bank and thus on the consolidated public sector. This would therefore amount to a fiscal expansion financed by short-term debt. Moreover, in such a framework, inflation control is largely left to the fiscal authorities: if inflation were to become too high, the government would have to raise taxes or cut spending. However, this could prove problematic. A democratically elected government would find it difficult to decide to raise taxes on corporate and household disposable income and growth, as this could cause it to lose the next election. This problem is not new. In fact, this is the very reason why independent central banks were created. The adoption of policies of the same type as those advocated by modern monetary theory would therefore imply a radical change in the current framework of an independent central bank as we understand it in Europe. Yet this risk is not limited to the demands associated with green quantitative easing or modern monetary theory. Since the crisis, central banks have strengthened their role and expanded the number of their missions. This has given them greater visibility, resulting in both demands on central banks to do more and criticism of their actions. Central banks are institutions at the service of society and are held accountable. Therefore, it makes sense  and healthy!  that their actions be examined. Yet past experience has shown that, for their actions to remain effective, it is important to preserve the independence of central banks. It also implies that our objectives should not be too broad: for many issues, including many of the challenges I have mentioned today, other authorities have more legitimacy and are better equipped to deal. 4. FINAL REMARKS PP 12 Let me conclude. After a decade of crises, monetary policy continues to face significant challenges, including in the euro area. Global risks and the persistence of low inflation continue to justify a very accommodative stance of monetary policy. That is why the Governing Council took additional steps this spring. We are also ready to intervene in the event of adverse events. In addition, new challenges are on the horizon for central banks: interest rates could remain low even "in normal times", while digitalisation and climate change could radically change the structure of our economies. Monetary policy will have to adapt to the new circumstances. However, we must bear in mind that monetary policy cannot do everything. On the contrary, other policies are better able to address many of the current and future challenges, both in terms of their root causes and consequences. This would give central banks more leeway to focus on their main objectives. Thank you for your attention. I am now available to answer your questions.

PP 10 Le premier concerne la diffusion des nouvelles technologies et le passage <88> l'<8e>conomie num<8e>rique. PP 11 Un autre d<8e>fi aux cons<8e>quences tout aussi incertaines pour la politique mon<8e>taire concerne le changement climatique. L'ann<8e>e derni<8f>re, lorsqu'il a re<8d>u le Prix d'<8e>conomie <88> la m<8e>moire d'Alfred Nobel, le professeur Nordhaus a qualifi<8e> celui-ci de <c7> d<8e>fi ultime pour l'<8e>conomie <c8>. Je ne pr<8e>tends pas fournir ici une analyse compl<8f>te des cons<8e>quences du changement climatique. <cb> bien des <8e>gards, nous <8e>tudions toujours ce qu'elles seraient. Je me pencherai plut<99>t sur certains des principaux canaux au travers desquels le changement climatique et les politiques adopt<8e>es pour le combattre pourraient affecter l'<8e>conomie, et sur ce que cela pourrait impliquer pour la politique mon<8e>taire. Dans la zone euro, l'impact pourrait <90>tre plus n<8e>gatif pour les pays du Sud que pour ceux du Nord, ce qui exacerberait la fragmentation. Cependant, les efforts visant <88> r<8e>duire la consommation de combustibles fossiles et <88> <8e>viter de tels r<8e>sultats d<8e>sastreux peuvent <8e>galement avoir de lourdes r<8e>percussions <8e>conomiques. Les voitures <8e>lectriques remplaceront les voitures <88> essence dans l'indice des prix comme s'il s'agissait d<d5>un produit diff<8e>rent : dans ce cas, l'indice des prix ne bondira pas. L'effet n<8e>gatif sur le pouvoir d'achat des m<8e>nages n'est donc pas visible dans l'indice des prix <88> la consommation. Il ne s'agit bien s<9e>r pas d'un ph<8e>nom<8f>ne nouveau, mais celui-ci pourrait se produire plus souvent <88> mesure que les r<8e>glementations imposent l'abandon des technologies <88> base de carbone. Il conviendrait de r<8e>fl<8e>chir <88> ces questions pour s'assurer que nos mesures de l'inflation continuent de refl<8e>ter les r<8e>alit<8e>s <8e>conomiques. Bien que l'impact final du changement climatique et des politiques visant <88> l'att<8e>nuer demeure incertain, il constituera un moteur essentiel du changement <8e>conomique (et social) au cours des prochaines d<8e>cennies. M<90>me si la transition vers des sources d'<8e>nergie plus propres <8e>tait parfaite, il pourrait avoir de lourdes cons<8e>quences pour la politique <8e>conomique. Les autorit<8e>s, y compris les banques centrales, ne devraient pas le n<8e>gliger. Mais que peuvent faire les banques centrales <88> ce sujet ? Comme d'autres institutions, entreprises et m<90>me m<8e>nages, les banques centrales peuvent adopter un comportement plus durable au quotidien. Depuis de nombreuses ann<8e>es, la Banque nationale de Belgique participe <88> des initiatives visant <88> la rendre plus respectueuse de l'environnement. Elle a obtenu trois <8e>toiles au label <c7> Entreprise <8e>codynamique <c8> de la R<8e>gion bruxelloise et est une entreprise certifi<8e>e <c7> neutre en CO2 <c8>. Avec d'autres banques centrales, la Banque participe <88> des groupes internationaux pour en savoir plus sur les risques et les cons<8e>quences du changement climatique et sur la transition vers une <8e>conomie plus verte. Nous participons par exemple au Network for Greening the Financial System, un r<8e>seau de 40 banques centrales et autorit<8e>s de surveillance qui a pour mission de d<8e>finir et de promouvoir les meilleures pratiques et de mener des travaux analytiques sur la question.
