Dans son r<99>le de superviseur et d<d5>autorit<8e> macroprudentielle, la Banque a entrepris des actions pour identifier, mesurer, g<8e>rer et mitiger les risques pour la stabilit<8e> financi<8f>re li<8e>s au changement climatique. Outre ces initiatives, les banques centrales ont <8e>t<8e> invit<8e>es <88> en faire davantage, notamment en recourant <88> des instruments de politique mon<8e>taire. Comme nous le verrons, un certain nombre de ces propositions poseraient d'importants probl<8f>mes pour la conduite de la politique mon<8e>taire. Je vais passer en revue certaines d'entre elles, en allant des actions les plus restreintes aux plus larges. Une premi<8f>re option consiste <88> ajuster l'<8e>valuation des actifs utilis<8e>s en garantie, en tenant compte du risque implicite plus <8e>lev<8e> qui entoure les industries li<8e>es <88> des <8e>missions de carbone plus importantes. Les actifs li<8e>s aux activit<8e>s <c7> brunes <c8> subiraient par exemple une d<8e>cote plus <8e>lev<8e>e. Par cons<8e>quent, les banques qui les donnent en garantie recevraient moins de liquidit<8e>s en <8e>change. Mais cela inciterait <8e>galement les banques <88> d<8e>tenir des obligations <c7> vertes <c8>, ce qui rendrait le financement des secteurs verts moins co<9e>teux. Cependant, il n'existe, <88> ce stade, pas de norme sur la fa<8d>on de d<8e>finir correctement les actifs verts et bruns, et les risques li<8e>s au climat n<d5>ont pas (encore) <8e>t<8e> incorpor<8e>s aux <8e>valuations des risques. Une proposition plus audacieuse sugg<8f>re de r<8e>orienter nos portefeuilles de politique mon<8e>taire vers des actifs <88> faible <8e>mission de carbone. Comme vous le savez tr<8f>s certainement, l'Eurosyst<8f>me d<8e>tient un large stock d'obligations <88> la suite des achats r<8e>alis<8e>s en vue de soutenir la progression de l'inflation vers son objectif. L'Eurosyst<8f>me d<8e>tient pr<8f>s de 20 % de l'ensemble des obligations vertes <8e>ligibles dans le cadre du programme d'achats du secteur des entreprises, ce qui repr<8e>sente environ six milliards d'euros. Ce montant est proportionnel <88> la part des obligations vertes sur le march<8e> des obligations <8e>ligibles dans le cadre du programme d<d5>achats du secteur des entreprises, l'un des principes de ce programme <8e>tant d'<90>tre aussi neutre que possible <88> lgard du march<8e>. Pourtant, pour certains, nous devrions aller plus loin et r<8e><8e>quilibrer davantage nos achats en faveur des obligations vertes. S<d5>agissant des initiatives du secteur public, je souligne le fait que nos politiques accommodantes ont cr<8e><8e> une consid<8e>rable marge de man<cf>uvre financi<8f>re suppl<8e>mentaire que les gouvernements peuvent utiliser pour financer des investissements publics verts. Certaines propositions vont toutefois encore plus loin et sugg<8f>rent que les banques centrales financent directement de telles initiatives du secteur public, par le biais d'un nouvel <c7> assouplissement quantitatif vert <c8> ou d<d5>un <c7> h<8e>licopt<8f>re mon<8e>taire vert <c8>. De telles initiatives s'inscrivent souvent dans le cadre de la <c7> th<8e>orie mon<8e>taire moderne <c8> (Modern Monetary Theory). Il ne faut cependant pas perdre de vue que notre principale mission consiste <88> maintenir la stabilit<8e> des prix et que toutes nos initiatives doivent d'abord et avant tout la respecter. En revanche, ce dernier type de propositions pourrait dangereusement m<8e>langer les politiques et les objectifs mon<8e>taires avec les politiques et les objectifs budg<8e>taires. Voyons par exemple ce que pr<99>nent les partisans de la th<8e>orie mon<8e>taire moderne. Le point essentiel de cette th<8e>orie est qu'un souverain qui <8e>met sa propre monnaie ne peut pas faillir. Il peut donc alourdir sa dette <88> l<d5>envi, puisque, en cas de besoin, la banque centrale peut imprimer de la monnaie pour la rembourser. Le gouvernement pourrait ainsi prendre des initiatives ambitieuses pour favoriser la transition vers une <8e>conomie plus verte (ou poursuivant d'autres objectifs) sans se soucier du caract<8f>re soutenable ou non de sa dette. Aussi attrayant qu<d5>il puisse para<94>tre, un tel cadre soul<8f>ve plusieurs probl<8f>mes. Pour commencer, la dette des diff<8e>rents pays de la zone euro n'est pas libell<8e>e dans une monnaie nationale mais dans celle de l'union mon<8e>taire, et les <83>tats membres ne peuvent pas en <c7> imprimer <88> volont<8e> <c8>. C'est la raison pour laquelle le Pacte de stabilit<8e> et de croissance est crucial pour garantir la soutenabilit<8e> des finances publiques. En outre, le Trait<8e> interdit le financement mon<8e>taire pour pr<8e>server la <c7> dominance mon<8e>taire <c8>. De mani<8f>re plus g<8e>n<8e>rale, l'<8e>conomie envisag<8e>e dans le cadre de la th<8e>orie mon<8e>taire moderne devrait <90>tre examin<8e>e avec prudence. En r<8e>alit<8e>, par <c7> imprimer de la monnaie <c8>, on entend que les fonds propres de la banque centrale sont transform<8e>s en r<8e>serves porteuses d'int<8e>r<90>ts d<8e>tenues par le secteur priv<8e>. Lorsque les taux d'int<8e>r<90>t augmentent par rapport <88> leurs niveaux n<8e>gatifs actuels, cela impose un co<9e>t <88> la banque centrale et donc au secteur public consolid<8e>. Cela <8e>quivaudrait donc <88> une expansion budg<8e>taire financ<8e>e par de la dette <88> court terme. De plus, dans un tel cadre, le contr<99>le de l'inflation est dans une large mesure laiss<8e> aux autorit<8e>s budg<8e>taires : si l'inflation devait devenir trop <8e>lev<8e>e, le gouvernement devrait augmenter les imp<99>ts ou r<8e>duire les d<8e>penses. Cela pourrait pourtant se r<8e>v<8e>ler probl<8e>matique. Un gouvernement d<8e>mocratiquement <8e>lu aurait en effet du mal <88> d<8e>cider d<d5>accro<94>tre les imp<99>ts qui p<8f>sent sur le revenu disponible des entreprises et des m<8e>nages et sur la croissance, car cela pourrait lui faire perdre les prochaines <8e>lections. Ce probl<8f>me n'est pas nouveau. En fait, c'est la raison m<90>me pour laquelle des banques centrales ind<8e>pendantes ont <8e>t<8e> cr<8e><8e>es. L'adoption de politiques du m<90>me type que celles pr<8e>conis<8e>es par la th<8e>orie mon<8e>taire moderne impliquerait donc un changement radical du cadre actuel de banque centrale ind<8e>pendante tel que nous l'entendons en Europe. Pourtant, ce risque ne se limite pas aux demandes associ<8e>es <88> l<d5>assouplissement quantitatif vert ou <88> la th<8e>orie mon<8e>taire moderne. Depuis la crise, les banques centrales ont renforc<8e> leur r<99>le et <8e>tendu le nombre de leurs missions. Cela leur a donn<8e> une plus grande visibilit<8e>, ce qui s'est traduit <88> la fois par des demandes adress<8e>es aux banques centrales pour qu<d5>elles en fassent davantage et par des critiques de leurs actions. Les banques centrales sont des institutions au service de la soci<8e>t<8e> et elles sont tenues de rendre des comptes. Par cons<8e>quent, il est logique <d0> et sain ! <d0> que leurs actions soient examin<8e>es. Pourtant, les exp<8e>riences pass<8e>es ont montr<8e> que, pour que leurs actions demeurent efficaces, il est important de pr<8e>server l'ind<8e>pendance des banques centrales. Cela implique <8e>galement que nos objectifs ne devraient pas <90>tre trop <8e>largis : pour de nombreuses questions, y compris plusieurs des d<8e>fis que j<d5>ai <8e>voqu<8e>s aujourd<d5>hui, d'autres autorit<8e>s ont plus de l<8e>gitimit<8e> et sont mieux <8e>quip<8e>es pour faire face. 4. FINAL REMARKS PP 12 Permettez-moi de conclure. Au terme d<d5>une d<8e>cennie de crises, la politique mon<8e>taire reste confront<8e>e <88> d'importants d<8e>fis, y compris dans la zone euro. Les risques mondiaux et la persistance d'une inflation basse continuent de justifier une orientation tr<8f>s accommodante de la politique mon<8e>taire. C'est la raison pour laquelle le Conseil des gouverneurs a pris des mesures suppl<8e>mentaires ce printemps. Nous sommes <8e>galement pr<90>ts <88> intervenir au cas o<9d> des <8e>v<8e>nements d<8e>favorables surviendraient. En outre, de nouveaux d<8e>fis se profilent <88> l'horizon pour les banques centrales : les taux d'int<8e>r<90>t pourraient rester bas m<90>me <c7> en temps normal <c8>, tandis que la num<8e>risation et le changement climatique pourraient modifier radicalement la structure de nos <8e>conomies. La politique mon<8e>taire devra s'adapter aux nouvelles circonstances. Nous devons n<8e>anmoins garder <88> l<d5>esprit que la politique mon<8e>taire ne peut pas tout faire. Au contraire, d'autres politiques sont mieux <88> m<90>me de relever bon nombre des d<8e>fis actuels et <88> venir, qu'il s'agisse de leurs causes profondes ou de leurs cons<8e>quences. Les banques centrales disposeraient ainsi d'une plus grande marge de man<cf>uvre pour se concentrer sur leurs objectifs principaux. Je vous remercie pour votre attention. Title: The challenges of the climate transition for the Belgian financial system and economy
text: The challenges of the climate transition for the financial system and for the Belgian economy Speech Gouverneur 11/10/19 FRDO Good morning and welcome to all. I am very pleased to welcome you to the Bank's premises for this day of reflection on the climate challenge and the role that the financial system can play in this regard. I have been asked to introduce the debates. I will leave it to the experts who will follow to provide more precise answers to the questions raised by the climate transition. For my part, I will limit myself to giving an idea of the stakes in economic terms and outlining the role that public authorities and, of course, central banks are and will be called upon to play in helping to meet this challenge. ***** As Governor of the National Bank, the challenges of the climate transition for the Belgian economy and the financial system are of course close to my heart. Climate change and, in particular, the climate transition will have an impact on the entire economy, and consequently also on the financial system. And, as you may know, the maintenance of an efficient and reliable financial system, in addition to monetary stability, is an important objective for us as a central bank, supervisor and macroprudential authority. Climate change is a major social problem that can have enormous social, economic, and financial consequences in the long term. We know that doing nothing is not an option. Churchill a dit : 93It92s better to take change by the hand before it takes us by the throat.94 According to the OECD, if we do nothing, Beyond the environmental and human damage, the purely economic impact of global warming would be a decrease in global GDP in the range of 1.0 to 3.3% by 2060 and 2 to 10% by 2100. Action is therefore needed. With the Paris climate agreement, important commitments were made to limit global warming to well below 2b0C by 2050, preferably close to 1.5b0C... And the good news is that it's not only doable, but at a reasonable cost. According to the European Commission, the cost of the so-called "mitigation measures" to limit heating could be limited to a maximum of 1.3% of GDP by 2050 (i.e. 4 bp of GDP growth per year, or much less than a typical revision of the figures of our national accounts). So let me start by saying that I am positive and hopeful. I am confident that with the right policy decisions and technological developments, these objectives can be achieved. But of course, this requires efforts and investments and a well-thought-out climate policy both at international and national level. In my opinion, the climate will be the challenge for the new regional governments and for the next federal government, in addition to job creation, an ageing population and putting public finances in order. However, it is important that such a transition takes place gradually, as it will also have a huge impact on the various economic actors. It is therefore crucial that everyone can prepare and respond to these changes in a timely manner. On the other hand, this transition must of course take place in a timely manner. If we wait too long, the actions that need to be taken will end up being much more stringent, with greater negative implications for many economic actors. There is therefore an urgent need for a clear and coherent policy that allows sufficient time to implement the policies in order to reduce uncertainty and increase predictability. Ik mij zeker inbeelden dat sommige groene investeringen minder risicovol zijn, bijvoorbeeld hypotheeklening toegekend voor een energiezuinige woning<c9> Maar dit moet zeker nog verder onderzocht worden. In elk geval zijn wij tegen het invoeren van een lagere kapitaalvereisten louter en alleen om groene investeringen aan te moedigen. Risico<d5>s zijn risico<d5>s, ongeacht hun kleur. Dit wil evenwel niet zeggen dat wij tegen het stimuleren van groene investeringen zijn, wel integendeel. Maar het moet gedaan worden door andere middelen dan en lager risico weging. Als toezichthouder kunnen wij ook zeker bijdragen aan het stimuleren van de markt van groene investeringen, door actief de ontwikkeling van een taxonomie te ondersteunen. Bovendien kunnen wij als centrale bank uiteraard actief onze eigen activiteiten en gebouwen meer duurzaam maken. Dat het Brussels instituut voor milieubeheer ons reeds sinds 2014 het label van ecodynamische onderneming heeft toegekend, met hoogst aantal sterren (3), getuigt dat wij hier al geruime tijd mee bezig zijn. Ook in het kader van onze externe reservebeheer worden sinds de tweede jaarhelft van 2018 concrete <d2>Environmental, Social and Governance<d3> (ESG) criteria toegepast binnen het segment bedrijfsobligaties, waarbij de voorkeur wordt gegeven aan bedrijven met hoge ESG ratings. ***** <c7> Dans un environnement qui change, il n<d5>y a pas de plus grand risque que de rester immobile <c8>. Vous avez reconnu la citation, abondamment rappel<8e>e ces derniers jours, de Jacques Chirac. La transition climatique est un enjeu majeur de nos soci<8e>t<8e>s. En toute franchise, je ne pense pas que la question centrale soit celle du financement des investissements n<8e>cessaires. Dans l<d5>environnement de taux actuel, l<d5>argent ne manque pas et les institutions financi<8f>res cherchent avidement des investissements potentiels. L<d5>enjeu principal est politique. Il r<8e>side dans la construction d<d5>un consensus suffisamment fort et durable, qui cr<8e>era le cadre propice au financement de la transition. Je vous remercie pour votre attention. Ik dank U voor uw aandacht. *****

Title: Interview De Morgen: 'We run the risk that the entire economy will collapse because there are no more staff'
text: Interview Pierre Wunsch 'We run the risk of the entire economy collapsing because there are no more staff' Pierre Wunsch: 'The better our response to the sanitary crisis, the less severe the economic impact will be.' Image Tim Dirven Pierre Wunsch: 'The better our response to the sanitary crisis, the less severe the economic impact will be.'Image Tim Dirven As governor of the National Bank of Belgium, Pierre Wunsch is helping to steer the crisis cell that is supposed to guide our economy through the corona crisis. He warns that the essential sectors must be able to continue to work. "If we are not careful, we run the risk that our entire economy will collapse because there are no more staff." Even the governor of the National Bank of Belgium does not escape the government's social distancing rules. "In the last five days, we largely met physically with the representatives of the banks, but were forced to wear a face mask. Now I don't go to the Bank anymore. I telework. It also takes some getting used to for me. Sometimes I get a phone call and three messages at the same time while I'm emailing. Just like in the financial crisis of October 2008, I have hardly been able to sleep for a number of nights because of the adrenaline." Wunsch (52) co-leads the Economic Risk Management Group (ERMG), which coordinates the Belgian response to this unprecedented crisis and proposes concrete support measures to the government. For example, the ERMG was involved in bridging loans and deferrals of payments for individuals and businesses, public guarantees for new corporate loans and measures taken by the insurance sector. Together with his European colleagues in the European Central Bank, Wunsch also voted for a financial bazooka of 750 billion euros. "The intervention of the ECB now facilitates the cheap financing of the states and banks. Most companies now know that they will not have liquidity problems." The governor is therefore cautiously optimistic that the eurozone has been propped up. "We prevented a collapse. The stock markets, bond markets and spreads stabilize after the initial panic." Nevertheless, the challenges remain enormous. "The coronavirus is helping to coordinate the course. The first line of defense remains the health front. The longer the sanitary measures have to last, the greater and heavier the impact on our economy." Do you have any predictions about how big the contraction of the economy will be this year? "The problem is that there is no lack of predictions. They go a bit in all directions. We have a contraction scenario of between minus 2 and minus 5 percent for Europe, depending on how long it lasts. We are also dependent on the situation in other countries. There are no certainties. The figures are subject to change. The better our response to the sanitary crisis, the less severe the economic impact will be." Pierre Wunsch: 'Europe will allow us to temporarily exceed the 3% budget norm. Nevertheless, the need for remediation will soon come back.' Image Tim Dirven To talk about our state itself, what does this mean for the already deep Belgian budget deficit? Where are we going to end? "We were already at almost 3 percent of GDP before the crisis. Roughly estimated, after the crisis we will end up with a budget deficit of at least more than 5%. (A budget deficit of 7 percent or more means more than 30 billion euros in absolute figures, MR). As we have done for taxes and mortgage loans, this means that there will be a postponement for a while. Europe will allow us to temporarily exceed the 3% budget norm. Nevertheless, the need for remediation will soon return. It is therefore of enormous importance that we only use the financial resources that are now available to bring the crisis under control where it is really necessary." Is this crisis like a war situation? "The analogy with war is good and bad. When it comes to fighting the virus, there is indeed a war that doctors and nurses must win. It is not a good analogy when we talk about the economy. It is not that our infrastructure, our businesses and our people have been bombed, that we will no longer have an economic fabric in two months or so. On the contrary, the message must be that our social infrastructure and economic potential has not been hit as in a war. It is important to avoid the technically unemployed or companies that are temporarily closed becoming permanently unemployed or bankrupt. All companies that were healthy before the crisis must be ready every day for the post-crisis resurgence. It is therefore important to bridge this period." What are the most urgent next steps? "The priority in the coming days is to find a good balance between the sanitary crisis and at the same time keeping our economy running as much as possible. Our estimate is that between thirty to forty percent of the Belgian economy is now paralyzed. If we are not careful, we run the risk of our entire economy collapsing because there are no more staff. Imagine if at some point, due to the interruption of the supply chain, the crucial sectors such as food or electricity could no longer be offered? That is precisely why it is important that we keep the essential sectors and their logistics supply chain running. "The message to the people is that, in order to soften the blow, we must now continue to work as much as possible. I know this is a bit at odds with the message 'stay at home'. Yet we need to find a balance between this public health crisis and the survival of our economy." Pierre Wunsch: 'If we start giving money to everyone, including people with a lot of savings or who are not affected, we will not be doing well.' Image Tim Dirven Pierre Wunsch: 'If we start giving money to everyone, including people with a lot of savings or who are not affected, we are not doing a good job.'Image Tim Dirven Who therefore needs financial support the most: the essential sectors or the supply chain? "We find that it is now really very difficult to distinguish between the two. For example, the operation of a food company also depends on the production of a packaging company. Now that the liquidity problems are more or less under control, we have to see who really needs a state intervention. Here too, we have to find a good balance, and that is not always easy. Today we already see that there are people who say that temporary unemployment is more advantageous than continuing to work, even if that is not always the case. We shouldn't give people incentives to stay at home. Even people who receive a wage do not have an immediate need for compensation. Elsewhere, there are requests to give premiums to those who continue to work. We have to be a little careful that regions, federal state and companies do not all start shooting together with premiums and at the end of the day we find a lot of overlaps and gaps in our financial instruments. The support measures taken by various governments of our country are rightly conditional. If we start giving everyone money, including to people with a lot of savings or who are not affected, we are not doing well." You are against the principle of helicopter money for everyone? "That's not a magic solution. Helicopter money must also be financed at the end and is equivalent to an additional government debt in the short term. The priority now is to provide financial support to people who really need it. Then we will see if there is a need for a more general, Keynesian, support for our economy. But even that is not yet clear. It is also possible that we will be confronted with pent-up demand, the phenomenon that fixed-income consumers have consumed very little for one or two months on luxury expenses such as restaurants and cars and then suddenly after the crisis can go back to shopping en masse with the hoarded money. That's kind of the experience of other crisis episodes in other countries. There is a limit to what we can do. We need to ensure that public debt remains manageable." Pierre Wunsch: 'We have to admit that countries such as Hong Kong and South Korea, which had more experience with infections in the past, are now coping much more quickly with the sanitary crisis and having a more limited economic impact.'Image Tim Dirven There are already more than one million people technically unemployed. How do you avoid that this will lead to permanent job losses? "Temporary unemployment exists and is appropriate in a first phase of the crisis. But perhaps we should now try to find an interim solution for some people between working a few days. and a number of days of non-work. That is one of the priorities for the coming weeks. "Already there are a number of companies that could work that are faced with a lack of staff. Every day we see that this problem is getting bigger. For example, some self-employed people also find it more advantageous to go full-time to a bridging right (a one-off support premium, MR), even though they can continue to work part-time. Nevertheless, we think it makes sense for the economy that they also continue to work partly. It must be possible to find a system in which they have partly their own income and receive a certain intervention from the state. Such a system will also be useful because the economy will not immediately be able to go to one hundred percent capacity in the run-up to the restart." Is there a risk that we will still have to deal with scarcity of food and other basic products if these problems last too long? "That's exactly what we want to avoid. That is why business continuity is now the priority" Catering businesses receive 4,000 euros to cover the first invoices. That's a drop in the ocean for some. How do we prevent that within a month we see many signs with 'Business to take over'? "I hope that the postponement of payments and the support for new financing  think of easy credit from a bank with a guarantee from a state  will help. But that's only part of the solution. I agree with you. Due to the losses they record in the meantime, there is a risk that some businesses will have a solvency problem and that they will virtually go bankrupt because they do not have enough equity to restart their business. That is what we will be looking at in the near future. The 4,000 euros was an urgent measure for small businesses and individuals. For SMEs with employees, this may be too little. We will see if interventions can be provided beyond what can now be offered." Do we also need a change in mentality to produce and buy more locally, so that our economy can absorb global shocks like this with shorter supplies? "I don't think so. Take, for example, the regions in Italy such as Lombardy that are in full lockdown. If they are autonomous economically and in lockdown, they have nothing left to eat. It is important that they are still able to import food. Also look at the pharmaceutical sector. GSK in Belgium produces vaccines that are important for the entire world population. It is unthinkable that everyone would have their own GSK locally. "We will of course have to learn lessons from this crisis. They will have much more to do with how we deal with the sanitary crisis and how we can ensure that the economy can continue to run at 80 percent, so that we have enough masks or can identify infected people more quickly, for example. That's where we admit that countries like Hong Kong and South Korea, which had more experience with infections in the past, are now coping much more quickly with the sanitary crisis and having a more limited economic impact." You are also a member of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB). You immediately announced a large-scale stimulus plan of 750 billion euros. How much of that will support our economy and will that be enough? "The ECB intervenes by buying government and corporate bonds in liquidity. In this way we facilitate lending and the financing of the state. At the same time, other discussions are ongoing such as corona bonds that could be financed with the European Stability Mechanism (ESM). This requires solidarity at European level." Is there such solidarity between the members of the Eurozone? "That is a very difficult discussion because we know that the single currency is opposed to fiscal rules that were not always applied by everyone, such as Greece in 2009. There was therefore a certain amount of mistrust between the northern and southern countries before this crisis. Now, this crisis is exceptional. It cannot be compared to the Greeks who did not follow the rules. In this case, the hard-hit Italy has done nothing wrong. I hope that this creates more room for solidarity than the last crises. But unlimited solidarity will not be possible in this Europe, I think. A lack of mutual trust makes that difficult." After this blow at the behest of Europe, will hard savings soon follow to close the debt pits, including ours? "This crisis is temporary. It is important that the support measures are also temporary. Then we can hope that there is a resurgence. We will gradually be able to reduce the deficit, but we will have to do so credibly vis-a-vis the markets and our European partners. Otherwise, we will come under pressure and we will have to take stricter measures, such as in the south of Europe after the previous crisis (where there was heavy cuts in the public sector, MR). We should avoid that as much as possible." What are credible austerity measures? "We will first have to demonstrate that we have a government that is capable of developing a multi-year strategy that will bring the deficit under control. Then I think it's enough. But the efforts will not be easy. Let that be clear." Pierre Wunsch: 'Unlimited solidarity will not be possible in this Europe, I think. A lack of mutual trust makes that difficult.' Image Tim Dirven Pierre Wunsch: 'Unlimited solidarity will not be possible in this Europe, I think. A lack of mutual trust makes that difficult.'Image Tim Dirven Do you expect a fast or very slow economic recovery? "If it doesn't take too long, we can hope it's a relative quick recovery will be. I've seen some forecasts that are already talking about 3 percent growth in 2021 after a 5 percent decline this year. That is a possible scenario, but it is still early to make a very reliable prediction about it." Are there any estimates yet of the number of jobs at risk? "It's too early for estimates. We will still have the economic impact of the crisis. Let us be very realistic: we will see bankruptcies in all European and non-European countries. It is not a crisis that we can bridge without job losses. What does give me confidence: Belgium and Germany were also able to cope with the previous crisis of 2008 very quickly. After a year, we have already created more jobs than the level of 2007. The impact on employment was limited, partly thanks to our system of temporary unemployment and the way in which the government also tackled the crisis in a targeted manner with as many temporary measures as possible in consensus with the social partners. If we do that again now, we can keep job losses to a minimum." It was precisely in the soft sectors that the corona patients now care for that savings had already been made in recent years. Does this crisis show that they deserve a better wage for work? "Look, I would be inclined to say yes but unfortunately it's a bit harder than that. Belgium is one of the countries in the world with the highest level of primary expenditure. And, bon, we have to make choices. It will certainly not be possible to give more to everyone after the crisis. On the contrary, after the crisis we will unfortunately have a higher public debt and fewer resources. So that's going to be a difficult debate." Should bonuses be paid out this year? "For the people who are now working 24 hours a day in this crisis, I do think that there should be bonuses this year. But I think that in such circumstances everyone expects people to behave in solidarity, and indeed to be attentive to the very difficult period that a number of people are going through. We need to show respect for the everyday heroes who work in primary care, such as doctors, nurses and caregivers in retirement homes."

Vandaag zien we al dat er mensen zijn die zeggen dat tijdelijke werkloosheid voordeliger is dan te blijven werken, ook al is dat niet altijd zo. We moeten mensen nu ook geen incentives geven om thuis te blijven. Ook mensen die een loon krijgen, hebben geen directe nood aan tegemoetkomingen. Er zijn elders dan weer vragen om premies te geven aan diegenen die blijven werken. We moeten een beetje oppassen dat gewesten, federale staat en bedrijven niet allemaal samen beginnen te schieten met premies en we op het einde van de rit veel overlappingen en gaten in onze financi<91>le instrumenten vaststellen. Dat is een van de prioriteiten voor de komende weken. <d2>Nu al zijn er een aantal ondernemingen die zouden kunnen werken die geconfronteerd worden met een gebrek aan personeel. Met de dag zien wij dat dat probleem groter wordt. Toch heeft het volgens ons zin voor de economie dat ze toch ook deels blijven werken. Het moet mogelijk zijn een systeem te vinden waarbij ze voor een deel een eigen inkomen hebben en een zekere tussenkomst krijgen van de staat. Zo<d5>n systeem zal ook nuttig zijn omdat de economie in aanloop naar de heropstart niet meteen naar honderd procent capaciteit zal kunnen gaan.<d3> Is er een risico dat we toch te maken zullen krijgen met schaarste van voedsel en andere basisproducten als deze problemen te lang gaan duren? <d2>Dat is precies wat we willen vermijden. Hoe voorkomen we dat we binnen een maand veel bordjes met <d4>Handelszaak over te nemen<d5> zien hangen? <d2>Ik hoop dat het uitstel van betalingen en de steun voor nieuwe financiering <d0> denk aan makkelijk krediet van een bank met waarborg van een staat <d0> zal helpen. Door de verliezen die ze in de tussenperiode boeken, bestaat het risico dat sommige handelszaken een solvabiliteitsprobleem zullen krijgen en dat ze virtueel failliet gaan omdat ze onvoldoende eigen vermogen hebben om hun zaak herop te starten. Dat is waar wij ons eerstdaags over zullen buigen. De 4.000 euro was een urgentiemaatregel voor kleine zaken en individuen. Voor kmo<d5>s met werknemers is dat mogelijk te weinig. We zullen zien of er tussenkomsten voorzien kunnen worden boven wat er nu aangeboden kan worden.<d3> Moeten we ook naar een mentaliteitswijziging om m<8e><8e>r lokaal te produceren en te kopen, opdat onze economie met kortere aanvoer globale schokken als deze kan opvangen? <d2>Ik denk van niet. Neem bijvoorbeeld de regio<d5>s in Itali<91> zoals Lombardije die in volledige lockdown zijn. Als ze autonoom zijn op economisch vlak <8e>n in lockdown, hebben ze niets meer te eten. Het is van belang dat ze nog in staat zijn om voedsel in te voeren. Kijk ook naar de farmaceutische sector. GSK in Belgi<91> produceert vaccins die belangrijk zijn voor de hele wereldbevolking. Het is ondenkbaar dat iedereen lokaal zijn eigen GSK zou hebben. <d2>We zullen uiteraard wel lessen moeten trekken uit deze crisis. Die zullen veel meer te maken hebben hoe we de sanitaire crisis aanpakken en hoe we ervoor kunnen zorgen dat de economie kan blijven draaien op 80 procent, zodat we bijvoorbeeld voldoende maskers hebben of sneller besmette mensen kunnen identificeren. Daar moeten we toegeven dat landen als Hongkong en Zuid-Korea, die meer ervaring hadden met besmettingen in het verleden, nu veel sneller de sanitaire crisis het hoofd bieden en een beperktere economische impact te hebben.<d3> U zit ook in de raad van bestuur van de Europese Centrale Bank (ECB). Jullie kondigden meteen een grootschalig stimulusplan aan van 750 miljard euro. Hoeveel daarvan zal onze economie steunen en zal dat voldoende zijn? <d2>De ECB komt tussen door het opkopen van staats- en bedrijfsobligaties in liquiditeit. Zo faciliteren we kredietverlening en de financiering van de staat. Tegelijk zijn andere discussies aan de gang zoals coronabonds die gefinancierd zouden kunnen worden met het Europees Stabiliteitsmechanisme (ESM). Daar is solidariteit voor nodig op Europees niveau.<d3> Is die solidariteit er tussen de leden van de Eurozone? <d2>Dat is een hele moeilijke discussie omdat we weten dat er tegenover de eenheidsmunt begrotingsregels staan die niet altijd door iedereen werden toegepast, zoals Griekenland in 2009. Er was daarom voor deze crisis een zekere vorm van wantrouwen tussen de noordelijke en zuidelijke landen. Nu, deze crisis is uitzonderlijk. Ze is niet te vergelijken met de Grieken die de regels niet volgden. In dit geval heeft het zwaar getroffen Itali<91> niets verkeerd gedaan. Ik hoop dat dit meer ruimte schept voor solidariteit dan de laatste crisissen. Maar onbeperkte solidariteit zal niet mogelijk zijn in dit Europa, denk ik. Een gebrek aan onderling vertrouwen maakt dat moeilijk.<d3> Volgen na deze klap op last van Europa snel harde besparingen om de schuldenputten te dichten, ook de onze? <d2>Deze crisis is tijdelijk. Het is van belang dat de steunmaatregelen ook tijdelijk zijn. Dan kunnen we hopen dat er een heropleving is. Wij zullen gradueel het tekort kunnen dempen, maar we zullen dat geloofwaardig moeten doen tegenover de markten en onze Europese partners. Anders komen we onder druk te staan en zullen we strengere maatregelen moeten nemen, zoals in het zuiden van Europa na de vorige crisis (waar zwaar gesnoeid werd in de publieke sector, MR). We moeten dat zoveel mogelijk vermijden.<d3> Wat zijn geloofwaardige besparingsmaatregelen? <d2>Wij zullen eerst moeten aantonen dat we een regering hebben die in staat is een meerjarenstrategie te kunnen ontwikkelen die het tekort onder controle zal brengen. Dan denk ik dat het genoeg is. Maar makkelijk zullen de inspanningen niet zijn. Laat dat duidelijk zijn.<d3> Pierre Wunsch: 'Onbeperkte solidariteit zal niet mogelijk zijn in dit Europa, denk ik. Een gebrek aan onderling vertrouwen maakt dat moeilijk.' Beeld Tim Dirven Pierre Wunsch: 'Onbeperkte solidariteit zal niet mogelijk zijn in dit Europa, denk ik. Een gebrek aan onderling vertrouwen maakt dat moeilijk.'Beeld Tim Dirven Verwacht u een snel of zeer langzaam economisch herstel? <d2>Als het niet te lang duurt, kunnen we hopen dat het een relatief snel herstel zal zijn. Ik heb een aantal prognoses gezien die het al hebben over groei in 2021 van 3 procent na een daling van 5 procent dit jaar. Dat is een mogelijk scenario maar het is nog vroeg om er een heel betrouwbare voorspelling over te maken.<d3> Bestaan er al ramingen over aantal banen dat op de tocht staat? <d2>Het is te vroeg voor ramingen. We zullen nog de economische impact krijgen van de crisis. Laat ons heel realistisch zijn: we zullen in alle Europese en niet-Europese landen faillissementen zien. Het is geen crisis die we kunnen overbruggen zonder jobverlies. Wat me wel vertrouwen geeft: Belgi<91> en Duitsland hebben ook de vorige crisis van 2008 h<8e><8e>l snel kunnen opvangen. Na een jaar hebben wij toen al meer banen geschapen dan het niveau van 2007. De impact op tewerkstelling was beperkt, mede dankzij ons systeem van tijdelijke werkloosheid en de wijze waarop de overheid ook toen de crisis gericht aanpakte met zoveel mogelijk tijdelijke maatregelen in consensus met de sociale partners. Als we dat nu opnieuw doen, kunnen we de jobverliezen tot een minimum beperken.<d3> Net in de zachte sectoren die de coronapati<91>nten nu verzorgen, was de voorbije jaren al bespaard. Toont deze crisis aan dat zij een beter loon naar werken verdienen? <d2>Kijk, ik zou geneigd zijn om ja te zeggen maar het is spijtig genoeg een beetje moeilijker dan dat. Belgi<91> is een van de landen in de wereld met het hoogste niveau van primaire uitgaven. En, bon, we moeten keuzes maken. Het zal zeker na de crisis niet mogelijk zijn aan iedereen meer te geven. Integendeel, we zullen spijtig genoeg na de crisis een hogere staatsschuld en minder middelen hebben. Dat wordt dus een moeilijk debat.<d3> Moeten bonussen dit jaar uitgekeerd worden? <d2>Voor de mensen die nu 24 uur op 24 uur in de weer zijn in deze crisis vind ik wel dat er bonussen mogen zijn dit jaar. Maar ik denk dat iedereen in zulke omstandigheden verwacht dat mensen zich solidair gedragen, en inderdaad attent zijn op de heel moeilijke periode die een aantal mensen meemaken. We moeten respect tonen voor de dagelijkse helden die in de eerste lijn werken, zoals dokters, verplegers en zorgverleners in bejaardentehuizen.<d3>

Title: Interview La Libre: Pierre Wunsch, governor of the NBB: "We must work as much as possible to avoid the collapse of the economy"
text: Pierre Wunsch, governor of the NBB: "We must work as much as possible to avoid the collapse of the economy" belga Published on 28-03-2020 at 12:16 pm - Updated on 29-03-2020 at 8:44 am Pierre Wunsch, Governor of the National Bank of Belgium The governor of the National Bank, Pierre Wunsch, wants Belgians to continue to work as much as possible, in order to mitigate the impact of the health crisis related to the coronavirus, he said in an interview with Morgen published Saturday. "I know it's a bit at odds with the message 'Stay home'. However, we need to find a balance between this public health crisis and our economy."Wunsch also warns of strong growth in bonuses and allowances, both for people staying at home and for those who work. "We must not give incentives to people to stay at home. As for people who still receive their salaries, they don't need compensation." "We must ensure that the Regions, the Federal Government and companies do not start distributing premiums together because we will ultimately see an overlap in these premiums and gaps in our financial instruments," continues Pierre Wunsch, co-president of the Economic Risk Management Group (ERMG), which is responsible for assessing the extent of the consequences of the coronavirus crisis on the economy and the financial sector. "The support measures taken by the various authorities in the country are rightly conditional. If we start giving money to everyone, also to people with comfortable resources or who are not impacted, we are not in the right place." For the governor of the NBB, the priority of the coming days is to find the right balance between the health crisis and the maintenance, as far as possible, of economic activity. "It is estimated that today, 30 to 40% of the Belgian economy is paralyzed. If we are not careful, we run the risk that our entire economy will collapse because there are no more staff." Technical unemployment is indicated initially, according to Wunsch. But we have to think beyond that. "We may now need to find an intermediate solution for some people between work for a few days and stopping for the other days. This is one of the priorities in the coming weeks. Today, there are already several companies that could work but are facing a lack of staff."

Title: Louvain[S] June 2020: P. Wunsch and J.-P. van Ypersele: time to choose
text: P. Wunsch and J.-P. van Ypersele: time to choose With eyes fixed on the impact of the covid-19 crisis on the economy, the question arises: how to cover the country's public finance deficit while anticipating future crises related to global warming? Attempted answers with Pierre Wunsch, Governor of the National Bank of Belgium and Jean-Pascal van Ypersele, climatologist. According to the scenarios of the National Bank of Belgium released at the beginning of June, the coronavirus crisis will have an impact of 9% on GDP in 2020. "We are working with scenarios because there is still far too much uncertainty to make estimates," says Pierre Wunsch, Governor of the SNB. "The V-shaped recovery scenarios mentioned (editor's note: rapid fall and recovery) now seem distant. I think it is important to look at the crisis over a period of more than a year. The two months of production lost this year will somehow reverberate in 2021. This crisis is more severe than 2008 but not in the same proportions. We will collectively come out poorer. There will be fewer ways to face the challenges that are the same as before the crisis including the climate, the aging of the population, public finances, low productivity gains, etc." Sophia, a transition plan However, debates on measures to reduce the impacts of global warming are present. Last May, the Resilience Management Group  100 scientists and 182 companies  presented the Sophia Plan, a 'transition plan for Belgium, for a sustainable post-COVID-19 recovery', i.e. more than 200 measures divided into 15 areas. "We must seize this extraordinary opportunity to revive the economy by not digging the ruts into which we risk falling later," insists Jean-Pascal van Ypersele, one of the project leaders. As The Economist writes, 'You have to seize the moment! The climate damage will be slower than that of the pandemic but it will be more massive and will last longer."1 "Whatever the difficulty of combining reflection and rapid decision-making, this restart must be directed in the best possible conditions." One of the opportunities is the carbon tax put in place for large European companies, believes the climatologist, but it does not sufficiently cover areas such as air traffic, gas, heating etc. "It is an opportunity to raise the necessary funds to replenish state budgets. Smart management of these budgets will ease the transition and avoid social effects.  Abundant renewable energy "The CO2 tax was already a good idea before the crisis," says Pierre Wunsch. "On the other hand, the impact on different sectors, such as the aviation sector, for example, is not going to facilitate discussions on tax increases, given the circumstances. For the economist, based on current technologies, the carbon tax must be practically infinite to achieve the goal set by Europe, namely zero carbon by 2050. "We have the capacity to reduce CO2 emissions by 60-70% at a limited cost to the economy. The last 30% require the implementation of technologies that do not yet exist. Still, I'm very optimistic about having renewable, abundant and cheap energy within 20 years. I don't think we're going to go to a world of energy scarcity or that we're going to have to live completely differently.  "The measures that were taken two years ago by the European Commission have made it possible to correct and provoke the rise in the price of a tonne of CO2," counter-argues Jean-Pascal van Ypersele. "What was modelled came true. By making it more expensive to use old technologies that do not reduce emissions, we encourage innovation and new technologies that will allow this reduction. But moving to another price overnight is neither realistic nor desirable. "We can, little by little, steer the whole economy and the techniques used in the right directions." Institutional tension "I think that the Sophia report does not take sufficient account of the institutional difficulty in which we find ourselves in Belgium," says Pierre Wunsch. "It focuses on participatory democracy, climate, etc., whereas today we have a problem of institutional tension and an economic structure in the south of the country that depends on transfers from Flanders. We are probably at 70% of public spending in Wallonia for 2021-2022. This means that we will be closer to a communist regime than to a neo-liberal regime that some people decry. This is not a unique situation, it exists elsewhere as in France. If we do not realize that the economic structure is not self-supporting, we are missing a debate on the restructuring of the economy. This is a significant financial issue. A public deficit of 6% is forecast for the next two years, which is not sustainable. We will have to make choices because there will be less money.  "You have to choose. Investing to achieve carbon neutrality will be expensive, not doing so risks costing even more," insists Jean-Pascal van Ypersele. "The crisis has shown the interconnection on a global scale. Here it is a virus that travels, with global warming, it can be refugees who will move by the millions. Installing barbed wire all around Europe is not going to solve anything. The governor says he is convinced that some companies are better able to anticipate the future and make meaningful choices. "The older I get, the more I realize that culture at large has a huge impact on the socio-economic success of countries. In Belgium, it is extremely difficult to mobilize for issues long-term. As soon as there is an economic crisis, environmental issues regress in priorities. In the polls of Belgians, the climate has fallen to the bottom of the pack.  Resist shocks Policymakers often have a limited time scale for the upcoming elections, the climate scientist notes, while accepting decisions that are difficult in the short term but beneficial in the long term is very important. The pandemic and the climate are known to impact the weakest and, he says, decisions do not sufficiently take into account the effects on the poorest. "The meaning of the containment measures has been understood and accepted. If we can explain the need for sometimes difficult decisions to protect the long term, I think we will have more good decisions. The researcher believes that a resilient society is better able to anticipate and withstand shocks, regardless of their origin. "This is in any case the ambition of the Sophia 2 plan." "Shocks can be very different in nature," says Pierre Wunsch. "When crises of this magnitude occur, we find that we have not invested enough to anticipate them. As soon as they move away, and this is partly in human nature, people are inclined to take certain risks. Honestly, I have not seen anything in the Sophia plan that reassures me that we will not experience a crisis in the next 50 years," he concludes. On sait que la pand<8e>mie et le climat impactent les plus faibles et, dit-il, les d<8e>cisions ne prennent pas suffisamment en compte les effets sur les plus pauvres. <c7> Le sens des mesures de confinement a <8e>t<8e> compris et accept<8e>. Si on arrive <88> expliquer la n<8e>cessit<8e> de d<8e>cisions parfois difficiles pour prot<8e>ger le long terme, je crois qu<d5>on aura davantage de bonnes d<8e>cisions. <c8> Le chercheur pense qu<d5>une soci<8e>t<8e> r<8e>siliente est mieux <88> m<90>me d<d5>anticiper et de r<8e>sister aux chocs, quelle que soit leur origine. <c7> C<d5>est en tout cas l<d5>ambition du plan Sophia 2. <c8> <c7> Les chocs peuvent <90>tre de nature tr<8f>s diff<8e>rente <c8>, rel<8f>ve Pierre Wunsch. <c7> Quand des crises de cette ampleur surviennent, on constate qu<d5>on n<d5>a pas assez investi pour les anticiper. D<8f>s qu<d5>elles sloignent, et c<d5>est en partie dans la nature humaine, les gens sont enclins <88> reprendre certains risques. Honn<90>tement, je n<d5>ai rien vu dans le plan Sophia qui me rassure sur le fait qu<d5>on ne vivra plus de crise dans les 50 ans qui viennent <c8>, conclut-il. Title: RTBF interview: Pierre Wunsch (National Bank): "This crisis is well managed, we have done little nonsense"
text: Pierre Wunsch (National Bank): "This crisis is well managed, we have done little nonsense" 04 September 2020 Is the economic crisis, the consequences of which we will bear the brunt of in the coming months, manageable? Everyone seems to agree on the principle: we need a recovery plan in Belgium to get out of the recession. The France has just presented its own, at 100 billion euros over two years  and Germany had already presented its own at the beginning of June. Should Belgium also invest massively in the coming months to save its economy? Interview with Pierre Wunsch, Governor of the National Bank of Belgium. It depends a bit on what is meant by a recovery plan. From the outset, I said that it was very important to forget about the deficit and do everything possible to avoid a collapse of the economy. That is what we have done, and I think we have done it well overall. It is a crisis that is very asymmetrical and that affects some sectors and people very strongly, and others less so. So take steps to deal with emergencies, certainly. Accelerate public investment before there is a recovery in private investment in the coming years, yes. And it is a crisis that from an economic point of view is well managed, both at European and Belgian level. But you have to be a little careful. A very high deficit is projected this year, 12%. Either. And we have taken essentially temporary measures that will disappear in the coming years. What is a little more worrying, however, is that we already had a deteriorating budgetary situation before the crisis, and that we are projecting a deficit of 6% in 2022. This means that structurally, sustainable measures cannot really be taken. So as long as we take measures that will be targeted and temporary, fine. And we certainly should not start by doing public sanitation next year or this year- On the other hand, to say that we can open all the valves without any attention and without thinking about how we will land later... Because that's what's very important: asking ourselves what our strategy is at the budgetary level to land in 2022-2023. At some point, we will have to return to a fiscal path that makes sense and we must think about it in advance. So, yes, a recovery plan. But if it's to throw money out the window and then realize that at some point all this is not tenable and that we have to go back abruptly, then I think we will have missed an opportunity. Investing public money while having a federal legislature that saves structurally  you've already argued for that  is a bit of a semi-opulence in the austerity that will come later. How is it possible to save on a legislature and at the same time to invest today? I know it may sound complicated, but I think a big part of the explanation lies in the word "temporary." Emergencies must be addressed. If we accelerate public investment in the next two years, because we know that it is too low in Belgium, and then we return to a budgetary path where we gradually find financing for these investments, we can perhaps already think a little about savings on certain items of expenditure. While on others, we continue to support the economy with measures for the sectors that are most affected. It is this balance, which is difficult, but which we will have to find, with a story behind it. I think it is very important to be able to tell the story of the strategy, so as not to have problems with the financial markets and loss of confidence in the ability to manage this situation. You talk about clear history, strategy. As we know, today there are a lot of companies that will go from a liquidity crisis  so from a lack of cash to hold on, to a solvency crisis  so an over-indebtedness that will weigh on their activities, or even threaten their survival. For the moment, in this change of reality for companies, we do not see at the political level a change of approach and certainly no clear strategy... This is something that was talked about some time ago in the SMR. And we realized that we were stumbling a little against an institutional problem: that the Regions  and perhaps more particularly Flanders  have indicated that it is a regional competence. It has therefore been difficult to take action in this area at the federal level. The Regions are now taking measures and we see that they are sometimes a little different from one Region to another. At the time, I called for more ambitious measures. The political context in Belgium today  the absence of a federal government with a strong majority, but also these differences between regional and federal competences  makes a coordinated response in this area more difficult. Are we unable today in Belgium to have a clear course, a clear strategy, in the economic management of what will happen to us in the coming months? I will not be so negative. I think that so far the crisis has been well managed, certainly as well as elsewhere, and perhaps even better in some respects. We have taken good measures, we have done little nonsense and it is important in a crisis to do little nonsense. We managed the crisis of the 80s very badly, we managed the crisis of the 30s, this crisis is well managed, but we are in a complicated country. This crisis is special: savings have increased, whereas the opposite usually happens in a crisis. Should we get this private savings, the money of the Belgians, to revive the economy? Yes, this is very unusual. In general, when there is a crisis, people tend to use some of their savings because they have a loss of income. Here, people, because they didn't have access to the store or because it wasn't always so cheerful to go to the store or the cinema, saved a little forced. The challenge is to recreate a climate of trust so that this naturally abandoned money is spent. So, in your opinion, we should not go and get it, we should not solicit it, we should not encourage Belgians who would be able to invest for example? One of the difficulties is that people who have a lot of savings and who have means, if we want to encourage them, it involves tax incentives. And so go and give money to people who already have money, so that they can spend it. This may be useful for the economy, but in redistributive terms, it may not be ideal.

Title: MNI Market News - Interview P. Wunsch - ECB Set To End PEPP In March - ECB Risking Wrong Inflation Message
text: 1. MNI Interview 1 -ECB Set To End PEPP In March -Belgium's Wunsch MNI Market News d0 David Thomas The eurozone economy should be strong enough for the European Central Bank to end its EUR1.85 trillion Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme on schedule in March, National Bank of Belgium Governor Pierre Wunsch told MNI, adding that the ECB should use its other tools to ensure monetary policy remains supportive. While a final decision on whether to end PEPP will depend on continued positive economic data and on the ECB's December projections, growth and inflation are going in the right direction, ECB Governing Council Member Wunsch said in an interview. "If I can extrapolate, to some extent, the good news we have had, then the logical conclusion would be that the emergency phase of the crisis is over and that we would stop the PEPP," he said, noting that the discussion on the matter has still to take place within the Governing Council. While ending PEPP will mean a fall in ECB bond purchases, the central bank has a "rich instrumentarium", including its Asset Purchase Programme and cheap loans to banks via its Targeted Longer-Term Refinancing Operations, he noted. Calendar-based elements "The normal thing would be to fall back on the instruments we had before PEPP, which is the APP, rate policy, TLTRO and others, and recalibrate these instruments to allow for a smooth transition, and for monetary policy to remain supportive. That should be enough," Wunsch said. "In case the APP would be recalibrated, I would be more inclined to inject some calendar-based elements, where we say that possible add-ons remain for at least so long instead of open-ended add-ons." While monetary policy will remain easy for the time being, the ECB should be clear that this stance will not remain in place indefinitely, he said, "Monetary policy is going to remain supportive as long we are not at our (inflation) objective," he said. But, he noted: "We have ideal conditions for inflation to converge with our 2% target." While pointing to the ECB's ability to respond flexibly to crisis, Wunsch said he would not be in favour of more formal coordination between the central bank and fiscal authorities. Market rate expectations "We have been able to deal with this crisis without any formal coordination, and it allowed us to be very flexible in what we do. We are independent and entering into discussions on formal coordination, I am not a big fan of that," he said, though he noted that it was inevitable that some degree of conditionality still had to be taken into account when the ECB decided on targeted policy actions, as foreseen under its Outright Monetary Transactions programme. MNI - Interview Pierre Wunsch Governor NBB d0 Published on 13.10.2021 2. "You still want some discussion somewhere on the fiscal position of different sovereigns," he said. "There is always this discussion as to whether we stick with the rule or be flexible with the rules." Markets are currently fully pricing in a 10-basis point rate increase by the ECB by the end of 2022. Wunsch said it was appropriate that investors adjust their expectations when the inflation outlook changes. "I see it as positive that from time to time that the markets pay attention because, otherwise you trade on habits and then suddenly you have a big shock and markets are taken by surprise, which can more easily turn into a financial crisis." he said. MNI Interview 2 - ECB Risking Wrong Inflation Message-Wunsch MNI Market News d0 David Thomas The European Central Bank should be careful not to over-emphasise the temporary nature of the recent surge in consumer prices, lest it create the impression that it does not want inflation to return to target, National Bank of Belgium Governor and ECB Governing Council Member Pierre Wunsch told MNI. "I am little bit concerned about our communications -we have stressed so much that it is temporary that it could create the feeling that we don't actually want to push inflation back to 2%," he said in an interview. "I do buy the argument that what we see today has a large temporary component. The big question is whether a succession of those shocks, combined with quite a tight labour market, might lead at some point to some second-round effects." For the moment, patience is required until the outlook for the recovery and inflation become more certain. "It's not like we have any signs -except directionally -that there are going to be strong second-round effects," he said, although he mentioned anecdotal evidence of emerging pay pressures. "People are paying more to get the people they want, and to some extent, we would want that, because we want inflation to go to 2%." Inflation expectations While inflation expectations remain contained below the ECB's 2% target, extremely supportive monetary policy could eventually drive a sustained increase in the rate of price growth, he said. "I don't mean this year or next year, but in the coming years and over our projection horizon, plus one or two years. You have a combination of factors that should contribute positively to inflation: we have a recovery of the economy, which is much stronger [than expected], you have supply constraints, you have energy prices going up, you have pent-up demand, you have NextGenerationEU, and you have the climate challenge," he said. Wunsch confirmed he dissented from the ECB's new forward guidance in July, which committed it to keep rates at present or lower levels until it sees inflation reaching 2% well MNI - Interview Pierre Wunsch Governor NBB d0 Published on 13.10.2021 3. ahead of the end of its projection horizon and durably for the rest of the projection horizon. The ECB also wants to be confident that underlying inflation is sufficiently advanced to be consistent with inflation stabilising at 2% over the medium term. "The forward guidance implies rates stay at present, negative, levels for several years if inflation does not pick up," he said, "as the cost benefit analysis of very easy monetary policy can evolve over time, I think that is an element we should have accounted for in our formulation." a1a1a1a1a1 MNI - Interview Pierre Wunsch Governor NBB d0 Published on 13.10.2021

Title: Climate change and the ECB: we need both enthusiasm and realism
text: Climate change and the ECB: we need both enthusiasm and realism Speech by Governor Pierre Wunsch CFO Award Trends-Tendances 21 October 2021 Ladies and gentlemen, It is a pleasure for me to have been invited here and to share my views on this very important topic.c9 As you know, climate change is one of the toughest challenges for the planet and the global economic system. All economic actors, including central banks, need to think about the role they can play to tackle it. This is exactly what the ECB has done recently, in the context of its strategy review. Our plan in that context d0 including some reflections that I have about it d0 will be an important part of my speech. Before jumping to my main messages, I should mention that I will only be talking about how climate change can affect the conduct of monetary policy. I will leave its implications for the other important job of central banks, namely financial supervision, for another occasion. So, let me start by summarising the five main takeaways of my speech: 1) Climate change is real and we need to act. That can be done at a reasonable cost. 2) The correct price for emissions is the key (but not only) instrument to steer our collective efforts. 3) Central banks have a rather limited role to play in this, given their mandate but also the instruments at their disposal. 4) However, the consequences of climate change for monetary policy and the central bank balance sheet need to be factored inc9 and the action plan that the ECB announced in July will just do that. 5) Funding the transition to net zero will benefit from advances in disclosures and taxonomy but making sure sustainable activities are profitable is the key priority. 1. Climate change is real and we need to act. That can be done at a reasonable cost. Letd5s start with my first message. Climate change is real. This has been made clear in many studies by renowned scientists and institutions. From these studies, it appears that the ecological, social and economic cost of no action is ultimately very high. While most forecasts predict that the consequences of climate change will be quite mild in Western Europe in the coming decade, the July floods have shown the devastating impact of extreme weather events. So, the risks related to climate change in our regions might need some re-assessment. But in any case, our focus should now be on mitigation measures. We have agreed to net zero in 2050. Letd5s do it! And letd5s do it while keeping the economic and social costs as low as possible. Even during the COVID-19 crisis, when large parts of the world economy came to a halt, carbon emissions only fell slightly. Positive news on the recovery implies that emissions will again start to grow if we do not take any additional measures. Clearly, we are currently not meeting our commitments. Emissions should come down by more than 5 % per year. We are not there yet! I am a strong believer in the capacity of markets to adapt to the new reality. But they need clear and stable rules of the game. I therefore welcome the new Commission package that aims to extend and deepen our climate toolbox, in particular the ETS system. Clear and ambitious long-term targets are essential, but they have to be translated into actual instruments to create the sense of urgency that is now required. Price signals and regulations are needed for climate considerations to be incorporated into the decision-making process of all economic actors. It should not be a matter of beliefc9 or a matter of being (or not) sensitive to peer pressurec9These rules should be binding so that we all act accordingly. But letd5s be honest. The path towards a carbon-neutral world will not necessarily be a happy transition. Taking the right measures to achieve this goal will have an economic cost. It will generate opportunities for some but be a burden for others. It will for sure disrupt current business practices and society at large. The precise cost for the economy is heavily debated and estimates differ substantially. The overall cost may well not be too high. According to the European Commission for example, the impact on aggregate GDP in 2030 could be negative or positive, depending on the hypotheses and assumptions that are used. To put this cost in perspective, let me mention a few numbers. Belgium emits some 110 million tonnes of CO2 each year. What about the average cost of abatement? It is not easy to pin down. Some green technologies are already competitive. Others are still expensive. Costs are also expected to fall as technology advances. In the industrial sector, carbon capture provides us with some upper bound for the costs. Estimates of the cost vary between 100 and 200db per tonne. I guess 150 euro per tonne is therefore a number we can use here as an d2upper boundd3 for the average cost of abatement in the entire economy. This would imply a cost of some 16-17 billion euro per year to reach net zero in Belgium. As a share of todayd5s GDP, that is some 3.5 %. But we have until 2050 to achieve net zero. Therefore, starting today, the yearly cost will gradually increase and reach the 16-17 billion figure in 2050. But by then, with a larger economy, it will probably be closer to 2 than 3 % of GDP. These numbers are smaller than the drop in GDP during the 2008-2009 great financial crisis and will come about much more gradually. Another way of putting it is that, each year, aggregate income growth would be some 0.1 of a percentage point lower between now and 2050. I know I am taking a risk in mentioning a number. But then, we will only know in thirty yearsd5 time. So, nobody can prove me wrong. Also, and most importantly, I strongly believe that we need a realistic message on the economic impact of climate change. It will not be d2party time with free moneyd3 BUT neither will it be all d2doom and gloomd3. Our best estimate is that the impact will not be any higher than that of previous economic shocks d0 like the oil shocks or financial crisis d0 but then spread over a much longer period. I might be wrong, but this is my best understanding of the issue from the many readings I have done on the topic. Anyway, even if the numbers suggest that the overall economic impact might not be too bad, some important remarks have to be made. First, they only consider the long-term impact on GDP and therefore overlook the intermediate period. The climate transition requires us to gradually factor in the cost to others from carbon emissions. This is a negative supply shock. It will constrain the means of production available to us. Also, part of the capital stock will be made economically obsolete earlier than foreseen or technically feasible. This is in addition to the negative impact on LT potential growth. There is therefore a trade-off between speed of action and the negative impact on the existing capital stock. Secondly, large investment will be needed to reduce emissions. Such additional investment can mean lower consumption. And green investment might even lead to other necessary investment being crowded out. This is probably less of a risk in the short run, given current low interest rates, but it cannot be ruled out, especially in the longer run if interest rates start rising again. Another way to look at this risk of crowding-out is perhaps easier to imagine: if virtually all research and innovation efforts in companies all over the economy are redirected to reduce emissions, other welfare-generating projects and activities could be put on hold or simply be abandoned. Productivity d0 the key source of welfare creation in an ageing society d0 would suffer. Last but not least, the costs might be very unevenly distributed across the population and economic sectors. Poorer households risk being hit harder, as energy represents a larger part of their expenses and they have less means to spend on clean investment. Some firmsd5 activities are very energy-intensive: that makes those firms very vulnerable to emission-reducing measures. Social coherence and competitiveness should therefore be kept in mind when charting a path towards net zero. Society-wide d0 yet targeted d0 support is needed to make the ecological transition a success. 2. The correct price for emissions is the key (but not the only) instrument to steer our collective efforts. For a successful transition, a green action plan needs to make economic sense. In that respect, economists agree that government action will be most effective if carbon is priced so that firms and households take the environment into account when consuming and investing. A carbon price and a clear announcement of its future path together form the most efficient way of doing that. All individual decisions can be taken with full forward-looking information and that naturally leads to the most cost-effective options to reduce emissions. In practice, the European Union has chosen to use the Emission Trading System (ETS) which fixes a maximum emission quantity. Emission rights are granted and traded, implicitly leading to a carbon price. In comparison to a carbon tax, an ETS has the advantage of directly fixing the target variable, that is carbon emissions. With quantities fixed, the price is the buffer and hence becomes more volatile. The current ETS has shown some success despite its disadvantages, like its rather limited scope. Fortunately, the European Commission has announced an extension of the system, which will remove or limit some of its weaknesses. By the way, even if higher ETS prices play a role in the recent very strong increase in energy prices, it is only one of many factors. The energy price boom is driven by several other market-specific factors affecting the price of energy products. It is therefore not the result of climate policies. But even after the planned extension, relying only on the ETS is risky. If people dond5t sufficiently internalise higher future CO2 prices, they could postpone necessary actions and the transition would be unnecessarily hard in the long term. Therefore, governments will also have to rely on regulation, impose minimum standards and forbid polluting activities. In addition, some techniques for reducing the amount of greenhouse gasses in the atmosphere are currently very expensive and will surely need public subsidies to be kick-started and ultimately be marketed. This is, for instance, the case for direct air capture (DAC)1, which will be needed to reach and accelerate to net zero, compensating for residual emissions. 1 DAC, which takes carbon from the air, should not be confused with carbon capture incorporated in industrial processes where the carbon concentration is much higher. It is also crucial to regularly review subsidy schemes in order to keep providing the right incentives and avoid windfall effects. This is complex, as it requires permanent monitoring of lots of elements, not only for the related technology but also for other technological alternatives. It is one of the lessons of the past that some technologies have been supported excessively. That has resulted in high costs for only small reductions of emissions. Policy-makers should support promising but still expensive technologies on a smaller scale. Innovative projects can then be an inspiration for everybody and kick-start private investment. Let me summarise this second part of my talk. A carbon price covering most economic activities is central to cope with climate change. It gives a clear market signal to all economic agents, who can then make the most cost-efficient choices. One could say that it gets into all the cracks of the economy. But only setting a carbon price might not be enough to reach the desired net zero target. Governments should correct the most adverse redistribution effects and could flank this price mechanism with regulation, for instance when network effects play a role. Temporary and targeted support of a limited number of promising flagship projects to get these off the ground and serve as a role model should also be part of the toolkit. 3. Central banks have a rather limited role to play in this, given their mandate but also the instruments at their disposal Everything I have said up to now, I consider to be the core of our collective efforts to reach net zero. I havend5t mentioned central banks and not even financial markets or financial institutions. So, letd5s turn to them now. What role should the ECB2 play in the fight against climate change? 2 For convenience, I refer to the ECB as the monetary policy authority for the euro area. To put things more specifically, the legal provisions apply to the ESCB, comprised of the Frankfurt-based ECB and the national central banks of the EU. 3 More precisely, it has been anchored in Article 127 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) and in the Statutes of the ESCB and the ECB which are annexed to that Treaty. 4 Referred to in Article 127 of the TFEU. The mandates of central banks differ widely all over the world. There are of course some common features, like the focus on the pursuit of monetary and financial stability or the fact that central banks should enjoy wide independence in the performance of their tasks. But the legal mandates also differ in the precise way they describe objectives, tasks and instruments. We should keep that in mind when comparing the actions of different central banks. In the EU, the mandate of the central bank is anchored in the Treaty3. In European Law, an EU institution can only have the competences which EU Treaties attribute to it. In other words, for each initiative, for each action, the central bank must find a legal basis in the EU Treaties. And I guess we all agree that Treaty change is only a theoretical possibility todayc9 Different views have been expressed as to the legal possibility for the ECB to take standalone actions on climate change issues, outside the pursuit of its primary objective of maintaining price stability. People arguing that such a legal basis exists often refer to the so-called secondary objective of the ECB4. The Treaty does in fact state that d2The primary objective of the ESCB shall be to maintain price stabilityd3. But it goes even further: d2Without prejudice to the objective of price stability, the central bank shall support the general economic policies in the Union with a view to contributing to the achievement of the objectives of the Union as laid down in Article 3 of the Treatyd3. If you read Article 3 of the Treaty, you will notice that it covers a very broad list of objectives without any priorities assigned to them. Sure, Article 3 refers to d2a high level of protection and improvement of the quality of the environmentd3 but only as one among many other objectives: balanced economic growth, a highly competitive social market economy, full employment, social progress, scientific and technologic advance, social exclusion and discrimination, equality of women and men, etc. I am an economist, not a lawyer. I shall therefore not venture further into these legal debates. But it is interesting that this legal possibility for the ECB to pursue a standalone action in the domain of climate change has only been discovered recently, while these provisions have been there for more than twenty years. In fact, I hear more and more voices d0 including from former central bankers d0 speaking about a risk of mission creep. For instance, the former Governor of the Bank of England, Mervyn King, expressed clear warnings when he wrote recently that central banks are risking their independence by entering into issues traditionally considered as being the domain of elected politicians5. Once politicians and activists see that central banks bend to pressure, he argues, they will push all the harder. In the end, that means central banks will find it harder to do what they are uniquely qualified to do: to provide monetary and financial stability. 5 6 7 Former US Treasury Secretary Larry Summers put it in even stronger words. He accuses central banks of trying d2to curry domestic political favor by focusing on issues like climate changed36. And, if you allow me a last reference, former Bank of England Deputy Governor Paul Tucker warned in his book d2Unelected Powerd3 that central banks should show d2self-restraintd3 in straying into areas where they do not have a mandate7. To offer yet another perspective on the question: how should we think about the effectiveness of euro area monetary policy to support climate objectives? Monetary policy is about supporting or slowing down aggregate demand in the euro area, depending on the outlook for inflation. Thatd5s in contrast with what is needed to tackle climate change, which is mainly about reinventing the global supply side of the economy. An overly proactive role on our side could perhaps even be a disincentive, maybe giving governments an excuse for postponing necessary, but sometimes difficult, decisions or reforms? Beyond the legal or political arguments, lies another one: monetary policy does not have efficient tools to deal with allocative efficiency. This is the reason why no economic textbook assigns us a role in this area. We have relatively blunt macro tools that are very far from a first-best Pigouvian price.
